#9973. Cloud Security Alliance Survey Finds Data Loss Prevention Often Detects Data Loss Only After It Happens

Research finds that, among respondents experiencing data loss, only 16% said DLP blocked their most significant incidents before data left the organization.

SEATTLE — (BUSINESS WIRE) — Data loss prevention (DLP) tools are often functioning as after-the-fact forensic systems rather than prevention controls, according to DLP in the AI Era, a new survey from the Cloud Security Alliance (CSA), the world's leading not-for-profit organization committed to AI, cloud, and Zero Trust cybersecurity education. The study, conducted in collaboration with Jazz, found that 73% of organizations said they experienced at least one confirmed data loss incident in the past 24 months. Among the respondents, only 16% said DLP blocked their most significant incident before data left the organization.

“Enterprise DLP has moved beyond the question of whether it should be deployed to whether it’s doing what it is intended to do. Enforcement is being softened, analyst capacity is consumed by noise, and new data-exit channels created through GenAI are exposing gaps legacy DLP was never meant to handle,” said Hillary Baron, AVP/Research, Cloud Security Alliance. “In the AI era, where employees and applications can move sensitive data through more channels than ever, organizations can’t afford to discover gaps after the fact.”

Related:External Teams Chats Anchor 15-Minute Malware Delivery

Perceived visibility exceeds demonstrated capability. While close to half (48%) of security teams ranked GenAI as their top exfiltration risk, less than a third (29%) are able to produce a routine 30-day report showing sensitive data sent to GenAI tools.

Modern risks lack modern enforcement. Paradoxically, the highest-ranked risks are among the least strictly enforced, and the lowest-ranked are among the most strictly enforced. Both GenAI (48%) and cloud storage uploads (41%) were cited as top exfiltration risks, but only 22% of organizations strictly block on GenAI and 19% on cloud storage uploads. Conversely, removable media, which ranked last (10%) as an exfiltration risk, is strictly blocked by 31% of respondents, the highest strict-block of any channel measured.

DLP alert overload fuels fatigue. Fifty-four percent of teams are triaging DLP alerts where the majority turn out to be false positives, and 90% report at least one measurable impact from alert fatigue in the past year, including 21% who report voluntary staff departures directly attributable to DLP alert burden.

Business friction determines enforcement posture. Seventy-one percent of respondents reported that their security teams received pushback on DLP enforcement during the past two years. Among those teams, 66% reduced enforcement for specific teams/use cases; 8% reduced enforcement broadly across the organization; and 3% reduced or paused the program entirely. Across the full respondent base, 54% softened enforcement in some form.

Related:TiDB Breach Exposes Flawed Cloud Security Assumptions

“Security teams know GenAI is creating new ways for sensitive data to leave the business, but many still cannot see the full impact,” said Ido Livneh, Co-Founder & CEO, Jazz. “Across the customer environments we observe, the average organization uses nearly 170 AI tools and fewer than 10 are sanctioned. Teams need to understand how data is actually moving so they can focus on real risk without blocking legitimate work.”

The survey was conducted online by CSA in June and July 2026 and received 433 responses from IT and security professionals. Respondents represented organizations ranging from fewer than 1,000 to more than 50,000 employees and were primarily located in the United States and Canada. Jazz funded the research and co-developed the questionnaire with CSA research analysts, while CSA independently performed the data analysis and interpretation.

Jazz is the DLP platform built to understand your business. Its agentic investigator, Melody, delivers pre-investigated findings with the business context already attached with no rules, no regex, and no browser extension required. A single lightweight agent runs at under 1% CPU and covers GenAI use, shadow IT, desktop applications, and personal cloud accounts. Jazz is a Gartner Cool Vendor and the winner of the 2026 CrowdStrike, AWS and NVIDIA Cybersecurity Startup Accelerator, selected out of nearly 1,000 startups. Learn more at jazz.security.

#9972. Marvell, Microsoft & Oracle Work to Standardize Data Center Hardware Security

The effort is aimed at standardizing a NIST FIPS 140-3 Level 3 integrated HSM for cloud and hyperscale data center infrastructure.

SANTA CLARA, Calif. — October 13, 2026 — Marvell Technology, Inc. (NASDAQ: MRVL), Microsoft Corporation and Oracle today announced a collaborative effort aligned with the Open Compute Project (OCP) aimed at standardizing a NIST FIPS 140-3 Level 3 integrated HSM for cloud and hyperscale data center infrastructure.

To direct this effort, the three companies have established a new OCP working group under OCP’s Security Track. The working group’s charter is to define open specifications for an integrated hardware security module for secure key caching and cryptographic key lifecycle management directly at the server level. This approach will reduce latency, improve scalability and strengthen the security posture of cloud compute workloads.

Most cloud and enterprise servers today rely on network-attached hardware security modules (HSMs) or software-only key management. This approach requires cryptographic keys to traverse the network or reside in unprotected, non-FIPS 140-3 Level 3 memory, exposing sensitive keys to potential security attacks. The working group will define an open specification for embedding a hardware security boundary, key vault and attestation chain directly into the server. This will ensure that cryptographic operations execute where data is processed, keys never leave a certified hardware boundary and workload integrity can be proven cryptographically to any relying party.

Related:External Teams Chats Anchor 15-Minute Malware Delivery

“An integrated HSM will allow cryptographic key operations to execute where the workload runs, satisfying both regulatory compliance and zero-trust architecture requirements, all without compromising higher performance for security,” said Cary Ussery, senior vice president and general manager, Multimarket Business Group, at Marvell. “By defining this as an open specification, we’ll make that capability available to the entire industry.”

“As AI transforms cybersecurity and quantum technology reshapes cryptography, protecting the keys and credentials at the heart of our digital infrastructure has never been more important,” said Mark Russinovich, CTO, deputy CISO and technical fellow, Microsoft Azure. “Through the Open Compute Project, industry leaders are coming together around a fully open-source integrated HSM, combining our collective innovation to advance interoperability, accelerate the adoption of post-quantum cryptography, and shape the future of hardware security.”

“An open specification for integrated Hardware Security Module (HSM) capabilities is an important step toward enabling cryptographic operations where data is processed, protecting keys within a hardware security boundary and supporting cryptographic verification of workload integrity,” said Pradeep Vincent, executive vice president, Compute and AI Infrastructure at Oracle. “This effort aims to establish a common foundation for adoption across the industry.”

Related:TiDB Breach Exposes Flawed Cloud Security Assumptions

The Open Compute Project (OCP) is a collaborative community focused on redesigning hardware technology to efficiently support the growing demands of compute infrastructure.

As founding members of the new OCP working group, Marvell, Microsoft and Oracle will collaborate with the broader OCP community to publish a joint technical specification, with an initial draft targeted for release around the 2026 OCP Global Summit and version 1.0 to follow. The companies plan to demonstrate the new technology in their exhibit booths and during Security Track presentations at the OCP Global Summit (October 12-15) at the San Jose Convention Center in San Jose, California.

Organizations interested in participating in the security working group are encouraged to join through the Open Compute Project.

Through a process of deep collaboration and transparency, we’re ultimately changing the way tomorrow’s enterprise, cloud and carrier architectures transform—for the better.

InfoQ Homepage News Google Discloses PageBreak AI Security Agent That Found 500+ XSS Bugs

Oct 31, 2026 2 min read

According to a paper published by Google, its AI-powered security agent has uncovered more than 500 XSS vulnerabilities across its web applications since entering full operation in January. Google PageBreak uses Gemini models to autonomously investigate potential vulnerabilities, but reports them only after deterministic validators successfully reproduce the exploit against a running application, resulting in a near-zero false-positive rate.

With PageBreak, every vulnerability hypothesis is tested against a running environment with a real exploit, such as executing JavaScript for XSS, writing to a world-readable location for path traversal, or triggering outbound DNS for RCE. Michał Bentkowski, information security engineer at Google, explains:

Early on in the development of PageBreak, we made a conscious decision to prioritize deterministic validation. Rather than simply hypothesizing bugs based on code patterns, the system closes the loop by verifying potential flaws against running environments. This approach results in a near-zero false positive rate, ensuring that we avoid overloading product teams with unverified vulnerability reports.

Google also retains non-deterministic findings internally to seed deeper future scans, identify gaps in its validation capabilities, and guide the development of new validators. These unverified candidates are not sent to product teams, keeping their attention focused on high-confidence vulnerabilities. Bentkowski writes:

While deterministic validation is our gold standard, we are aware that our validators are currently lacking in capabilities to cover all vulnerability types or complex scenarios. This comes with the risk of false negatives that might have otherwise been caught by non-deterministic validators.

In the separate article, "Google’s PageBreak Project – Real-World Findings," on Google Bug Hunters, Bentkowski describes three technical cases found by PageBreak: an XSS vulnerability, a cache-poisoning issue caused by a service misconfiguration, and a path-traversal vulnerability. On LinkedIn, Lukas Weichselbaum, senior staff information security engineer at Google, stresses the importance of reducing false positives:

A lot of AI-generated bug reports sound convincing but turn out to be wrong, and the teams that get them waste time checking each one. In PageBreak, the model can suggest whatever it likes, but a finding only counts once a validator confirms it with a real payload. The validators are plain code written by security engineers, not by the model and live outside the agent loop.

Bentkowski says PageBreak benefits from Google's engineering environment, particularly Google’s monorepo end-to-end code visibility, security signals that connect live HTTP traffic to source code, and existing scanning infrastructure that provides authenticated access to its web applications.

With the longer-term goal of reducing product-team involvement to validating AI-generated fixes, Google is integrating PageBreak with other agentic security initiatives such as CodeMender to automatically generate fixes for the vulnerabilities it discovers.

No independent validation of the 500+ vulnerabilities has been provided.

Presented by: David Iparraguirre - Senior Product Marketing Manager at Datadog, and Jessica Yang - Product Manager at Datadog

#9970. Fine-tuning a 350M Model for Better Structured Outputs in 100 GRPO Steps

This guide is a fully public, inexpensive recipe for making a small model substantially better at structured-output compliance. We fine-tune LFM2.5-350M with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) using the TRL library and evaluate it on the IFStruct benchmark. The full run takes around 500 samples and 100 training steps, small enough for a free-tier Colab or Kaggle GPU, and is available on GitHub. The results show that even a light fine-tuning procedure improves performance from 22.6% to 29.7% on the IFStruct benchmark.

Structured output is one of the most common real-world tasks for LLMs, yet most benchmarks fold it into broader reasoning or extraction scores rather than measuring it on its own. Whether a model reliably returns valid, parseable output in the requested format and shape — schema compliance — is often what decides whether it can be wired into a downstream system at all.

Note that the training pipeline described here is not the one used to train the RL model described in the IFStruct blog. This notebook doesn't aim to recreate the IFStruct benchmark score, but to show how task-specific fine-tuning of smaller models can improve performance and match that of far larger models.

This guide has two halves that run in different places:

We will need uv for the Python tooling and llama.cpp for serving. Following the Liquid AI llama.cpp deployment docs, install llama.cpp with Homebrew and verify that llama-server is available:

Before we begin, let's evaluate LFM2.5-350M on the IFStruct benchmark and see whether we can reproduce the reported score of 21.1%.

IFStruct is a benchmark for testing the validity of LLM outputs and schema adherence. The benchmark is open-source in Liquid4All/ifstruct, with the public benchmark dataset available on Hugging Face at LiquidAI/ifstruct-v1.0.

For the eval comparison, we serve the model locally on the MacBook with llama.cpp. We will use the BF16 GGUF (LiquidAI/LFM2.5-350M-GGUF).

Then we start the base-model server with the following command:

Once the server is running, we can run the full benchmark with 2000 samples:

The IFStruct release blog reports 21.1% for LFM2.5-350M. Our local llama.cpp/BF16 setup measures 22.6%, close to the 21.1% reported in the IFStruct blog. We use this local result as the baseline for the same serving stack comparison.

The full, runnable pipeline lives in the accompanying notebook. We will cover only the relevant pieces in this section.

We use nvidia/Nemotron-RL-instruction_following-structured_outputs, which pairs each prompt with a target JSON Schema and an expected field count. We use about 500 samples for training.

Because the Nemotron data distribution differs from the IFStruct evaluation, we augment the prompts to close two gaps between them:

We load LiquidAI/LFM2.5-350M and attach a LoRA adapter. Because LFM2.5 uses a hybrid attention/convolution architecture, we target the LFM-specific module names:

This trains ~6M parameters, about 1.66% of the model.

Then we define three reward functions, each on a [0, 1] scale, which score every completion on whether the extracted structure is correct:

We combine the three as a weighted sum with reward_weights=[1.0, 0.5, 2.0].

We train for 100 steps with 8 generations per prompt group, sized for a free-tier 16 GB GPU:

As you can see in the notebook, over the run, all three reward components climb, the KL from the reference model lifts off zero after warmup, and the truncated-completion fraction stays near zero.

Finally, we merge the LoRA adapter back into the base weights and save it as a single self-contained checkpoint, ready to convert to GGUF for serving:

After GRPO fine-tuning, we rerun the IFStruct evaluation. For this, we need to convert the merged model checkpoint into a BF16 GGUF. The converter script ships with the llama.cpp source, so we clone the repo once and install the converter's gguf package.

Then we serve the merged model with the following command:

Then, we will run the full IFStruct evaluation again with the fine-tuned model:

Comparing the two runs on the identical serving stack:

The gains land exactly where the training aimed: the JSON pass rate rises by nearly 14 points (18.0% → 31.9%), while YAML stays mostly the same. While this is still below the Qwen3.5-2B score of 33.15%, it shows that even light task-specific fine-tuning can bring a small model close to a larger one.

A short GRPO run with about 500 samples and 100 steps can lift a small 350M parameter model from 22.6% to 29.7% on IFStruct. The takeaway is that a cheap, task-specific reward signal can make a small model substantially more reliable about form, closing much of the gap to models several times its size.

#9969. TiDB Breach Exposes Flawed Cloud Security Assumptions

Cloud providers may be storing sensitive customer data, without either party knowing it. But when a provider is breached, the unseen information comes to light.

A breach of an open source database provider may have inadvertently highlighted a serious gap in the way companies think about their cloud security.

On Oct. 19, software maker PingCAP, which sells an SQL database program called TiDB, disclosed that it had been breached. According to PingCAP's website, it serves major American corporations like Atlassian, Square, and Pinterest, as well as major players in China's AI space, including Manus, Kimi, and more.

The perpetrator — the somewhat deceptively named "Fulcrum Security," or FulcrumSec, for short — is a relatively new extortionist group whose leak site already includes major organizations like LexisNexis, Novo Nordisk, and the Manchester Airports Group (MAG). Earlier this fall, FulcrumSec appears to have compromised PingCAP, enjoying something shy of unfettered access to all of its cloud management, financial, analytics, storage, and other systems for a month or more.

Related:External Teams Chats Anchor 15-Minute Malware Delivery

The even bigger issue is whether the breach exposed downstream customers' sensitive data. Investigators are still working out the details, but early evidence suggests that customers may be at some risk. Though their actual databases weren't breached, the information their vendor stored about them may have been enough to cause serious issues.

In a security notification published 12 days after first having discovered the incident, PingCAP acknowledged that hackers had access to its systems from Sept. 9 to Oct. 7. Using stolen service account credentials, the company wrote, the unauthorized party accessed internal company systems and then copied data and source code.

PingCAP's own third-party-assisted investigation found no evidence that attackers ran malicious commands or maintained persistent access in their systems, nor did they access any customers' databases. Instead, it said, the threat actors accessed customers' billing and other business data, such as contract terms and pricing, as well as various information pertaining to cloud accounts and product usage — email addresses, SQL editor text and errors, etc. They also exported a table with encrypted API keys, though investigators said the encryption protected the keys from actually being used maliciously.

Dark Reading reached out to PingCAP for comment. A company spokesperson provided the following statement:

"Between September 9 and October 7, 2026, an unauthorized party used stolen service account credentials to access certain PingCAP internal systems, copy data, and obtain source code. PingCAP identified the activity on October 7 and began disabling the affected credentials that day. As of October 14, all identified compromised credentials have been invalidated, all identified unauthorized access paths have been blocked, and four vulnerabilities reported by our external incident response firm have been fixed and independently verified as remediated.

Related:Marvell, Microsoft & Oracle Work to Standardize Data Center Hardware Security

"Our investigation, supported by outside counsel and third-party forensic specialists, has found no evidence that data stored by customers in our TiDB cloud production services was impacted, and no evidence that the attacker ran commands or maintained persistent access in the production systems reviewed. Exported records included certain TiDB Cloud account information, business and billing details. API-key values in the exported data were encrypted, and we have found no evidence that any were decrypted or used. As a precaution, we have advised all customers to rotate their TiDB Cloud management API keys and remain alert to targeted phishing attempts. We will notify affected customers directly as customer-specific impact is confirmed, and we will continue to share verified updates on our Trust Hub: pingcap.com/trust-hub."

FulcrumSec, however, painted a bleaker picture.

Related:Cloud Security Alliance Survey Finds Data Loss Prevention Often Detects Data Loss Only After It Happens

In a name-and-shame post to its leak site, the hackers claimed to be in possession of all of PingCAP's service management records, its financial records, its files stored within Google Cloud, Jira support tickets, customer relationship management (CRM) data, analytics data, source code, plus a four-year-long log of every connection every one of its customers ever made to the TiDB Cloud service.

Crucially, the hackers did not claim to have stolen any TiDB databases straight up. Instead, they indirectly obtained a wealth of potentially exploitable user data like those aforementioned API keys and other secrets, and potentially sensitive internal data exposed by cloud database commands.

The attackers fingered individual enterprises caught in the crossfire: brand-name US companies like Airbnb and Booking.com, Asian corporate giants like Baidu and Fujitsu, and a few of the world's biggest video game companies, including Capcom, Konami, and Square Enix. Asia represented the biggest slice of the pie, with nearly 2,000 affected organizations in Japan, China, and Hong Kong, with another 500 from India.

Additionally, FulcrumSec said its unauthorized access lasted for nearly two months, not just one. It was so comprehensive and unthreatened that, in the meantime, they were able to stand up a mirror of PingCAP's own service management system. Instead of having to manually exfiltrate data, their replication feed automatically pulled fresh copies of the company's internal database every six hours, for 22 days.

Claims made by threat actors must always be met with a degree of skepticism, and Dark Reading did not independently confirm FulcrumSec's. Still, the group does have some record of reliability.

Last summer, for example, the group breached Manchester Airports Group (MAG), claiming to have stolen 86GB of data. That data turned out to contain far more genuine personally identifiable information (PII) than MAG copped to, according to reporting by BleepingComputer. And whereas some hackers exaggerate their winnings, this case was something of the opposite: That initial 86GB claim represented compressed data. The hackers clarified that the actual, uncompressed total stolen was 640GB.

Even if one were to completely ignore the hackers' account and take PingCAP's more limited assessment as the truth, it would still represent a potentially serious risk to customers.

Arguably the most acute dangers — more than the broad customer data, or the API keys if they are in fact protected — lie in the less obvious exfiltrated data. This includes Jira tickets, SQL histories, and places where organizations unknowingly leak internal data. For instance, when customers use their cloud-managed database services, they send commands to the vendors' servers. Those interactions can often carry corporate secrets or sensitive data of many other types.

"Vendors don't typically set out to store secrets. However, customers often pass them over to use features built for convenience, and the data can settle in places few people think of as credential stores," explains Crystal Morin, senior cybersecurity strategist at Sysdig.

Take PingCAP's SQL editor text and errors, for example, she says. "That's query history and error output, which is where secrets can accumulate when someone pastes a connection string to debug something on the fly," Morin adds. In FulcrumSec's name-and-shame post, for example, it highlighted exfiltrated SQL statements that listed in full view one medical clinic's roster of patients, and another's list of medical professionals.

Keeper Security chief information security officer Shane Barney seconds Morin's point. "The PingCAP incident illustrates a daily reality in enterprise security: Attackers do not need to compromise a customer's primary database directly if they can systematically harvest upstream credentials," he says. "In modern software-as-a-service (SaaS) ecosystems, customer metadata, API keys, and diagnostic query logs routinely seep into vendor environments through everyday operational telemetry. When service account credentials or administrative API tokens are stolen from a provider, that aggregated operational data transforms into a road map for exploitation."

Barney emphasizes the importance of cloud security hygiene — such as rotating vendor-facing API keys and eliminating hardcoded and long-lived secrets in developer workflows — and vetting one's managed service providers by demanding continuous third-party risk assessments and independent certifications and attestations such as SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001.

Morin urges organizations to ask a few specific questions when vetting cloud providers. "Teams should seek to understand what customer-provided data the vendor retains and what its retention policy is. They should also ask whether they scan for secrets at ingest and redact what they find," she says. "Teams may also want to understand how service account credentials are handled, whether they’re short-lived, how they’re scoped, how often they rotate, and what detections fire on anomalous credential or account use."

And, she says, don't forget: "Inquire about breach notification, specifically the timeline and what triggers it."

This story was updated at 9 p.m. ET on Oct. 22 to reflect a statement from PingCAP.

#9967. UAE Transitions 50% of Government Services to Agentic AI

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

The United Arab Emirates says it's creating a foundation of security and safety as it transforms its public service footprint.

The United Arab Emirates (UAE) plans to move half of its government operations, services, and sectors to autonomous AI agents over the next two years, prompting a conversation around how it intends to secure and monitor those AI agents.

To that end, the UAE has implemented a "control tower agent," conducts audits using agents and humans, and considers monitoring and establishing trust as critical to its efforts, Omar Sultan Al Olama, minister of state for artificial intelligence, told attendees on Oct. 14 at the World Economic Forum's (WEF) Annual Meeting of Global Future Leaders in Dubai. Security and trust are critical to achieving the nation's goal of autonomous government systems that improve quality of life and to not risk harm to citizens, he said.

"There is an oversight that ensures that we understand what agents are doing, how they're taking certain actions — there's a continuous audit that is being done," Al Olama told attendees. "There's an audit that's done by agents, and there's an audit that's done by humans to ensure that this doesn't go haywire in any way, shape, or form."

Related:Third Serengeti Sweep Tops 1,400 Arrests as Investigations Mature

In April, the UAE Cabinet unveiled a framework to transition 50% of the federal government's sectors, services, and operations to agentic AI within two years. The effort aims to redesign government policies and processes to embrace AI capabilities, creating "smart systems" that take proactive actions to reduce operational costs, provide more efficient services to citizens, and make government more efficient, according to public notes from the meeting.

The UAE's plans for agentic AI should not be surprising. While global AI diffusion — a measure of the number of adults who used a generative AI product in a specific period — hit 19% in the second quarter of 2026, the United Arab Emirates has taken the lead globally with more than 73% of the population using AI during the quarter, according to Microsoft's "Global AI Diffusion: Q2 2026 Trends and Insights" report.

Yet at the same time, the risk landscape is changing, often because of AI use. The UAE has already faced significant increases in attacks over the past two years, many powered by AI agents, as political tensions and military conflicts continue to build in the region.

The government's Agentic AI Project will roll out in several phases across ministries and federal entities, it said. On Oct. 9, the Ministerial Council for Artificial Intelligence and Development reviewed the first phase of the project, focused on "building government capabilities, surveying and assessing government services, operations and tasks, and setting priorities," according to a statement announcing the review. The second phase will establish a national technical ecosystem for agentic AI, under the name "FedAI," that will enable government agencies to develop and operate agentic services and conduct internal competitions, such as hackathons, to develop applications.

Related:Australian Gov't Weighs Mandatory AI Incident Reporting

The UAE leads other nations with 73% of its population using generative AI at least once in the quarter. Source: Microsoft

The coming phase includes training for government employees in agentic AI development and generative AI technology to provide a foundation for the future, Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahya, one of the UAE's two vice presidents and deputy prime minister, said in the statement.

"We are building a government system that is smarter, more flexible, and more proactive; a system that leverages agentic AI to develop services, operations, and tasks, and to shape policies and decisions," he said. "This should be achieved in a secure and reliable digital infrastructure, in a way that strengthens the readiness of the UAE Government for the future and reinforces its leadership in developing government work models."

Security and trust are critical for operations conducted by agentic AI systems, and that means monitoring and auditing agentic activity, says Evin McMullen, co-founder and CEO of AmanTrue, an Abu Dhabi-based startup creating a governance control layer for agentic AI.

Related:EU Cyber Resilience Act to Enforce New Reporting Requirements

"Any institution, certainly a government that's adopting AI agents at scale, [and] especially related to internal operations or citizen services, should be able to show who acted in the event of an agent action," she says. "Which agent, who authorized it — which human being and associated institution — and what the limits or definition of the task was."

Governance is a key problem facing deployments of AI agents. Because of their often transitory nature, their ability to obscure on whose behalf they are acting, and their occasional penchant for going rogue, agents and their actions need to be tracked closely. However, 29% of security teams have discovered unknown AI agents running in production that were never registered, and nine in 10 organizations had a security incident in the past year attributable to agentic AI, according to an Oct. 20 report released by cloud-computing and AI-infrastructure platform ServiceNow.

As more organizations adopt agentic services, governance becomes more important, especially when multiple organizations work through agents on the same data and services, says AmanTrue's McMullen.

"When many services intend to act through the coordination of agents, an institution has to be able to show which agents specifically accessed a given data record on whose authority, within what defined limits, with what output," she says.

Gaining trust in autonomous systems will require that the AI agents are closely monitored, tracked, and controlled, the UAE's Al Olama said at the World Economic Forum event.

"The government's only currency is trust," he said, adding that "if the government makes one wrong decision, you lose a lot of that currency. ... The same would be true with AI. Once we have one breakthrough event, where AI exits the sandbox and goes and harms people, I think it's going to take a long time for us to regain that trust."

Rob is an award-winning, veteran technology journalist of more than 30 years, reporting on global cybersecurity issues, the latest offensive and defensive technologies, malware incidents, cyber conflict, and AI's impact on software and cybersecurity.

A former research engineer, Rob has written for more than two dozen publications, including CNET News.com, Dark Reading, MIT's Technology Review, Popular Science, and Wired News. He has received five awards for journalism, including Best Deadline Journalism (Online) in 2003 for his coverage of the Blaster worm. Rob also analyzes data on various trends using Python and R for both his reporting and his clients. Recent reports include analyses of the shortage in cybersecurity workers, annual vulnerability trends, and annual threat reports.

Rob holds degrees from Cornell University in Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (double major).

#9966. NeoMME: an efficient Multimodal-native and Multilingual Encoder

We introduce NeoMME, a family of 260M and 800M multilingual multimodal encoders. Unlike many generative visual language models, NeoMME does not use a separate pretrained vision tower or a causal language model. A single bidirectional Transformer processes both text tokens and raw image patches, and we train the entire model from scratch with a masked discrete-diffusion objective.

We fine-tuned NeoMME for visual document retrieval using ColPali's page-image approach. NeoMME-Retriever returns dense and late-interaction embeddings in one forward pass. Both model sizes lie on the ViDoRe v3 Pareto frontier for nDCG@10 and model size. At a matched 2048×2048 image input size on an NVIDIA L40S GPU, the 260M model encodes about 51 pages per second, or about twice ColModernVBERT's throughput. Hierarchical token pooling and asymmetric quantization reduce late-interaction index storage from roughly 1.5 MB to 6 kB per page (255× smaller) while retaining more than 95% of baseline nDCG@10.

NeoMME is available in Hugging Face Transformers. We release all model checkpoints under the Apache 2.0 license.

Many recent visual document retrievers are adapted from pretrained generative visual language models. A separately pretrained vision encoder produces visual features, which a projector maps into the language model's input space. A causal decoder then processes the combined image and text representations. Retrieval, classification, and token labeling do not generate text autoregressively, so they do not require a causal decoder or the parameter and compute overhead of this architecture.

ModernBERT brought efficient architecture and training improvements to bidirectional encoders. For visual document retrieval, ModernVBERT applied a bidirectional ModernBERT-style text encoder while retaining a separate pretrained SigLIP2 vision tower. We wanted to push this even further by designing and training a multimodal encoder without having to carry over the parameter and compute overhead of a VLM.

NeoMME (pronounced "nee-oh-me", IPA /ˈniː.oʊ.mi/) is a multilingual, multimodal foundation encoder that generates vector representations for input text and/or images using a single Transformer encoder. It is not based on an existing pretrained vision tower, text encoder, or text decoder.

Images and text use the same computational path, so NeoMME can more easily support pretraining, fine-tuning, parallelization, and serving across both modalities.

NeoMME comes in two sizes, 260M and 800M. Both variants share the same architecture:

We pretrain NeoMME from scratch as a discrete masked-diffusion text denoiser. For each text-only example, we sample a corruption rate uniformly between 0 and 1. Each eligible text token is then independently masked at that rate.

Multimodal examples use corruption rates between 0.3 and 1. The image patches remain visible while NeoMME reconstructs masked text. With light masking, the model can often recover a missing word from the surrounding text alone. For example, "cat" is a plausible completion of "The [MASK] sat on the mat," even without an image. But high masking forces the model to learn image-grounded descriptions with little to no signal from the non-masked input text tokens.

Pretraining mixes multilingual text, code, mathematics, natural images, and document images. Each model processes about 524 billion packed input tokens, including 290 billion tokens from text-only examples. This text budget is relatively small compared with ModernBERT's 2 trillion training token budget. Hence, we chose the NorMuon optimizer to improve data efficiency during training.

To get a meaningful downstream evaluation of the backbone, we fine-tune NeoMME for visual document retrieval using the page-image methodology introduced by ColPali. While traditional text-based retrieval consists of retrieving text chunks, NeoMME-Retriever ranks document page screenshots and bypasses all the preprocessing OCR steps necessary to extract text from PDFs. Treating the pages as images preserves layout, charts, tables, font type and size, and other visual clues that cannot be captured even by a perfect OCR model.

NeoMME-Retriever reuses the NeoMME backbone but adds two jointly trained heads on top of it for retrieval:

Omar Khattab, who introduced late-interaction in ColBERT, explains why the term is more precise than "multi-vector." It describes the granularity and learnability of the scoring function, not simply the number of stored vectors.

To learn more about late-interaction, we recommend reading this crash course by Amélie Chatelain.

One NeoMME-Retriever forward pass returns both representations, which gives you flexibility no matter your use case and infrastructure. We recommend using late-interaction embeddings in general since they are more powerful and can be used easily with open-source libraries like NextPlaid. However, if you have a very large corpora, you can run a single forward pass with NeoMME-Retriever to get the dense embedding, retrieve a small number of documents through an ANN index, and then use late-interaction to rerank the retrieved candidates.

We report nDCG@10 on ViDoRe v3. NeoMME-Retriever-260M reaches 0.523, the highest score among evaluated models strictly below 800M parameters. It is within 0.002 nDCG@10 of ColQwen2.5 while using about 14× fewer parameters. NeoMME-Retriever-800M reaches 0.556, within 0.009 nDCG@10 of the similarly sized Vultron Retriever Flash (0.8B). Both NeoMME-Retriever models lie on the model-size Pareto frontier.

ViDoRe v1 and v2 use nDCG@5. On both benchmarks, NeoMME-Retriever-260M outperforms ColModernVBERT and the twice-larger ColSmol-500M. NeoMME-Retriever-800M outperforms ColPali v1.3 while using 3.6 times fewer parameters.

† Scores from MTEB. ‡ Results from our own evaluations.

Late-interaction storage scales linearly with the number of vectors in the output embedding. Higher-resolution images contain more patches, so they produce larger embeddings. For example, a 2048×2048 square page produces embeddings containing 4,200 vectors with NeoMME-Retriever, or about 2.1 MB in float32. Across the ViDoRe v3 benchmark, the measured average is about 1.5 MB per document.

To reduce the storage footprint of the late-interaction index, we combine two complementary compression methods:

We tested this setup on ViDoRe v3. With a pooling factor 10 and int8 queries and documents, storage decreased from about 1.5 MB to 39 kB per page, a 39× reduction, while keeping more than 99% of the baseline nDCG@10. A more aggressive configuration uses pooling factor 8, int8 queries, and binary documents. That version uses 6 kB per page (255× smaller) and keeps more than 95% of the original retrieval quality.

Users can pick a compression setting from that frontier based on storage budget and required retrieval quality.

Before you can search a corpus, a retriever model must turn your documents into embeddings, which will be stored in a vector store like Qdrant, Weaviate, or Milvus. Faster encoding makes building and adding new documents to the index faster, thus reducing the GPU uptime and compute cost required.

So we measured image encoding speeds for NeoMME-Retriever against other multimodal document retrievers. We used preprocessed image tensors and calibrated the batch size separately for each model and image size. At a matched 2048×2048 input size on one NVIDIA L40S, NeoMME-Retriever-260M encodes about 51 pages per second, nearly twice ColModernVBERT's 26 pages per second. Both 260M and 800M NeoMME-Retriever models are also faster than the other models we compared on smaller input images.

NeoMME-Retriever (260M and 800M) returns dense and multi-vector embeddings together. The example below scores two text queries against two document-page images with MeanMaxSim late interaction and dense cosine similarity.

We provide separate dense and late-interaction checkpoints for fine-tuning with Sentence Transformers v6. Following the same pattern as text encoders such as ModernBERT, Sentence Transformers loads the backbone through NeoMMEModel rather than the dual-head NeoMMEForRetrieval class. Sentence Transformers currently supports one retrieval head per model, so each checkpoint lets you fine-tune the dense or late-interaction head independently. To train both heads together, use NeoMMEForRetrieval with a custom Trainer.

Visual document retrieval can be used as the first stage of a visual retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system. Unlike text RAG, which retrieves extracted text chunks, visual RAG retrieves the original page images and sends them to a visual language model. The model can then use tables, plots, diagrams, and page layout that text extraction may flatten or omit. Here is how visual RAG works:

You can test visual RAG directly with NeoMME-Retriever in our HF Space: 🤗 tonywu71/neomme-retriever-demo.

NeoMME replaces separate pretrained image and text encoders with one long-context bidirectional Transformer. We train it from scratch to process both multilingual text tokens and raw 32×32 image patches.

NeoMME-Retriever is a fine-tuned version of NeoMME for visual document retrieval. One forward pass produces both dense and late-interaction representations. The 260M model outperforms all evaluated models strictly below 800M parameters and, at a matched 2048×2048 input size, encodes pages at about 2× ColModernVBERT's throughput. To reduce the large storage footprint of late-interaction embeddings for high-resolution documents, we experimented with hierarchical token pooling and asymmetric quantization and managed to reduce the late-interaction embeddings from roughly 1.5 MB to 6 kB per page, a 255× compression, while retaining more than 95% of the baseline nDCG@10.

We release all NeoMME model checkpoints and a day-zero Hugging Face Transformers implementation to allow practitioners to build efficient multimodal and multilingual representation models on top of our work.

NeoMME began as a side quest between two good friends. We worked with limited time and compute, and we decided to share the results so the community can build on them. We thank H Company for supporting the work and providing the compute used to train NeoMME.

#9965. As AI Risks Grow, Insurers Split on Covering the Damage

Cybersecurity In-Depth: Feature articles on security strategy, latest trends, and people to know.

Some build specialized agentic AI coverage, while major carriers quietly exclude it — leaving enterprises exposed without their knowledge.

Following a rash of data breaches this year, several insurance companies have begun offering proactive policies related to artificial intelligence (AI) to cover enterprises that might be targets of unprovoked attacks or the source of attacks from AI agents going rogue. Meanwhile, other carriers are intentionally side-stepping this emerging risk, leaving enterprises to figure out how to manage it.

Insuring an enterprise against attacks from rogue AI agents that attack the enterprise, or perhaps those created within the enterprise that breach the corporate environment and attack third parties, is uncommon coverage. Many enterprises mistakenly believe their cyber and liability insurance policies covers AI-related risks.

As corporate insurance policies get ready to renew at the end of the calendar year, CFOs, general and outside counsels, CISOs, and other corporate executives tasked with insurance responsibilities should be examining them closely to determine their current AI risks and identifying exclusions that might be baked in. This is also a good time to meet with insurers that offer AI-specific policies to learn what types of coverage are available that the existing policy does not cover. Insurers are warning that the increased use of AI and AI agents is not keeping pace with enterprises’ governance. Rogue AI incidents, like the recent Open AI attacks against Hugging Face and other servers, have only heightened insurers’ concerns.

Related:Rethinking Cybersecurity Awareness in the AI Era

Last year, insurance coverage specifically for AI-related losses was in its infancy. Carriers often included minimal coverage in generic Errors and Omissions (E&O) policies, Directors and Officers (D&O) liability insurance, or simply in the liability policy, but many of those policies are inadequate to address AI's actual risks.

Today, several specialty insurance firms have coverage for AI-related incidents, either as endorsements, language included in technology E&O policies, or as standalone policies. Among the insurance companies and specialty providers that sell purpose-built policies, affirmative endorsements, and specialized coverage targeting AI risks are Armilla, Coalition, Corgi Insurance, Cowbell, Munich Re, and Beazley.

However, several large carriers are restricting or excluding AI-related risks and autonomous machine behavior from commercial general liability policies, adopting the Verisk/ISO exclusion endorsements. The exclusions address gaps in policies that were written prior to generative AI becoming ubiquitous within enterprises, according to insurance industry trade publication Insurance Business. The ISO endorsement removes coverage for bodily injury, property damage, and personal and advertising injury arising from generative AI. Chubb, Travelers, Berkshire Hathaway, AIG, and W.R. Berkley are among those adopting this endorsement, according to the publiction.

Related:Trust Is Not What It Seems — and Fraudsters Are Counting on It

So how can companies protect themselves from possible losses from potential risks from rogue AI agents? Here's what you can do today to reduce risk and improve your ability to qualify for AI-specific insurance:

Review your existing cyber and corporate liability insurance to determine which AI-related losses are covered and where your security exposures remain.

Analyze your network infrastructure to determine whether you have sufficient guardrails, along with specific policies and procedures, for addressing incoming and outgoing AI agent attacks.

Have your general or outside counsel review third-party contracts to ensure your supply chain is protecting you from potential AI threats.

Require your supply chain partners to demand their supply chain partners are protected; enterprises need protections multiple levels back down the supply chain.

Have your engineering team determine the different design patterns and architectural principles your vendors are using to build their AI applications. Not all AI development is compatible and responds to security software the same way; treating incompatible architectural principles the same could leave security gaps.

Be sure your AI applications have the minimum system rights and credentials required to do their jobs.

Treat Agentic AI as you would service accounts or endpoint detection and response systems. They're not "set them and forget them." They need to be monitored and maintained.

AI is not a panacea for every problem a company might face. It is a tool with specific use cases and configurations. If you use it as a catch-all for whatever ails your network, you will be compromised. Only use AI for specific tasks for which you have written rules, expectations, and results, and then ensure the AI applications are meeting those specific goals.

Related:Security Threats Don't Stop at the Office: Why Executives' Families Need Training, Too

Coverage for AI-based risks sometimes fall outside the purview of cyber insurance coverage. Because of AI's ubiquity in the enterprise, coverages for its potential failures likely will appear in other specialties as well.

For example, AI is used extensively by human resources departments in enterprises as a hiring tool, says Andrew Correll, head of underwriting for Armilla, a Lloyd's coverholder writing policies for the London syndicate. Coverage for AI tools that hallucinate or display a bias that triggers an insurable event might well be included in the enterprise's liability coverage or in coverage specific to use cases that are separate from a dedicated cyber insurance policy, he adds.

AI coverage addresses more than just a corporate computer being attacked and completely disabled, notes Craig Linton, AI and Emerging Risk Strategy Lead at Beazley. In some cases, a system only needs to be purged of unwanted data brought in by an AI agent. Taking systems offline for that purpose could interrupt business operations but is different than a common malware attack that forces the system to go offline or fail, which is a covered event. Beazley offers dedicated policies for defenses against the attack and endorsements that he calls "AI voluntary shutdown coverage," Linton says.

In order for enterprises to qualify for AI-related coverage, underwriters "look at the body of controls holistically," Correll says.

"Human review is obviously a component of that," he says. "But we also look for what kind of guardrails and rules are in place."

The Beazley application for AI coverage includes dozens of questions focusing on roughly 15 security controls, Linton notes. While most of the security controls are essential for cyber insurance coverage ­— multifactor authentication, backup and recovery, and training and network protection — the carrier also includes inquires about operational technology security, mergers and acquisitions, and Payment Card Industry (PCI) security.

He cautions teams buying AI insurance ­— often the general or outside counsel, chief financial officer and senior executives ­— that employees might be using unsupervised AI on their corporate and personal devices. Like similar shadow IT challenges companies faced in years past, employees will turn to shadow AI they can obtain easily and inexpensively if the tools are not provided by their employer and secured by the IT team. With AI, he says, this can introduce significant risks.

One challenge several sources mentioned is addressing the common problem of generative AI large language models (LLMs) hallucinating and displaying bias. For Corgi Insurance, coverage for hallucinated, inaccurate, or biased model outputs may fall under the Technology E&O policy/Generic Tech E&O policies written before generative AI technologies were widespread could be silent or ambiguous about how they treat model outputs. The company recommends looking for explicit AI-output language and reviewing algorithmic-bias exclusions carefully. When selecting an AI-centric policy, the proverbial devil is in the details, says Jack Kudale, co-founder and CEO of Cowbell. Does the policy wording address a nonmalicious system failure? Does it address an unauthorized disclosure without any external intrusion? Does that fall within a cyber coverage? Does it fall in a technology errors and omission, or does it in a completely different risk altogether? Questions like these will determine whether the policy or rider will address the threat the enterprise is trying to insure against or whether there is a possible exclusion, such as the Verisk/ISO exclusion endorsements and similar limitations employed by the top-tier insurers. If an exclusion is found in an existing policy during a corporate review, the enterprise then can purchase specialty coverage to mitigate that risk.

Protecting your enterprise from potential rogue AI agents and other AI risks requires that enterprises proactively ensure that three risk areas are protected: infrastructure, data pipelines, and your supply chain, Kudale says.

Protecting the infrastructure includes making sure that you have no misconfigured servers, overpermissioned identities, or exposed public endpoints. Safeguarding the data pipelines includes ensuring the storage architecture is secured from breaches, compromises, and poor decision-making, he adds. Finally, organizations need to secure their supply chain well beyond their direct vendors. Threats can come from secondary, tertiary, or further back in the supply chain.

"It's one thing we worry about the most," Kudale says. "We don't worry about hallucination and bias as much as others. We worry about supply chain more."

Stephen Lawton is a veteran journalist and cybersecurity subject matter expert who has been covering cybersecurity and business continuity for more than 30 years. He was named a Global Top 25 Data Expert for 2023 and a Global Top 20 Cybersecurity Expert for 2022. Using Hacktron, we found that an email address like a`touch${IFS}/tmp/savane-rce-proof`@attacker.example gave any registered user code execution on its backend. From there, we made our account a superuser, impersonated Bash's maintainer, and confirmed we could add an SSH key with push access to the upstream Bash repository. An unpatched kernel gave us root access and access to a GNU backup server. We reported it to the FSF on May 11, 2026. #9963. Les supermarchés de l'UE paient d'un firmware de réfrigérateur non mis à jour

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

Des centaines de magasins ont subi des pertes se chiffrant en millions d'euros parce qu'ils avaient fait appel à des tiers pour gérer le micrologiciel OT obsolète qui pilotait leurs systèmes de climatisation.

This translation is provided by our internal AI translation tool.

Des centaines de supermarchés français ont subi cette semaine des pertes s'élevant à plusieurs dizaines, voire plusieurs centaines de millions d'euros, à la suite de cyberattaques qui ont perturbé leurs systèmes de réfrigération.

Dans la nuit de lundi, des pirates informatiques ont piraté les contrôleurs des systèmes de réfrigération commerciaux de grandes chaînes de supermarchés françaises. Ils ont transformé les réfrigérateurs, les congélateurs et les chambres froides en appareils de chauffage, faisant grimper leur température jusqu’à 50 degrés Celsius (plus de 120 degrés Fahrenheit), ce qui a complètement abîmé tous les aliments qu’ils contenaient et aurait même provoqué quelques petits incendies. L’identité et les motivations de l’auteur de cette attaque restent inconnues.

Les contrôleurs de réfrigération permettent aux commerçants de régler et de surveiller à distance la température de leurs réfrigérateurs, 24 heures sur 24 et 7 jours sur 7. Il s’ensuit donc que les gérants de magasin auraient pu être alertés ou se rendre compte manuellement que quelque chose n’allait pas. Pour empêcher cela, des sources françaises indiquent que les attaquants ont prolongé les cycles de dégivrage des systèmes ciblés — processus au cours duquel les congélateurs font fondre intentionnellement le givre et la glace accumulés — afin que le réchauffement passe pour un entretien de routine.

Related:EU Grocers Pay a Steep Price for Unpatched Fridge Firmware

Selon les propres rapports des entreprises, les attaques ont touché un peu plus de 700 magasins d’alimentation et commerces de détail, tous au cours de la même nuit. Un analyste de la société française de cybersécurité Sekoia a déclaré à Reuters que l’Espagne, le Portugal, la Pologne, l’Allemagne et la Belgique avaient également été touchés, et qu’une grande chaîne de supermarchés aux Pays-Bas avait mis ses systèmes hors service par mesure de précaution, selon l’AP. Une seule chaîne française, Intermarché, a fait état de pertes s’élevant à plusieurs dizaines de millions d’euros.

Pire encore, les experts soulignent que ces attaques auraient très certainement pu être évitéesgrâce à des mesures élémentaires de cybersécurité.

Les premiers rapports suggéraient que les attaques de lundi étaient liées aux contrôleurs de réfrigération du fabricant danois Danfoss. Danfoss occupe une place importante dans le domaine des solutions de contrôle pour les supermarchés et la grande distribution alimentaire, avec plus de 50 000 installations de sa technologie à travers le monde, selon son site web.

Related:Taiwan Bullet Train Hack Highlights Cybersecurity Gaps in Rail Systems

Le 9 août, des chercheurs en cybersécurité de l’équipe Team82 de Claroty ont révélé trois vulnérabilités dans la plateforme AK-SM 800A de Danfoss. Ces failles — référencées sous les numéros CVE-2025-41450, CVE-2025-41451 et CVE-2025-41452 — permettaient aux attaquants de procéder à l’exécution de code à distance (RCE) ou à un déni de service (DoS) contre les parcs de réfrigération des entreprises. Danfoss a corrigé ces failles mais comptait sur ses clients pour mettre à jour eux-mêmes leurs systèmes.

Dans une déclaration à Reuters, Danfoss a rejeté la responsabilité sur les clients utilisant un micrologiciel obsolète, indiquant qu’elle « conseillait depuis longtemps à ses clients de maintenir les systèmes pris en charge à jour avec le dernier micrologiciel et de migrer les systèmes hérités vers des solutions de dernière génération ».Le fabricant d'équipement d'origine (OEM) a fourni davantage d'informations à une publication spécialisée dans la réfrigération, Cooling Post. Selon lui, la « majorité » des unités concernées fonctionnaient sous AK-SM 800 ou son prédécesseur, l'AK-SC355. Ces deux systèmes ont depuis longtemps atteint leur fin de vie : le premier en 2021, le second en 2016.

Related:AI-Driven Cyberattack on Mexico Couldn't Breach OT Systems

Mardi, le CERT national français (CERT-FR) avait identifié qu’une autre plateforme de contrôleurs de réfrigération — « XWEB », des fournisseurs Dixell et de sa société mère Copeland — avait également été impliquée dans les attaques. Il n’a pas précisé quelles vulnérabilités ou versions de micrologiciel pouvaient être en cause, bien que les indices circonstanciels indiquent désormais clairement que les auteurs de ces menaces s’appuient sur les recherches de Team82. Le jour même où ils ont révélé ces vulnérabilités affectant Danfoss, ces mêmes chercheurs ont divulgué 23 autres touchant XWEB Pro, dont 21 de gravité élevée.

Le 26 août, une série étrange de rapports similaires a commencé à filtrer depuis des installations militaires américaines.Les groupes frigorifiques tombaient en panne. Dans chaque base où cela se produisait, les gens ont probablement pensé qu’il s’agissait d’un problème électrique inhabituel. Mais peu à peu, de plus en plus de sites ont signalé le même phénomène.

Après être tombée sur ces rapports étranges sur les réseaux sociaux, une journaliste indépendante a émis une hypothèse hasardeuse. « Je suis suffisamment lucide pour savoir que cela semble insensé, mais je vous demande de me suivre », a écrit M. Elizabeth sur Substack. « Je pense qu’il y a une probabilité non nulle que quelqu’un ait piraté les congélateurs des commissariats. »

À ce jour, l’armée américaine n’a pas confirmé qui ou quoi était à l’origine des pannes survenues dans les cantines réparties sur au moins 14 bases de l’armée de l’air, installations de la marine et postes de l’armée de terre distincts. Il se pourrait que ce soit une coïncidence que ces attaques aient eu lieu seulement deux semaines après la divulgation des vulnérabilités par Danfoss.

Ce serait d’autant plus une coïncidence que la Defense Commissary Agency (DeCA) — l’agence centrale du ministère de la Défense (DoD) chargée de superviser les magasins militaires — a explicitement mentionné avoir utilisé les technologies de Danfoss par le passé. Par exemple, dans un modèle de cahier des charges techniquedestiné aux prestataires des magasins militaires datant de juin 2022, la DeCA citait le Danfoss AK-SM 800A comme « base de conception » pour les différentes unités de contrôle.

Fort de son expérience, Bill Moore, PDG de Xona Systems, se souvient : « Dans bon nombre de ces magasins physiques — mais aussi dans les usines de fabrication, les centrales électriques, les sites pétroliers et gaziers, c’est le cas partout —, le plus gros problème est que les organisations parviennent plutôt bien à segmenter leurs propres réseaux. Mais en matière de technologies opérationnelles (OT), il y a tous ces équipementiers et tiers qui ont besoin d’un accès. Et les entreprises n’y ont pas vraiment prêté attention. »

En accordant à de nombreux fournisseurs et équipementiers l’accès à leurs systèmes, les entreprises finissent par s’exposer à des attaques à distance. « Et il n’y a littéralement aucune visibilité ni gouvernance sur bon nombre de ces connexions. Je dirais que c’est vrai dans un pourcentage élevé de cas — la moitié, peut-être plus, dans l’ensemble. Elles laissent en quelque sorte tous leurs équipementiers agir à leur guise, mais nous avons constaté que de nombreux pirates compromettent ces connexions tierces », déplore-t-il.

Dans un e-mail adressé à CNBC, Les Mousquetaires — société mère d’Intermarché et de Netto — a expliqué que l’attaque avait eu lieu via un prestataire de services chargé des systèmes de réfrigération dans certains de ses magasins.

« En résumé : déconnectez vos équipements d’Internet », déclare Andrew Ginter, vice-président chargé de la sécurité industrielle chez Waterfall Security Solutions. Les recherches effectuées cette semaine sur Shodan ont par exemple révélé des milliers de systèmes Danfoss exposés sur Internet, dont environ 1 500 rien qu’en France.

« Dans un monde idéal, les entreprises protégeraient leurs systèmes de contrôle derrière un accès à distance contrôlé par du matériel », explique M. Ginter, « mais même un simple pare-feu entre ces appareils et Internet serait déjà utile. »

Pour les pare-feu de base, il conseille aux entreprises :

De mettre en place une règle « tout refuser »

De n’autoriser les connexions qu’à partir d’adresses IP spécifiques

D’appliquer un mot de passe et une authentification à deux facteurs à ces connexion

De mettre à jour automatiquement le pare-feu, pour éviter de l’oublier

Utilisent des appareils de qualité commerciale ou industrielle, et non grand public ; de nombreux appareils grand public ne proposent pas de mises à jour, ou ne se mettent pas à jour rapidement

Enfin, ajoute-t-il, « Remplacez le pare-feu strictement tous les quatre ans. Pourquoi ? Parce que si nous avons des appareils exposés à Internet, neuf fois sur dix, nous n’avons pas d’équipe de sécurité, et nous ne remarquerons pas quand nos pare-feu ne seront plus pris en charge et que les mises à jour automatiques cesseront. »

« Les mesures de base ne suffisent pas pour les infrastructures critiques de grande envergure ou l’industrie lourde, mais elles contribueront grandement à empêcher les hacktivistes de s’introduire dans vos congélateurs », conclut Ginter. « Retirez vos équipements d’Internet. Faites-le de toute urgence. »

Nate Nelson is a journalist and award-winning scriptwriter. In addition to Dark Reading he writes for Darknet Diaries, the most popular show in cybersecurity across all media.

He began his career as a freelancer, ghostwriting Forbes and CNBC op-eds for executives in tech and finance. Then he transitioned to journalism at Threatpost, where he covered cybersecurity news and trends. Throughout those years he co-created a cybersecurity podcast, Malicious Life, which in its day climbed into the Top 20 technology podcasts charts on Apple Podcasts and Spotify.

He holds degrees from New York University and Bard College. As a born and bred New Yorker, he enjoys a superiority complex, but is polite enough to keep it to himself.

#9962. Rebuilding AUTOMATIC1111 with Gradio Workflow

In our last post, we built five small gr.Workflow graphs and hinted at what it would take to build something as complex as AUTOMATIC1111's stable-diffusion-webui. In this post we walk you through Workflow1111, where we have rebuilt most of AUTOMATIC1111's feature set as a single workflow canvas.

Workflow1111 is a graph of eleven media pipelines built using seventy-three nodes. It brings together SOTA models for text-to-image, hi-resolution fix, image-to-image, prompt-matrix grids, VLM interrogate, detection-to-inpaint masks, ControlNet-style annotators, background removal, PNG Info storing, and image-to-video.

You can run any of these pipelines by signing in with your Hugging Face account or providing an access token. Once you sign in, the model calls use your own quota.

👉 Try Workflow1111, or duplicate the Space and start rewiring it for your own use case.

All the media pipelines are built from the same four operator kinds covered in our last post and the official guide. Each node on the canvas wraps one operator, and the operator's inputs and outputs become the ports you connect edges to. As a quick reference on our four operator kinds: fn is a Python function, model is a model called through InferenceClient, space is another Gradio Space, and dataset is a row from a Hub dataset.

Let's go through the pipelines one by one.

This is the core pipeline. It has the controls you'd expect from A1111's txt2img tab: negative prompt, steps, CFG, seed, width and height, plus a model_id field for choosing the checkpoint. The prompt goes through a prompt-builder fn node first, which appends the selected style preset and cleans up the text, then into a model node that calls the checkpoint through Inference Providers. A post-process fn node writes the generation parameters into the PNG's metadata on the way out, which is what the PNG Info pipeline reads back later.

In Automatic1111, hi-resolution fix first upscales the txt2img output and then runs a second denoising pass. Here it's a two-node detour instead. The text-to-image result goes into a FLUX.1-Kontext model node with a refine instruction ("enhance fine detail and micro-texture, keep the composition identical") and comes back sharper and larger.

That same Kontext node doubles as the image-to-image tab. Upload an image, describe the change you want, and it returns the edited image.

Start with a rough prompt like "A lighthouse in a storm." This pipeline sends it to a Qwen3-4B model node, and a small fn node turns the reply into a clean list of tags, capped at forty: "stormy sea, wet rocks, dramatic composition, low angle shot, volumetric lighting, ominous tone." You can connect any diffusion model node to this output to render the image.

There's no custom node involved, unlike in ComfyUI. In a Gradio workflow the LLM and the diffusion model are both ordinary model operators on the same canvas.

This is like AUTOMATIC1111's Interrogate button, with a VLM doing the interrogating instead of CLIP. Qwen2.5-VL looks at a night-market photo and writes a prompt that could have produced it. A ViT classifier node reads the same image and returns labels: restaurant 51.9%, tobacco shop 15.6%, toyshop 9.1%.

Both nodes use the same image input, so gr.Workflow runs them in parallel and you get both answers in roughly the time it takes to run one.

AUTOMATIC1111 makes you paint an inpaint mask by hand. This pipeline generates one from a detector instead. DETR finds six objects in a street photo (three people, a dog, a bicycle, and a car), and from there the workflow splits into two branches: one draws the detected boxes on the original image, the other turns them into a mask you can feed into an inpaint pipeline downstream.

The drawing and the mask creation both happen locally with Pillow and NumPy. Only the detection call leaves the machine.

This is like AUTOMATIC1111's prompt matrix. A base prompt, "a lone oak tree," gets combined with four suffixes (at sunrise, in a thunderstorm, under the Milky Way, in autumn fog) by a fn node, and each variant goes to its own text-to-image node. A final node stitches the four results into one contact sheet.

gr.Workflow has no loop operator, so the four text-to-image nodes sit side by side on the canvas. Since they're at the same dependency depth they run in parallel, and all four images start generating at once.

This is like the Extras tab in Automatic1111. There are two upscaler nodes, and they take different routes. The first is a local Lanczos resample in an fn node, which needs no network call and finishes as fast as Pillow can resize. The second is AuraSR ×4, and it's the first space node on the canvas: it calls a Space on the Hub and treats the result like any other node output.

Background removal works the same way. BRIA RMBG-2.0 is another space node, so the whole model lives in its own Space and this canvas just calls it in.

Canny, line art, sketch, luma-depth, and posterize are the preprocessors you'd normally get from the ControlNet extension in Automatic1111. Here, each one is a fn node written in plain NumPy, with no model behind it. On a pre-loaded example photo of a building facade, each annotator takes about half a second on CPU.

There are 36 operator nodes in the app, 32 are fn nodes, and 22 of those run entirely in-process without a network call. Roughly two-thirds of the canvas keeps working if you lose your connection. Since these are regular Python functions, you can also test them directly, with no canvas, server, or GPU involved.

AUTOMATIC1111 stores generation details in the PNG's parameters text chunk, and the PNG Info tab reads them back. Workflow1111 does the same. The post-process node on the text-to-image pipeline writes the metadata, and this pipeline reads it back out, including the prompt, negative prompt, steps, CFG, seed, image size, and model.

The image node that PNG Info reads from also feeds a Wan 2.2 I2V A14B node, which animates it; in the demo example a sleeping fox wakes up and starts moving. There's no second upload box because one reference node can feed as many downstream pipelines as you need, so a single upload gets its metadata read and gets animated on the same canvas.

So far every model call has gone to someone else's hardware, through Inference Providers or a Space. That's why you can build and run something like Workflow1111 without a GPU of your own.

A fn node is just Python, though, so it can equally load a model locally and run it on your own GPU. FastVideo/fastvideo-fasth3-preview is a gr.Workflow app that does exactly that. It runs FastH3, a four-step distillation of MiniMax-H3, and generates video with a soundtrack on ZeroGPU.

The whole app comes down to one bound function:

ZeroGPU gives the function a GPU when it needs one, then releases it when the call is done. gr.Workflow doesn't need to know about any of that. It just calls the fn node.

This isn't specific to Spaces either. Point bind= to a function that loads a local checkpoint, run .launch() on your own machine, and the Workflow1111 canvas can drive your own GPU.

Every output node on the canvas becomes a REST endpoint, with no routes written by hand. Workflow1111 exposes nine of them: /image, /edited_image, /generated_prompt, /recovered_prompt, /detected_objects, /x_y_grid, /upscaled_local, /annotator_map, and /png_info.

The same endpoints are also MCP tools. Launch with mcp_server=True (guide) and every output node shows up as a tool an AI assistant can call. Point Claude Code, Cursor, or any MCP client at the server URL:

Now an agent can generate an image, read a prompt back out, or run detection as steps in a larger task, with no glue code. Each caller sends their own token in the X-HF-Token header, so the Space holds none of its own.

AUTOMATIC1111 gave us the feature list, but the tool Gradio Workflow really gets compared to is ComfyUI, since both are node graphs. For a lot of what people want to build and ship, gr.Workflow covers the same ground.

The result is a multi-model pipeline that people can open in a browser, sign into, use right away, and call from code.

Workflow1111 has 73 nodes, but it started with just this:

bind= turns your functions into nodes, edges= connects them, and .launch() opens the canvas in your browser so you can keep editing there. When it's ready, gradio deploy puts the whole thing on a Space. The gr.Workflow guide has the full details, including the JSON schema and every operator type.

If you'd rather start from something that already works, open Workflow1111, hit Duplicate, and pick one of the eleven pipelines to change: delete nodes, swap models, rewire the flow. If you'd rather start smaller, the previous post has five workflows you can get running in about a minute each.

Whatever you build, post it on X and tag @gradio. We'd be happy to amplify your workflows.

4-step MiniMax-H3 — video with a matching soundtrack

Automatic1111-style studio on one gr.Workflow canvas

Really impressive breakdown the part that stands out most is how the graph structure gives you free parallelism (the prompt-matrix and interrogate examples) without any extra orchestration code. The mix of fn, model, and space node types on one canvas also makes the ComfyUI comparison land well: you get custom-node flexibility from plain Python, but zero-code REST/MCP endpoints for free. Curious how complex a canvas can get before performance or maintainability becomes a concern has anyone pushed past 73 nodes

Analisis yang sangat mengesankan, bagian yang paling menonjol adalah bagaimana struktur graf memberikan paralelisme gratis (contoh prompt-matrix dan interrogate) tanpa kode orkestrasi tambahan. Perpaduan tipe node fn, model, dan space pada satu kanvas juga membuat perbandingan dengan ComfyUI tepat: Anda mendapatkan fleksibilitas node kustom dari Python biasa, tetapi endpoint REST/MCP tanpa kode secara gratis. Saya penasaran seberapa kompleks sebuah kanvas dapat dibuat sebelum kinerja atau pemeliharaan menjadi masalah, apakah ada yang pernah melampaui 73 node?
