#9961. An outsider's perspective on Scion and Mononoke

Recently, Anthropic wrote a blog post about their new centralized version control system Scion. As someone working on the Source Control team at Databricks, where we have a huge monorepo and are exploring different options, I figured it might be useful to share my perspective here.

(Obligatory disclaimer: This post represents my own views, not my employer’s.)

I recommend reading Anthropic’s post before continuing to read this one. You may also want to pre-read Rain Paharia’s Anthropic’s Scion is heavily inspired by Mononoke and the follow-up More on Anthropic’s Scion ripping off Mononoke.

Before we get into the weeds, it might be helpful to you to know where I’m coming from. If you’re not interested in this, you can jump to the Technical Commentary section.

I have never worked at Facebook, but one of my all-time favorite tech talks is Durham Goode’s Scaling Mercurial at Facebook from Git Merge 2017.Goode was the longest-serving and most senior member on Facebook’s Source Control team. (source)

The talk covers various interesting aspects for both the server side and the client side. For the server side, some of the topics include solving push contention with server-side rebasing (pushrebase), using scalable object storage for commits, moving various source control queries to the server, etc. For the client, there’s mention of the smartlog and other CLI commands for easier manipulation of history (compared to rebasing in Git).

However, more so than the technical aspects of the talk (which are interesting in their own right!), the main thing that has stayed with me throughout these years is the deep care for users that is reflected in Goode’s tone and words. It’s a bit difficult to convey this without the power of voice,You should watch the presentation! but here are some quotes which reflect this:

In the context of hg smartlog:hg smartlog gives you a focused view of your branches and how they relate to the development trunk.

I know Git can produce this kind of UI if you know the incantation, but the critical thing here is not that it can be done; it’s that it becomes the default view of their source-control environment. That is where the power comes from: making it really intuitive for users to use source control and understand the concepts without reading a man page.

In the context of hg absorb:hg absorb auto-magically identifies the right commits in a stack to squash fixes into and rewrites history accordingly. This makes it easier to work with stacked changes.

This is the type of UI that we need to be inventing for our users: ones that match their intent and do it to the best of their ability, without making the user understand everything they have to do. It’s a little bit magic, but it’s magic in a very clean way. I think a lot of user experiences could benefit from this approach.

If you want to undo an amend or undo parts of a commit in Mercurial, you just run unamend and uncommit. You don’t have to understand a reflog; you don’t have to get a PhD to understand reset anymore. It just works, and it gives users confidence that they can recover from mistakes. That’s one of the most important things we can do: provide user experiences that give them confidence in what they’re doing.

On the user experience side, we as a source control community need to do a better job of building UIs that are accessible, intuitive, and that enable novice users to be power users. Everything I just talked about is how we are trying to do that for our users at Facebook. If the Git community could do that, the massive number of Git users taking advantage of it has the potential to redefine productivity for an entire generation of users.

Over the years, the possibility of these workflows lingered in my mind as I continued working with Git. I tried building my own wrappers on top of the git CLI to do some of these things, but I couldn’t get the performance to be reasonable since everything shelled out to git all the time, and I didn’t understand Git’s internals well enough to do something better.

I ended up sticking with vanilla Git until Waleed KhanWaleed worked at Facebook on dev tools, and later did work at Twitter related to version control. created git-branchless, with support for a smartlog, in-memory rebases, undo and more. I eagerly adopted it. I also used Stephen Jung’s git-absorb quite a bit. Even today, the initial bit of git absorb’s README cites the mention of hg absorb on a Mozilla mailing list as the key inspiration.

Finally, earlier this year (2026), I mostly switched to using jj, after having bounced off of it a couple of times. jj was created by Martin von Zweigbergk, who previously contributed to Git and later joined Google and worked on their internal Mercurial client for the monorepo.Source: Mercurial at Google (2023).

So even though I have almost exclusively worked with Git throughout my career, I am in a way indebted to the work on Mercurial by Goode and numerous other contributors.

I’ve talked a bit about my personal usage of version control tooling. Let me briefly describe work I’ve done related to version control.

From late 2021 to late 2025, I worked at Sourcegraph on code indexing and navigation. For the last two of those years, I worked more on the backend written in Go, where the code navigation was coupled to version control.This is because code navigation data could be uploaded for ~any commit.

During this time, one of the recurring sources of incidents was the (non-)incremental updates for the commit graph structure that was mirrored into Postgres, in order to be able to efficiently compute what code navigation data (stored in Postgres) was “visible” at which commit.

I recall being frustrated with that, and half-jokingly proposing that it would be good to move to a more custom storage solution or have custom indexes next to Git’s storage itself. That proposal didn’t particularly go anywhere (not that I expected it to), but the frustration with Git as a hard-to-operate database stayed with me.

Since around March 2026, I’ve been working on Source Control at Databricks. Some of the things I’ve worked on include:

So in a way, I’ve been ~responsible for monitoring and maintaining the health of thousands of git checkouts (of our huge internal monorepoDepending on the specifics of compression, the history of the master branch ends up in the range of 20-50GB. ) for the past few months. (Life lesson: don’t get upset at a database for being hard-to-operate lest the monkey’s paw curls? 😄)

Apart from my main work, I have spent dozens of hours studying jj, Mononoke (the open-source server for Facebook’s VCS), TigerBeetle and, to a lesser extent, RocksDB and papers on LSM trees. I also prototyped a minimal code storage server in Tiger Style.

Over this time, I was also fortunate enough to attend Git Merge 2026.Interestingly enough, the sponsors included OpenAI, Google, GitHub, Cursor, etc., and the attendees included a bunch of employees from Meta who work on Sapling/Mononoke, but no Anthropic employees were present AFAICT.

Whew, that was a lot of words! At least, I hope that this helps you understand where I’m coming from when I write the points below.

This section covers what I think of the overall design and development processes that have been described in the post on Scion.

Having studied Sapling/Mononoke, and having spent some time thinking about how to build a version control server, the following bits felt obviousI understand that the post is written for a broader audience, so it makes sense to repeat things which may be “obvious” to people who work in the area. That said, I think there’s value in separating out/clarifying to readers what is common knowledge within a given area vs what is genuinely novel. For example, if you were writing an academic paper, common knowledge would go into a Background section, not into the later sections. (and hence not worth emphasizing) and/or copied (without clear attribution):

In order to support this growth, we built Scion, an in-house version control system, and fully migrated our monorepo from git in five months. We also built and shipped a code review surface (called Antique), code search, a rich source control IAM system, novel ways of managing and landing large amounts of reviewed code, and more, all in that same time period.

This was done by a team of 7 people and an undisclosed number of Claude tokens.

On reading this, my first thought was, “That’s still quite a lot of work.” With Git, it’s very easy for people (or agents) to come up with complex operations to do specific things, which can be difficult to easily map to other VCSes as-is. So it’s impressive that they managed to rip out Git fully regardless.It’s not 100% clear in the post if they’ve done so, but I’m assuming this based on the wording in the post.

I’m guessing that one or more of the following are true: (1) their monorepo lacks a file-based OWNERS system (2) the OWNERS system largely goes through with automated approvals from Claude (and hence does not bottleneck on human approvals) or (3) they used some targeted bypasses to go in and change people’s code to use their custom scn client instead of git.

we created Slack channels where we tasked Claude with being obsessively focused on the health of a single component. We call these Claudes “superfans.” We have a scion-daemon superfan, a scion-cache superfan, an Antique merge queue superfan [..] They have access to our telemetry and logs, and act like an experienced engineer who has nothing better to do than to refresh charts and look for anything strange. We also have traditional alerts for all of our systems, but our superfans can detect subtle and novel issues that make these alerts seem one-dimensional by comparison.

This is a pattern which I (personally) have not heard of being deployed elsewhere, presumably in large part due to the cost of frontier-model tokens. I’m guessing this will become more widespread as token prices fall.

It would’ve been nice if they’d given some examples of what “subtle and novel issues” these superfans found.

The development lifecycle in Scion discourages refs (pointers to commits, such as branches and tags), except for the main ref or release branches, because global state that every server has to agree on is a looming scaling problem.

This point didn’t quite add up for me. The amount of data associated with a ref is very small – it’s the ref’s name and the ID of the object it points to. If you separate out temporary refs (for landing/organizing work) and long-lived refs (for release branches), then temporary refs can be automatically cleaned up and would be proportional to the number of changes in flight. The long-lived refs would keep adding up anyway (and potentially contribute to whatever scaling problem is anticipated).

So how does not using refs in the dev loop help?

I can see a downstream correctness argument for avoiding refs, where it’s easy to accidentally write a job which (if it works with refs) accidentally pulls in two different commits (as the ref moves) instead of detecting ref movement and triggering failure/retry. However, it’s also easy to make a different kind of mistake just working with commit IDs – you could keep running the job for a commit that has become unreachable due to a push.

There are several points in the article related to resource utilization which didn’t add up in my head.

Beyond these, there are standard workarounds for large monorepos, like internal git mirrors and repository snapshots (seeds) kept in blob storage. We’ve used all of them—at our peak, we operated several hundred internal git mirrors to deal with the load.

At Databricks, we do something similar with reference repos which are updated every ~2 hours, and we have fewer than 10 git mirrors to deal with CI load, despite the repo size being within the ~same order of magnitude. Even with this many mirrors, the CPU load is well under control, and increasing the frequency of snapshots from 2h to, say, 1h or even 30min – which would reduce CPU load on the mirrors – would be doable with a bit of work.

So it’s difficult for me to think of what kind of workload would necessitate “several hundred” git mirrors. Maybe very wide fan-outs for tests in CI?

Similarly, there’s another point about maintaining the mirrors later on:

At our peak, we ran several hundred git mirrors, which significantly strained capacity and no longer scaled once the repo outgrew the mirrors’ disks or memory limits

It’s unclear how a repo with 100GB of history on the main branch could outgrow the disks on modern cloud instances, which can have several TB of storage. Yes, it requires some level of care wrt. maintenance, but disk limits and memory limits should generally not be the major problems here. Memory in particular is even more odd, because most accesses will likely be for the most recent data, which can easily stay resident in a few GB of RAM at most.

Many of the pre-migration numbers provided on the chart (which make the Scion numbers look impressive) seem way too high, and some of the ones post-migration also seem unusually high. As one example, the charts show that the p50 for ‘pull latest’ fell from 87s → 3.5s. Each of these feels off for different reasons.This is one of the places where the post – by going wide instead of deep – makes it difficult to understand what’s actually being said. For example, percentiles can easily be skewed downwards due to automated background loops (esp. those running at high frequency) if most operations short-circuit to no-ops.

Pre-migration: At our scale, fetching the changes at the start of a day can take over a minute, but after that, fetches are much faster. So even the p90 for fetch operations ends up being under 1 minute. Granted, “fetch” and “pull latest for the trunk” are not equivalent operations. However, I’m not sure what it would take for things to be so bad for the p50 to be at 87s if you do background pre-fetching once a devbox has booted up.

Post-migration: 3.5s seems surprisingly high, given everything else. With sparse checkouts, presumably this number should be proportional to the size of the diff within that subset between pull operations. For example, naively, I’d expect network to be the limiting factor: even at 2GbpsGCP doesn’t appear to have ingress bandwidth limits for instances within a VPC, so I’m using the “2Gbps per vCPU” (for egress) as a rough guide/underestimate of available bandwidth. you could transfer 875MB in 3.5s. I can’t imagine the amount of data being transferred for a p50 “pull latest” being even close to that, so there must be something else that’s the bottleneck. Maybe the query for determining what data should be pulled is the slowest bit? Too many RPCs? Serialization/deserialization overhead? 🤷

Before we explore what we built, we should acknowledge how unusual our workload is. Unsurprisingly, Anthropic uses Claude to write software far more than almost any other company, so we’re often the first to see where tools built for human scale start to strain. Source control is just one example of this. While we don’t expect many organizations to have these problems in the very near term, we suspect it won’t be too long before others who use AI coding tools experience these same pressure points, which is why we wanted to share what we built and what we learned.

The vibe of this paragraph captures the vibe of the rest of the article. It is simultaneously:

As Rain put in their post More on Anthropic’s Scion ripping off Mononoke:

It is always good to situate your work in the larger context. We all stand on the shoulders of giants! There is nothing wrong with borrowing and adapting existing work to new contexts — that is the vast majority of what I do as an engineer. When you position your work as derivative, you are acknowledging those that came before you, as you hope to be acknowledged by those who come after you.

Given how they’ve framed their work and how they’ve recognized prior work only with cursory nods (this changed somewhat after they got called out for it!), I’m now much less surprised by their absence at Git Merge 2026. Historically, companies and developers have joined communities to learn from other people’s expertise, and to be able to recruit people interested in the same areas.

Now that companies can increasingly point LLMs to clone your codebase, it is understandable that some of them no longer feel the need to engage with the corresponding communities in the same manner.

One of the major problems with the blog post is that it is unclear as to what primary purpose it is meant to serve and who the target audience is.

Perhaps because of the lack of a clear audience in mind, even though the post was (thankfully!) not LLM-written, many parts of it suffer from LLM-isms like:

Historically, using version control has been a fairly human-centric activity. While you might have a sprinkling of deterministic automations, such as for bumping dependencies, reverting PRs which introduced regressions, etc., the main user was the developer.

As increasingly more companies use LLM agents for increasingly more parts of the development lifecycle, it is understandable that LLMs become the primary “user” for a VCS, and the developer is abstracted away from the VCS. In such a world, if you’re focused on the LLM as the “user”, you could ask questions about metrics like error rates/undo rates/latency for tool calls.

If you take a broader view and are interested in the end-to-end developer experience, you might still care about questions such as “what are the problems people face when trying to use the VCS via LLMs”, as well as “which operations are slow but frequent, and could be replaced with fast and deterministic tooling instead.”

But the post really does not touch upon either of those points, and overall ends up having no clear narrative arc as a result.

The post starts out with a relatively vague motivation:

the latent demand for merging code is practically infinite, and every bottleneck we remove immediately leads to a further increase in the amount of code we produce. In order to support this growth, we built Scion [..]

However, near the end of the post, the wins are stated in terms of reduced CPU utilization (which translates to increased capacity for other things) and simplified systems (I understand why this is a win, but it seems like this was not the original motivation for pursuing this path).

I understand that the new VCS is able to support the current growth, but the implied thesis that the VCS was the bottleneck and removing that bottleneck actually unlocked the growth lacks compelling evidence in the post – one is left to wonder how much of the growth is attributable to increased background automations vs. model changes vs. other factors.

For example, were people frequently blocked from landing PRs because CI was at capacity and runs remained queued for a long time? If so, did freeing up capacity help reduce the time from PR creation to merging, which in turn led to more PRs being created? Maybe! But the reader is basically left to just guess all of the intermediate details without a clear connecting thread.

When I first started reading the post, I went in with high expectations. After all, it has historically been rare for companies to build their own version control systems, and given how much money and talent Anthropic have at their disposal, I thought the post would’ve been a lot more interesting than it actually turned out to be.

Overall, had Anthropic clearly stated up front what parts of the design were copied from other systems with proper attribution, and focused the post on how they managed the migration, I think the post would’ve been more honest, more streamlined and also more useful to people outside Anthropic. Specifically:

The post does none of that,It’s understandable that they wouldn’t want to open-source the code itself, as untangling it from the rest of the monorepo and having development in multiple places would add friction for themselves for unclear benefit. presents several previously established ideas as seemingly original without a clear separation between the two, and frames the high-level description as a “gift” to the developer ecosystem/Source Control community.

InfoQ Homepage News LocalStack for Azure Enters Public Preview with Security Settings Stored but Not Enforced

Oct 31, 2026 3 min read

LocalStack has put its Azure emulator into public preview, free and self-serve, with general availability expected in early 2027. Its own documentation is candid about the gap between emulating a resource and emulating its behavior.

The product runs Azure services on a developer machine and accepts existing ARM and Bicep templates, Terraform modules, Pulumi programs, and Azure CLI scripts without rewrites. The pitch is to test applications, as LocalStack puts it, "without waiting on a dev subscription or paying for every iteration." The service list is broad, covering AKS, Container Apps, Functions, App Service, Cosmos DB, Service Bus, Event Hubs, Key Vault, App Configuration, Managed Identity, API Management and more, and is wider than the announcement itself suggests. Each developer gets an isolated sandbox, and LocalStack positions it for development and testing rather than as a replacement for Azure.

The project is led by Paolo Salvatori, a Microsoft principal who spent 28 years at the company before joining LocalStack, and the creator of Service Bus Explorer. He sets the fidelity contract in one line:

If your solution runs perfectly on Azure but fails on our emulator, that is our bug to fix.

The documentation covers 24 resource providers and reports how much of each API is implemented. Storage Accounts covers 13 of 81 operations. App Service covers 143 of 616. Virtual Network covers 10 of 29.

The more useful pattern is what happens to the operations that are implemented. Configuration is frequently accepted, stored, and returned without taking effect. On App Service:

Keys, access restrictions, authentication settings, and publishing credential policies are not enforced.

The same page records that httpsOnly is not enforced and the emulator serves HTTP, that custom host-name bindings are stored and listed while the app answers only on its default names, that VNet integration is stored and returned with no network effect, and that backup configuration is stored while backup and restore are not implemented.

Networking follows suit. The Virtual Network page states plainly that "the emulator does not route network traffic or enforce security rules," that peering is unsupported, and that VPN gateways, ExpressRoute circuits, Load Balancer, Application Gateway, and Network Watcher are not implemented. Private DNS zones accept only A records.

Several Storage divergences land on authentication. Data-plane requests with a bearer token succeed whenever a token is present unless RBAC enforcement is enabled. A user delegation SAS does not re-check the principal’s RBAC when used. A SAS restricted to the caller’s public IP is refused because the emulator sees a Docker or loopback address. Unsupported request headers are silently accepted rather than rejected, and the x-ms-version header is not validated at all.

That promise is about code that runs in Azure and fails locally. The documented gaps mostly describe the reverse: an app with httpsOnly set serves HTTP here, and a data-plane request carrying any bearer token gets through. Both pass locally, and nothing in the run flags the difference.

Three behaviors will surprise people before any of that does. A web app created on a Windows plan runs its code in the Linux runtime. The Oryx build image ships for amd64 only, so on Apple Silicon a code deployment’s build fails, and the app starts without its dependencies. App Service state is held in memory and lost when the emulator stops.

Microsoft’s own local tooling is narrower and older. Azurite emulates Blob, Queue, and Table storage, the Cosmos DB emulator covers that database, and Azure Functions Core Tools runs Functions locally. None compose into a single environment where an ARM or Bicep deployment can be exercised end to end, which is the gap LocalStack aims to fill.

LocalStack also pitches the sandbox at AI agents, somewhere they can "deploy, break, and retry" without live credentials. An agent iterating there gets access restrictions stored rather than applied, and any bearer token accepted. Both come back as passes.

Developer experience features, including App Inspector, snapshots, and the chaos APIs, are not in preview. Pricing arrives at general availability, and preview access ends there. The transition terms are not settled: the product page still carries "[30 days]" as a literal placeholder and an unfilled next-steps section.

#9958. My favourite laptop

I’m not a big owner of things, but the best laptop I’ve ever owned is a roughed-up 2015 Thinkpad X250.

For the flex, here it is running a GUI shell sat on top of the microkernel I’m currently working on (blog post about this incoming… eventually).

Here’s a list of things that I think make it brilliant. I don’t want to pretend that any of these things are uniquely exemplary: far from it. It is the confluence of them, and not any one in particular, that makes me love using it.

It’s pretty tiny. Its form-factor fits snuggly into the footprint of an A4 piece of paper, so it sits alongside books and folders when placed in a small rucksack without risking damage.

It weighs almost nothing too: even with the extra capacity battery, it’s only about 1.45 Kg. Light enough that you almost don’t notice it when travelling.

Mine has an i5-5200U: 4 logical cores, maxing out at 2.7 GHz. I upgraded it to 8 GB of RAM a while back: more than enough for some light on-the-go programming.

Even at full pelt, I’ve never heard the fan kicking up much of a fuss. Now that I think about it, I’m not even certain that it works.

The X250 has both an internal battery and an external battery slot. I’ve opted for the largest after-market external battery I could find. When doing casual work the laptop will easily survive for north of 10 hours without a charge, stretching to 12 hours if I’m careful.

The X250 was quite popular and replacement parts retail very cheaply on ebay. It’s not the easiest to disassemble Thinkpad by any means but I can tear it apart entirely with the pocket phillips I keep on my keyring. I have previously replaced:

Every time you open up a laptop you run the risk of damaging something important either via a slip of the hand or simply the accumulated toll of loosening and tightening dozens of tiny screw threads. Despite that, my X250 has proved remarkably resilient and has never sustained any major damage despite more than more than a dozen tear-downs.

As with most Thinkpads, the keyboard feels lovely to use. When you spend a lot of time writing code the reliability and sensitivity of a keyboard starts to matter a lot. Coupled with my text editor, the experience of writing code on the thing is beautifully snappy.

I opted for Endeavour OS. In the usual Arch Linux tradition, it favours native package installs over sandboxed applications. As a result my install sits at around 30 GB. A 128 GB M.2 SSD raided from another second-hand machine is more than enough to cover that and everything I’m working on.

I’ve slimmed down my systemd setup as much as possible and the thing boots from cold in about 8 seconds.

Here’s where the X250 beats out most competition. I bought mine second-hand for about £100 in 2018. They’ve only got cheaper since then. I’m not afraid to take it anywhere because it’s barely worth stealing and would be cheap to replace even if that were to happen. Its value is very much not in its on-paper specs and instead in how I use it.

I get a certain glee in keeping older or second-hand hardware running as a daily driver. It sounds silly, but it feels like a quiet revolt against bigger-faster-costlier consumption culture. Come the end times, this is the machine I’ll be riding it out with.

#9957. What We Missed: Feds Lasso Texas Laptop Farms

Cybersecurity In-Depth: Feature articles on security strategy, latest trends, and people to know.

In this video, Dark Reading editors discuss some of the news they didn't get a chance to cover, from busting up North Korea's stateside infrastructure in "Operation Lonestar Justice" to Staples' gift card bonanza.

The US government is striking back against the ever-persistent threat of fake IT worker schemes run by the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK).

In this episode of "What We Missed," Dark Reading's Rob Wright and Alex Culafi discuss some of the recent news events and topics that didn't make it into the publication, starting with FBI raids across more than 40 Texas residences that were allegedly running "laptop farms."

The law-enforcement action, dubbed “Operation Lonestar Roundup,” seized 187 devices, charged 14 people, and arrested individuals accused of facilitating North Korean threat actors running fake IT worker schemes. The schemes disrupted by Operation Lonestar Roundup impacted more than 70 US companies, according to the FBI.

Fake IT worker schemes typically involve DPRK actors masquerading as IT professionals and developers, either using fake or stolen identities, to gain employment at US companies. The threat actors then use their positions to exfiltrate sensitive data, steal intellectual property, and gather intelligence.

Related:Ex-OpenAI Engineer Detained After Planting Secret Recorder at HQ

Also discussed on this episode: Russian police arrested alleged members of a cybercriminal group known as the "DataSuckers," which has taken credit for several breaches against companies in Russia and Ukraine; and according to a report from 404 Media, a Chinese criminal operation breached Staples' internal customer support system and used it to issue thousands of gift cards, worth $5 million.

For all of our Dark Reading news videos, please check out our YouTube channel and our curated video articles.

This transcript has been edited for clarity and length by Informa TechTarget's internal AI assistant. For the full experience, please watch the video.

Organizations at every level are dealing with North Korean operators trying to either get paychecks to send back to North Korea or to get data that they can use to exploit later, and it's — I don't know if it's getting uglier, but it remains very ugly a few years later.

#9956. Async GRPO with LoRA across HF Jobs: a bucket, a proxy, and no NCCL

LoRA support recently landed in TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer with PR #7017, and ships with TRL v1.14. The asynchronous trainer can now train an adapter instead of the full model, and it syncs only the LoRA adapter to vLLM. This post covers a real-world project built on top of it, where training and inference no longer share a machine.

LoRA training is particularly suited for RL, as shown in Thinking Machines's blog LoRA Without Regret. They show that LoRA can match full fine-tuning for policy-gradient RL, even with rank 1. This stems from the fact that the advantage function only gives ~O(1) bits of information per episode, so there is not that much to learn from each step, from a total-bits-of-information point of view. A rank-1 adapter has enough capacity to absorb it.

There is also a systems consequence of LoRA training. A rank-1 adapter for a 1.5B model is a few megabytes, while the full model is around 3 GB. Instead of sending the full policy to the inference workers after every update, we can just send the adapter. vLLM can also keep several adapters loaded at once. Old rollouts finish with the policy they started with, while new rollouts use the latest one.

TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer already separates training and generation. The trainer and vLLM can run on different machines and at their own speed. This is easy in a single-node or cluster setting where both processes share a filesystem or can form an NCCL group.

What we want is to run the same setup with Hugging Face Jobs. Essentially, an HF Job is one container running on one VM. This means that one Job cannot spawn multiple nodes (at least for now) to hold a trainer and a fleet of vLLM servers (we are limited to 8xH200 at most per node). The AsyncGRPOTrainer is built for exactly that kind of scale, so the question became: how far can we get if we drop the requirement that the trainer and the inference servers share a node?

Well, with a full-weight sync, the answer would be "not far". Every update would have to move gigabytes between machines, which is what NCCL is for in a dense cluster, but Jobs can't communicate across nodes. There is no shared local disk and obviously no shared localhost. With LoRA, a sync is only a few megabytes. For the filesystem part, HF Jobs provide volumes backed by Storage Buckets! These buckets can then be mounted as a FUSE filesystem in every Job and are enough to work as a shared FS between nodes. No network path between the Jobs is needed at all.

The new adapter-only sync path in AsyncGRPOTrainer works like this. The trainer does not send tensors to vLLM. Every few optimizer steps, it saves the adapter under /.vllm_lora/trl-policy-v{N}, publishes the directory with an atomic rename, then sends its path to vLLM's /v1/load_lora_adapter endpoint. vLLM loads the files from disk, so the rollout worker can then request model="trl-policy-v{N}".

This is how runtime adapter loading already works in vLLM. The endpoint takes a path, not tensors, so the trainer and the server are expected to share a filesystem. On a Slurm cluster, that is the network filesystem. On Jobs, we get the same thing by mounting a Storage Bucket as a volume at the same path in every Job, as we mentioned earlier. Under the hood, it uses hf-mount, which exposes the bucket as a POSIX filesystem inside the container:

Nothing in TRL or vLLM had to change for this. The trainer writes to /lora//.vllm_lora/ and the servers read from the same path. The path sent in the POST request is already valid inside every container.

Note that we also store the checkpoints and the final adapter in the bucket. The HF Jobs are ephemeral, but a preempted trainer can resume training, as the final adapter is always persisted to the bucket and is never lost when the Job stops.

Each replica uses one GPU and the stock vllm/vllm-openai image. We only need to enable runtime LoRA loading and reserve enough adapter slots.

The number of adapter slots follows from max_staleness. In AsyncGRPOTrainer, every weight sync bumps the policy version by one, and max_staleness is how many versions a rollout sample may lag behind the current policy before the trainer discards it. With max_staleness=4, a sample generated under trl-policy-v3 is still used for training while the trainer is at v7. A rollout that started under v3 must also be able to finish under v3. So at any moment, vLLM has to serve the current policy plus the four before it. That is why the trainer keeps max_staleness + 1 adapter versions registered and unloads anything older. Each sync loads the new version before it unloads the oldest one, which needs one more slot during the swap. That gives --max-loras 6. With only five, vLLM would silently evict a policy that still has rollouts in flight at every sync.

We pin vLLM to v0.27.1. vLLM moves fast, and the flags above and the runtime LoRA endpoints are the ones that version exposes, so treat the version as part of the recipe.

There is another possible design where the trainer keeps only the latest adapter and always publishes it under the same name. We did not go that way, because vLLM keys its prefix cache by adapter name. With a single name, KV blocks computed under the previous weights would still match after the swap, so the prefill would not be redone and a rollout could get its prefix from one policy version and its decode from the next. The trainer would have no way to tell, and it would show up as ratio drifting away from 1. Versioned names make this impossible: a name always means one set of weights, and a cached prefix can never match a newer version.

We chose sail/Sanity-Test-R1D-1.5B, the dataset from Defeating the Training-Inference Mismatch via FP16 (Qi et al., 2025). The reproduction code is in sail-sg/Precision-RL.

The authors generated 40 answers for each MATH problem with DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B. They kept problems with a success rate between 20% and 80%, yielding 1,460 questions. This dataset is really good for RL validation because the questions are neither already solved nor completely hopeless for that model, meaning the model can get a good early signal to train on and improve.

This is awesome as a robust end-to-end test: if one vLLM replica silently serves the base model under an adapter name, we want to see that in the curve within a few dozen steps. Also, this dataset is small enough to cycle through in less than two hours.

We also take the hyperparameters from the paper's LoRA scripts in oat/scripts/lora: Qwen/Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B, LoRA rank 1 with alpha 2, a learning rate of 4e-5, 8 samples per prompt, 128 completions per step, a maximum of 3,000 generated tokens and a 4,096-token context.

The trainer uses the same vllm/vllm-openai:v0.27.1 image with TRL installed on top. We ran the PR branch at the time; the same code now ships in TRL v1.14. The training script is a normal AsyncGRPOTrainer script. The only Job-specific values are the output directory and the server URL.

During initialization, TRL calls /server_info. If it finds a lora_config, it uses adapter-only sync. Configurations vLLM cannot serve directly, such as DoRA, modules_to_save, or a rank above --max-lora-rank, fall back to merged-weight sync with a warning. The log should contain Adapter-only vLLM sync enabled.

Now onto the fun stuff. We need a proxy between the trainer and the vLLM Jobs for two reasons:

Exposed Job ports require an Authorization: Bearer header on every request. The proxy is where that header gets added, so TRL does not need to know about it.

We want more than one GPU generating. On a single vLLM server, the usual way to get that is --data-parallel-size > 1, but TRL refuses adapter-only sync in that mode, for a good reason: a call to /v1/load_lora_adapter only reaches the DP rank that answers it, so the other ranks would keep serving the base model under the new policy name. On Jobs the question does not even arise, since each replica is its own machine. So the data parallelism has to live one level up, in something that fans the adapter load out to every replica.

We therefore run a small proxy at 127.0.0.1:8000 on the trainer Job and point TRL to it as if it were a single vLLM server. Besides adding the header, the proxy does two things functionally:

A quick reminder of why this matters. Generating a completion has two phases with very different workload profiles:

Those keys and values are the KV cache. Because attention is causal, the KV of a token depends only on the tokens before it, not on what comes after. Two requests that share a prefix therefore share the KV of that prefix, and a replica that already has it in cache can skip that part of the prefill entirely. The whole game now is to find that replica, so a request can benefit from landing on the replica that has already seen its prefix.

vLLM stores its prefix KV cache in blocks of 16 tokens. Because of GRPO, the rollout worker sends G requests with the same prompt (in our case G=8). If they all reach the same replica, the first request computes the prefill and the next seven reuse it. With round-robin routing, half would go to a replica that doesn't have the prefix cached, and those four requests would redo the prefill work and waste valuable GPU compute.

The job of our router is to track which replica has seen which block hash. One important detail is that the hashes are chained, so the hash of block 3 represents blocks 1, 2 and 3, not just block 3. This mirrors causal attention: the KV of block 3 is only valid if blocks 1 and 2 are the same too. We also seed the chain with the adapter name because the KV cache also depends on the adapter that generated it: a prefix cached for policy v3 is useless for policy v4!

The video walks through the entire decision process for choosing a replica. The steps below go through a real 135-token completion request example (from the Sanity dataset problems):

1. Split the prompt into blocks. The router receives token ids and cuts them into 16-token blocks, just like vLLM. It only hashes complete blocks, so the last 7 tokens are ignored here.

2. Hash the prefix. Each block is hashed with the previous hash, starting from the adapter seed. h3 therefore identifies blocks 1, 2 and 3 in order. Two prompts with the same first k blocks get the same hashes up to hk. Once one block changes, every hash after it changes too. This is why we seed the hashes with the adapter name: the same prompt under trl-policy-v4 starts from another seed and cannot match entries from v3. This is what we want because the old KV blocks were computed with different weights.

3. Compare two prompts. Problem 1 has 103 tokens. Both prompts start with the same 23-token chat template. Their first block is identical, but block 2 already contains the problem text. The hashes differ from there.

4. Store the owners. For every hash, the router remembers which replicas served it and which hashes came after it (we cap the successor set at two because we only need to know whether a block has one continuation or several). After a few prompts, the template block h1 is owned by both replicas and already has several successors, h2 to h8 are owned by A only and each has a single successor, and h2' to h6' are owned by B only.

In practice, every prompt in a run starts with the same tokens. Here, it is the chat template and the system prompt, which amount to the first 23 tokens of all 1,460 problems. In an agent setting, it would be the tool descriptions, and in a multi-turn environment it would be the shared conversation history. These blocks are in every replica's cache within seconds, so matching on them tells us nothing about where a particular prompt lives.

A block is common if every replica has served it, or if it has more than one successor. Common blocks are ignored during routing because they do not identify a particular prompt. More on this below!

5. Pick a replica. The router counts how many leading blocks match on each replica and removes the common prefix. What is left is the number of blocks specific to this prompt. Then:

Here is the rule applied to four requests. Start from a state where replicas A and B both have 3 requests in flight, and only the template block h1 is known on both replicas.

6. Reuse the prefill. Request 2 is the reason for doing all this. It reuses the prefill computed by Request 1: blocks 1 to 8 are already in A's KV cache, so A skips straight to decoding the completion. Had it gone to B, B would have prefilled all 135 tokens again while A's cache sat unused. Request 3 shows why the common rule is needed. Without it, the shared chat template would make every new prompt look like a cache hit. Request 4 keeps the load bounded. Saving one prefill is not worth letting a replica fall far behind.

The common prefix is the annoying part. Every request starts with the same system prompt and chat template. A simple longest-prefix match would give the first replica a match for almost every new prompt. We detect the shared prefix through fan-out instead: a block with several different successors is common, while a block that always leads to the same successor belongs to a particular prompt. Only the blocks after that common prefix count as affinity.

The proxy also needs to broadcast the adapter loads to every replica. We treat the operation as all-or-nothing. Each replica has its own bucket mount, so they do not necessarily see a new adapter at exactly the same time. A No adapter found for error usually means that one bucket mount has not caught up yet, and we retry only that replica. For any other error, we unload the adapter from the replicas that accepted it so that a policy name never exists on only part of the replicas.

We also broadcast /pause, /resume and /v1/unload_lora_adapter in the same way. /health returns 200 only if every replica is healthy. /server_info and /v1/models only need one answer. From TRL's point of view, the proxy is a single data_parallel_size=1 server, so it selects adapter-only sync.

We initially wondered whether a Python asyncio proxy would become a bottleneck. It does not (at least at this scale). There are at most 128 non-streaming JSON requests in flight, and routing only computes a few hashes. One thread handles this easily. A more refined router that needs to handle more traffic would probably need to be written in a faster language (We see you 🦀).

The numbers below come from the trainer's logged metrics on trackio. The run uses Qwen/Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B, LoRA r=1 on all-linear, 128 completions per step and 8 rollouts per prompt. It runs for 500 steps and saves a checkpoint every 50 steps. The trainer uses an h200x2 Job and each of the two vLLM replicas uses one h200 Job. Running all three costs ~$20 per hour.

All 252 adapter loads succeeded 🎉: 126 syncs times 2 replicas. Six succeeded on the second attempt and 246 on the third.

At the end of the run, after 64,728 rollouts, the proxy's counters read:

With 8 rollouts per prompt, at least one of the eight requests must be cold. The theoretical minimum is therefore 12.5 %. The router gets 14.2 % unmatched requests, 84.5 % affinity hits, and 1.3 % spills. There is not much left to gain here unless we start looking at each replica's load using deeper inference-side metrics based on real measured load.

The first configuration has a pretty obvious problem: the trainer is the bottleneck, not generation. Over the 500 steps, we have:

The rollout queue stays full, and the worker is mostly blocked by backpressure. The second replica is basically useless in this configuration. We'll see later in the post how we went through runs that moved the bottleneck between training and generation to make the run 3.9× faster.

Figure 1. trackio run r1-dp2. Panels: reward with its 20-step rolling mean and 50-step block means, and ratio on a 0.99 to 1.01 axis. Reward climbs from 0.15 to 0.44 over 500 steps; ratio stays between 0.9993 and 1.0004 throughout.

500 steps took 3 h 27 min. Mean reward goes from 0.145 over the first 20 steps to 0.438 over the last 20. More importantly for this test, ratio stays at 1.000 for every step! The policy served by vLLM always matches the one used by the trainer to score the rollout. This held across all 126 syncs. Mean staleness was 1.5 policy versions, against a maximum of 4. The trackio dashboard has the full curves.

We have our undeniable proof that LoRA AsyncGRPO works! Let's now see how we can improve our training runs by looking at the recent detailed AsyncGRPO metrics.

Async RL is a pipeline between training and generation. Making one side faster does nothing if the other side cannot keep up. Fortunately, in AsyncGRPOTrainer we've added enough timings and metrics to see this directly.

All the useful metrics are documented in the Logged metrics section. perf/rollout_wait_s tells us how long the trainer waits for samples. rollout/backpressure_s tells us how long generation waits for space in the rollout queue. They are diametrically opposed to each other and should not both be high. Together with the queue size, they tell us which side is slow.

We ran five experiments. Each one starts from a problem visible in the previous run's dashboard. Unless mentioned otherwise, the model, recipe and three-Job layout stay the same. The names below are the trackio run names.

We keep these four groups of metrics visible:

The diagnosis is simple: a full queue with zero rollout wait and high backpressure means the trainer is too slow. An empty queue with rising rollout wait and no backpressure means generation is too slow. Comparing perf/mfu_wall_clock with perf/mfu_fwd_bwd also shows how much time the trainer GPUs spend waiting instead of training.

Figure 2. trackio run r1-dp2. Panels: perf/step_s, perf/fwd_bwd_s, sample/rollout_queue_size, rollout/backpressure_s. Step time and forward+backward overlap almost completely; the queue sits pinned near 476 of 512 and backpressure never drops below 11 s per rollout group: trainer-bound.

perf/step_s is 22.9 s and perf/fwd_bwd_s is 21.9 s. Forward and backward take 96 % of the step time. The queue stays full and the trainer waits only 0.02 s for rollouts, and the rollout worker spends 15 seconds per group blocked by backpressure. The two vLLM replicas generate faster than the trainer consumes. The reported 4.6k tokens/s is not their actual limit; they simply have nowhere to put more output.

The batch metrics explain the terrible 3.9 % MFU. batch/microbatches_per_step is 64 and batch/samples_per_row is 1.0. Each rank processes one sequence of around 1.2k tokens, 64 times per step. This comes from the reference recipe's per_device_train_batch_size=1. For a 1.5B model on an H200, this is completely latency-bound.

The fix is not to change the batch size. We keep 128 completions per optimizer step and only change how they are laid out on the GPU: instead of one sequence per microbatch, we pack many sequences densely into each row. The trainer supports this through token-budget batching. With token_budget > 0, it packs several samples into one padding-free row per rank. An optimizer step processes gradient_accumulation_steps rows. We set token_budget=16384 and gradient_accumulation_steps=6.

Figure 3. trackio runs r1-dp2 and r1-dp2-tb16k overlaid over their first 154 steps. Panels: batch/samples_per_row, batch/microbatches_per_step, perf/step_s, perf/fwd_bwd_s, perf/mfu_fwd_bwd, rollout/generated_tok_s. Packing takes samples per row from 1 to 13, microbatches from 64 to 6, step time from 23 s to 5.9 s, and generation from 4.2k to 27.5k tok/s with no change on the vLLM side.

batch/samples_per_row goes from 1.0 to ~12.7 and the number of microbatches drops from 64 to 6. The rows are 95 % full! Forward and backward fall from 21.9 s to 5.6 s, while MFU rises from 3.9 % to 19 %. We now train on around 150 samples per step because the rows pack better than the mean-length estimate predicted.

Generation also jumps from 4.6k to 25k tokens/s, even though we changed nothing on the vLLM side. The queue is no longer constantly full, so the replicas can finally run. This is why we do not like optimizing pipeline stages in isolation. We need to be careful to evaluate the whole system, as a slow stage can hide the real performance of everything before it.

perf/fwd_s is 1.34 s while perf/fwd_bwd_s is 5.6 s. A normal backward costs roughly twice the forward, and with frozen base weights it should be closer to once. A ratio of 3.2 is suspicious.

The reason is that AsyncGRPOConfig defaults to gradient_checkpointing=True. Every microbatch recomputes its forward during the backward. This also explains why a 16k-token row only uses 25 GB on a 141 GB H200! It's a memory optimization for this trainer, but we don't need it in this specific case: the model is small enough to fit into VRAM with the activations kept for the backward.

Figure 4. trackio runs r1-dp2-tb16k and r1-dp2-tb16k-nockpt overlaid over their first 134 steps. Panels: perf/fwd_s, perf/fwd_bwd_s, perf/weight_sync_s, sample/rollout_queue_size, perf/rollout_wait_s, perf/mfu_fwd_bwd. Forward+backward drops by one forward; the queue falls from ~420 to ~60, and rollout wait rises from 0.02 s to 0.5 s: the bottleneck shifts to generation.

With gradient_checkpointing=False, forward and backward drop to 4.6 s, almost exactly one forward less, and MFU reaches 23 %. The queue now falls to 71 and rollout wait rises from 0.04 s to 0.6 s. The trainer consumes samples faster than two replicas generate them. We successfully moved the bottleneck to generation.

This exposes two more costs. A 7.6-second weight sync every four steps now takes 25 % of wall-clock time. It was only 8 % when each step took 23 seconds. Also, backward is still 2.5 times slower than forward. With frozen base weights, there are around 2 seconds per step that do not look like normal model math.

Since generation was now too slow, we added a third replica. We also reduced the adapter retry interval from 2 s to 0.5 s in the proxy and disabled fsdp_reshard_after_forward to check whether FSDP2 re-gathers caused the extra 2 seconds in backward.

Figure 5. trackio runs r1-dp2-tb16k-nockpt and r1-dp3-tb16k-nockpt overlaid over their first 134 steps. Panels: perf/weight_sync_s, rollout/generated_tok_s, rollout/inflight, perf/fwd_bwd_s. Sync falls from 7.6 s to 5.8 s; generation and forward+backward do not move; rollout/inflight reads 128 in both runs, which is the cap the third replica ran into.

Weight sync falls from 7.6 s to 5.8 s, so the shorter retry helps. Forward and backward stay at 4.6 s, which rules out resharding. Generation moves from 25k to only 26k tokens/s. The third replica does basically nothing.

The reason was sitting in rollout/inflight: 128 in every run. The proxy shows those requests split as 44 + 43 + 41 across the three replicas. max_inflight_tasks limits concurrency for the whole rollout worker, not per replica. A 1.5B model on an H200 processes 43 and 130 concurrent sequences at almost the same cost per token. Splitting 128 requests over three GPUs gives nearly the same throughput as splitting them over two.

So vLLM was not the limit. Our own client-side constant was. We had set it conservatively because we did not know how hundreds of long HTTPS requests would behave through the public Jobs proxy. At this point, 130,000 rollout completions had crossed it without a single transport error.

max_inflight_tasks=384 and queue_maxsize=768, nothing else.

Figure 6. All five trackio runs (r1-dp2, r1-dp2-tb16k, r1-dp2-tb16k-nockpt, r1-dp3-tb16k-nockpt, r1-dp3-inflight384) overlaid, x-axis in steps. Panels: perf/step_s, reward, sample/rollout_queue_size, sample/staleness_mean. Step time falls from 22.9 s to 4.8 s across the series while the reward curves stay on top of each other; the last run's queue refills to ~690 of 768 and its staleness settles at 2. Runs 2 to 4 were stopped early once the dashboard had answered the question.

With 384 requests in flight, each replica gets 128. The queue quickly fills to around 690 out of 768 and stays there. Backpressure returns to 5 seconds and rollout wait falls to 0.03 seconds. Training is the bottleneck again! Forward and backward take 4.6 seconds, weight sync adds an amortized 1.5 seconds, and median step time is 4.8 seconds.

Mean staleness rises from 1.5 to 2.0 versions because samples wait longer in the larger queue. This is still below max_staleness=4, and ratio remains very close to 1.000.

Figure 7. trackio runs r1-dp2 and r1-dp3-inflight384, reward against wall-clock minutes since the first optimizer step. Same recipe, same 500 steps, same final reward; run 5 gets there in 52 minutes instead of 3 h 26 min.

The final run is 3.9× faster and trains on 31 % more samples, with basically the same reward curve. Packing, disabling checkpointing and raising the in-flight limit made the difference. In each case, the dashboard made this clear within the first ten minutes.

Show tracked I/O statistics in a visual dashboard

LoRA training is particularly suited for RL, as shown in Thinking Machines's blog LoRA Without Regret. They show that LoRA can match full fine-tuning for policy-gradient RL, even with sportzfy rank 1. This stems from the fact that the advantage function only gives ~O(1) bits of information per episode, so there is not that much to learn from each step, from a total-bits-of-information point of view. A rank-1 adapter has enough capacity to absorb it.

Really interesting take on how LoRA changes the systems side of RL training, not just the training itself. The idea of separating training and inference across different machines while only moving a small adapter instead of the full model makes a lot of practical sense, especially when working with HF Jobs. The “bucket, proxy, and no NCCL” approach feels like a good example of simplifying distributed infrastructure by moving the communication boundary to something much smaller and easier to manage.

I also like the connection to the LoRA Without Regret work, particularly the point that policy-gradient updates may not require huge adapter capacity to capture the useful signal. Sending only a few MB instead of several GB after updates can make a massive difference in both bandwidth and iteration speed. Would be really interested to see more details on how the bucket/proxy setup behaves at scale and whether there are any noticeable trade-offs once the number of inference workers or concurrent rollouts increases.

#9955. Microsoft Links Storm-0940 to ConnectWise Supply Chain Attack

The China-linked actor used an AI-enabled penetration-testing tool to automate and accelerate its attack on more than 2,200 tenants.

A China-linked threat actor that Microsoft tracks as Storm-0940 used an agentic AI penetration-testing framework to accelerate a supply chain attack involving ConnectWise Cloud Backup.

The attackers used compromised application credentials associated with the service to attempt to access the Microsoft 365 environments of more than 2,250 downstream customer tenants. In multiple instances, the attackers obtained privileged access to an organization’s cloud infrastructure in less than three hours after initial targeting, Microsoft said in an analysis published this week.

The activity demonstrates how threat actors are integrating agentic AI into existing offensive security workflows and scaling their operations exponentially, Microsoft researchers wrote. "While the majority of the targeting wasn't successful, Storm-0940 achieved privileged cloud persistence at many organizations in a brief time," they said.

Related:One Compromised Laptop, Billions Lost: The Binance Attack-Path Warning

ConnectWise provides software and IT management technology that managed service providers use to deliver a broad range of services to their customers, including backup and recovery for Microsoft 365 data. Delivering these services requires the company to have authorized application access to customer Microsoft 365 environments to back up and restore data.

On Oct. 16, ConnectWise disclosed unauthorized access to application identities associated with its Cloud Backup product. The company subsequently published additional details and containment guidance but has not publicly explained how the attackers initially gained control of the application identities.

Microsoft described the incident as part of a broader Storm-0940 campaign that began as early as September and targeted hundreds of organizations worldwide across several industries including manufacturing, aerospace, chemicals, energy, defense, and financial services. The threat actor has been using an AI penetration-testing framework called ARTEX to automate and accelerate its operations.

"In multiple affected environments, Microsoft observed AI-accelerated follow-on activity through Microsoft Graph, including reconnaissance, application credential changes, and attempts to modify privileges that could enable expanded or persistent access," Microsoft said.

In the ConnectWise incident, Storm-0940 used ARTEX to accelerate reconnaissance and scanning, password spraying, and OAuth application abuse. The threat actor used ARTEX to attempt sign-ins to more than 2,250 tenants, generating as many as 2,900 sign-in attempts per minute. That pace left defenders with little time to detect and respond to the activity, Microsoft noted.

Related:Microsoft's AI Risk Report Misses This Key Detail

"Storm-0940's activity illustrates how a threat actor with a broad target set can use an agentic AI tool and privileged authentication material to quickly attempt to compromise many organizations," the company said.

ConnectWise suspended its Cloud Backup service and also took its SaaS Security and Cloud Management services offline following the incident. In an Oct. 22 update, the company noted it was continuing work on restoring disrupted services and urged customers to keep affected ConnectWise application connections offline until further notice.

"Investigation and monitoring continue alongside restoration. Existing backup archives remain encrypted, isolated and preserved, with no indication of compromise," the company said. ConnectWise called on customers to review their individual Microsoft 365 environments using the company's technical investigation and remediation guide and related information.

Microsoft meanwhile highlighted its own mitigation and protection guidance, which included recommendations like reviewing every Microsoft 365 tenant that might have been tied to ConnectWise and to preserve logs and other forensic evidence before making any changes.

Related:PapRAT Cyber-Espionage Campaign Leaves a 'Bitter' Taste in South Asia

Ross Filipek, CISO at Corsica Technologies, says that before reconnecting with ConnectWise, affected organizations should have a clear understanding of what might have happened inside their environment. He pointed to Microsoft's discovery of application credential changes that could give attackers a way back in to compromised environments. Organizations are going to need to investigate whether their Microsoft 365 environments are safe before they reconnect, he says.

"Keep affected connections disabled in line with vendor guidance. Investigate unauthorized changes that could leave another way in. Preserve evidence without delaying containment," Filipek tells Dark Reading. "There's also an immediate business question: Are backups still running? Assign someone on each side to check coverage during the interruption. A restored connection needs verification that backup jobs are completing and recovery works."

Going forward, organizations need to have a recovery plan that takes into account the potential of their losing access to a service that they normally would depend on for recovery, Filipek adds. Incident responders should know which applications connect to the organization's Microsoft 365 tenant and how to quickly sever those connections when necessary, and exercise that scenario with their service provider.

"Establish who checks backup coverage during containment and who decides whether the business can tolerate the interruption. Leaving those responsibilities implied is how both sides end up assuming the other has checked," he says.

Jon Baker, vice president of threat-informed defense at AttackIQ, wants affected organizations to preserve sign-in and audit records and to investigate application sign-ins, Microsoft Graph activity, new credentials, privilege changes, and unusual data access. "Remove confirmed unauthorized access and verify vendor and tenant remediation separately," he advises. "After containment, controlled validation can test whether comparable application behavior can still reach sensitive resources or establish another foothold."

InfoQ Homepage News Kubernetes Confidential Containers Get Fortanix Attestation and Key Management

Oct 31, 2026 2 min read

Fortanix has announced support for Confidential Containers in its Confidential AI platform. The integration connects Kubernetes workload attestation to encryption-key release, so workloads that meet security policy can decrypt models and sensitive data inside hardware-based trusted execution environments (TEEs).

Confidential Containers (CoCo), a Cloud Native Computing Foundation project, runs Kubernetes pods inside confidential virtual machines backed by hardware-based trusted execution environments (TEEs). Unlike ordinary containers, whose isolation depends largely on the host operating system, confidential VMs use hardware protections to encrypt memory and restrict access to the workload while it runs. This helps protect data in use, not just data at rest or in transit, and can let teams run sensitive workloads on shared infrastructure. Those protections still depend on trusting the guest software and configuring attestation and key release correctly.

Fortanix's technical overview describes plugins connecting CoCo workloads to two services: Confidential Computing Manager (CCM), which verifies the environment, and Data Security Manager (DSM), which releases keys only to environments CCM has verified. The company says CCM can attest the processor and graphics processing unit (GPU) together, a check that depends on configuration.

CoCo moves image pulling and unpacking into the confidential guest. Its Attestation Agent collects hardware evidence, and its Confidential Data Hub obtains secrets after verification. In Fortanix's described workflow, keys stay in DSM if attestation fails, so the workload cannot decrypt protected models or data.

Fortanix chief product officer Anuj Jaiswal said in the announcement: "With attestation and key management in one platform, teams can adopt standard CoCo without building the trust layer themselves." Fortanix says CCM and DSM run clustered, with 24x7 support, as a hosted service, on-premises or air-gapped.

Fortanix's Intel TDX deployment guide offers two GPU settings: Required makes CCM validate GPU evidence through NVIDIA's attestation service; Ignored checks only that evidence is present and disregards the result. The guide also notes that the Fortanix CoCo Helm chart does not configure host firmware or kernel settings, which must be completed beforehand.

Attestation and conditional secret delivery already exist in CoCo's open-source Trustee components. Trustee separates evidence appraisal from resource authorisation. Its attestation service compares platform claims with reference values, then its Key Broker Service applies a user-defined policy before releasing secrets from local storage, a plugin or an external key store. A successful attestation still requires that policy to authorise the request. Trustee also accepts GPU evidence bound to the processor's attestation report.

Microsoft's Azure Secure Key Release offers a managed alternative in Key Vault Premium and Managed HSM, integrated with Azure Attestation. It releases exportable keys, not secrets or certificates.

The pod's guest kernel and helper processes sit inside the trust boundary, so teams must trust them too. CoCo's trust model explains that hardware measurements usually cover the guest environment, with container verification forming a separate stage. It also warns that an enclave application can still expose a dangerous external interface and excludes denial-of-service protection and hardware side channels. Attestation does not establish that an AI application handles data safely.

Fortanix says CoCo support is available now, and its deployment guide documents installing the Fortanix CoCo Helm chart. The announcement also says Fortanix is developing open-source plugins for CoCo, without naming repositories or versions. CCM's 17 September release notes added CoCo application registration for AMD Secure Encrypted Virtualization-Secure Nested Paging (SEV-SNP) and Intel Trust Domain Extensions (TDX).

#9953. Your Agent Aced the Task. Will It Do It Again?

Your agent works in rehearsal, but during the live demo, it takes a different path and fails the same task.

That is embarrassing onstage. In production, it is a reliability problem: a workflow that succeeded once may fail the next time a user makes the same request. For mission-critical work, such as reconciling a financial transaction or checking a contract for an obligation, that can be a showstopper.

Most benchmarks hide this variability behind an average. On AppWorld, a ReAct agent using GPT-4.1 succeeded on 77.4% of runs across five repetitions. But it succeeded in all five runs for only 53.0% of tasks — a 24.4-point consistency gap.

Most benchmarks report the first number. We built a way to measure the second — and improve it.

In an earlier post, we introduced ALTK-Evolve — a system that turns an agent's own past trajectories into reusable guidelines, distilled automatically and injected back at inference time. It measurably improves task success, but those results only asked the average-case question too. This post introduces consistency guidelines, a new guideline type in altk-evolve built on top of a diagnostic tool we call the Consistency Analyzer, that targets this gap directly.

Standard agent evaluation reports Mean@k: run a benchmark k times, average the pass rate. Often k=3, sometimes just 1. It's the number on every leaderboard, and it's what "77% accurate" means in practice.

Mean@k answers "how good is this agent, on average?" It does not answer the question a real user cares about: will it still be good if I ask this exact question again? For that you need Pass^k: the fraction of tasks where the agent succeeds on all k runs.

⚠️ Pass^k is not Pass@k. The familiar Pass@k is optimistic — it asks whether at least one of k attempts succeeded, the right question when you can verify and retry. Pass^k is its pessimistic mirror image: every attempt must succeed. Same letters, opposite question. Pass^k ≤ Mean@k ≤ Pass@k, always.

A ReAct agent backed by GPT-4.1 posts a Mean@5 of 77.4% — genuinely strong. But Pass^5 is only 53.0%. Nearly a quarter of the benchmark consists of tasks the agent can sometimes solve and sometimes can't, with nothing about the task changing between runs. We call this gap — Mean@k minus Pass^k — the consistency gap.

This isn't a capability problem you fix with a bigger model. It's an orthogonal axis: an agent can be capable and inconsistent at the same time.

Every time an LLM agent decides something — which API to call, what argument to pass, whether to retry — that decision comes out of a probability distribution over next tokens. What matters is the shape of that distribution. A sharp one puts most of its mass on a single token: the runners-up are far behind, and the same choice comes out run after run. A flat one spreads comparable mass across several near-tied tokens, and which one wins is close to a coin flip.

The shape decides how much noise it takes to change the outcome. Sharp distributions are resilient — GPU floating-point non-associativity, request batching, and other platform-side effects nudge the numbers slightly, but nowhere near enough to reorder a clear winner. Flat distributions are vulnerable to exactly that nudge: near-ties may reorder under small perturbations. And because a trajectory chains dozens of decisions, a small per-step chance of flipping compounds into a large chance that some run goes differently. That's where a 24-point gap comes from.

This is also why the problem survives your decoding settings. Greedy decoding and a fixed seed both govern how a distribution gets turned into a token — they say nothing about the distribution itself. On a hosted endpoint the probabilities shift slightly from run to run, so the same prompt to the same model at temperature zero can still resolve a near-tie one way today and the other way tomorrow.

Our setup: the ReAct agent runs at temperature 0.0, so none of the variance above is ordinary sampling.

Which turns the problem into a search: which steps in a given trajectory were the flat ones — and what do you do about them once you know?

Consistency guidelines come out of a two-stage pipeline that plugs into ALTK-Evolve's existing machinery — with a new source signal driving what gets written.

1. Detect — the Consistency Analyzer. Given one recorded trajectory, the analyzer replays each decision step through controlled resampling, measuring how much the model's output actually varies at that point. Concretely, that's one additional model call per decision step, done once offline — issued with the sampling parameter set to draw k completions at once (k=5 by default) — replayed against the already-recorded context, not new tool calls, not new environment interactions, and not a second end-to-end rollout of the task. This yields a consistency score per decision step that is written into a scorecard to pinpoint exactly which decisions are at risk of flipping on the next run. Detection is fully black-box — no logits, no model internals, no instrumentation beyond the trace you already have.

2. Generate — targeted guidelines. Every flagged step becomes a candidate consistency guideline in the standard ALTK-Evolve format, so it slots into the existing storage and retrieval pipeline. Here's a real example, generated by GPT-4.1 from a trajectory of the AppWorld task "How many activities are done in my bucket list as per my SimpleNote note?":

[Guideline 1] When counting checkbox-style markers in note content, use a line-anchored regex match rather than a plain substring count — note titles often repeat the marker symbol in a legend line.

[Guideline 2] Always verify search results for note queries by checking for multiple matches and confirming the correct note before proceeding.

Nothing here is task-specific trivia. String-counting bugs and unverified search results are decision points that show up with high uncertainty across many AppWorld tasks. That's the point: the analyzer targets instability, not failure — so it catches steps the agent happened to get right this time but could easily get wrong next time.

Watch the 2-minute demo — five parallel runs of the agent split 3-2 on this task because of agent uncertainty about the counting strategy, then run again after these guidelines in context: all five agree.

We evaluated on AppWorld test_normal (168 tasks) with a ReAct agent on GPT-4.1, generating consistency guidelines from a single baseline trajectory per task and testing them on 5 fresh runs.

Mean@5 (%), aggregate — same scale as Pass^5 above.

The consistency gap is cut roughly in half. Aggregate Pass^5 rises 53.0% → 69.0% while Mean@5 rises 77.4% → 81.0%, narrowing the gap between "looks capable" and "can be counted on" from 24.4pp to 12.0pp. Nearly a third of previously-inconsistent tasks become tasks the agent passes on every single run.

The middle and hard tiers gain most. Medium +22.9pp (+44% relative), Hard +14.3pp (+45% relative) — effectively tied in relative terms, with Medium ahead absolutely. Easy gains +12.2pp, having had the least room. This is consistency guidelines doing what they're designed to do: finding and stabilizing the specific decision points where an agent's own uncertainty was leaking into the outcome.

Mean@5 never drops. Preserving average accuracy was a hard requirement, not a nice-to-have: a system that boosts Pass^5 by trading away Mean@5 would just be shifting unreliability around, not fixing it. Mean accuracy holds or improves at every difficulty level.

Applied to a different but related task in the same AppWorld scenario — another variant of the scenario the guidelines were mined from — consistency guidelines still lift Pass^5 by +13.0pp, only 3 points below the same-task number. A guideline derived from one run isn't just patching that run; it's capturing something that transfers.

The sharper evidence comes from a weaker model, gpt-oss-120b. Same-task Pass^5 rose +6.0pp from a much lower baseline (10.1% → 16.1%) — and, interestingly, the similar-task generalization number (+8.7 pp) actually exceeded the same-task gain, suggesting the guidelines were capturing genuinely reusable failure patterns rather than memorizing one trajectory's specifics.

Try the ALTK-Evolve — the open-source repo now includes the Consistency Analyzer and consistency-guideline generation used in these experiments — or read the technical report on arXiv for the complete methodology.

If accuracy numbers you can't reproduce on your own tasks sound familiar, we'd like to hear about it — concrete examples of flip-prone behavior in your own agents are exactly the kind of feedback that shapes what we build next. Open an issue or a discussion.

Great perspective on agent reliability. Measuring consistency alongside accuracy seems especially important as AI agents move into workflows where reproducibility matters. The Consistency Analyzer approach is a fascinating way to identify unstable decisions without requiring full task replays.

The useful split is the one most dashboards still refuse to print: Mean@k answers “how good is this agent on average?” Pass^k answers “will the same request still succeed if I ask again?”

Once you’ve watched a trajectory chain dozens of near-tied tool choices, a strong average with a wide consistency gap is exactly the demo that fails live. Capability and consistency are orthogonal — buying a bigger model can lift Mean without closing the gap.

What I want teams to take from the Consistency Analyzer framing is operational, not the guideline machinery itself: treat flip-prone decision steps as first-class eval targets. One offline resample pass over a recorded trace is a cheaper reliability signal than another end-to-end leaderboard screenshot.

Practical ask for anyone shipping agents from this: do you report Pass^k (even k=3) next to Mean@k in the release gate, and do you refuse the “stable” label when the consistency gap is still large on your hard tier?

Reproducible reliability will not remove disagreement about which guidelines to inject. It will make the disagreement about the right metric.

Thanks, and you've landed on exactly the operational takeaway we hoped for: flip-prone decision steps should be eval targets in their own right. Beyond that, knowing where they are also turns the eval into a diagnostic: a consistency gap tells you that an agent is unreliable, while the flip-prone steps tell you where and why.

On your release-gate question: we'd strongly encourage it, and k=3 is a sensible default. A few things we'd suggest to anyone adopting Pass^k as a gate:

I'd like to understand your closing point better. In our experiments, we didn't choose among individual guidelines: for each new task, we injected the guidelines derived from the most similar task. I'm curious where you see the disagreement about which guidelines to inject arising.
