There was absolutely no way to enter the correct settings menu without a navigation SD card inserted. In fact, the menu definition pointing to the Settings applet was read from the SD card itself, and without one inserted containing the right menu definition, the unit didn't even know how to enter the Settings applet.This decision by TomTom (or Renault) is still baffling to me.What made things worse was that this needed to be a legitimate SD card. This would run the rootfs /bin/sh and execute our script with it as root.Being able to execute arbitrary binaries also turned out to be useful even without arguments, since I needed to somehow get a program to crash, triggering a coredump. Using a DoS vuln to crash the script parser or the main UI itself wouldn't work very well, because this would immediately trigger a reboot of the whole system, killing my script.I used my emulator setup to execute pretty much every single binary on the system, and found that /bin/dbus-monitor raised a SIGABRT if it couldn't connect to the system bus (which the unit didn't run), triggering a coredump. This was perfect.Putting it togetherMy final master.script turned out to be quite simple:#define LOGFILE ../../proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern LOG |/bin/sh /media/sdcard/payload.sh SHEX /bin/dbus-monitorI initially confirmed success by simply calling reboot in the payload.sh script. I was very pleasantly surprised when booting the unit with the SD card inserted and pressing "Yes" at the "Execute master.script?" prompt, the unit rebooted, confirming that I had code execution.The first thing I did was use this to create a full backup of the internal eMMC using dd. With a more complete dump of the system, I pretty quickly figured out that the date & time settings that I'm interested in are in /mnt/flash/settings.dat, which is a custom binary format. After some more reverse engineering, I figured out the exact offset in the file which held the currently set timezone, and wrote a script to patch it to be UTC+2.That is how I was finally able to fix my car's timezone.

This decision by TomTom (or Renault) is still baffling to me.What made things worse was that this needed to be a legitimate SD card. The system had DRM checks which rejected SD cards without the correct CID (a unique ID burned into the card) and files with signatures based on that specific CID, so I couldn't even copy the files to a blank SD card. I'm guessing the DRM was in place to prevent people from pirating maps.I don't want maps. I have a phone that I use for navigation. I just want to change the damn time.I checked online and found some third parties selling the card I presumably needed, but with shipping to Estonia, it would've cost me roughly 60 EUR, which I really didn't feel like paying.Fine. I'll just root it and do it myself.Easy wins?I couldn't find anyone online who'd jailbroken one of these before. I found some old forum threads with long-expired image links that had some pretty generic information about the unit itself and the general consensus was that it was difficult to root.I didn't expect a Linux 2.6 system from 2011 to be incredibly hard to hack, so I naively went in looking for some easy wins.My first idea was to modify the ext3 update image itself. It seemed like I could easily just mount the filesystem, modify some init scripts to do what I want, and copy it to a blank SD card for the unit to pick up my modified image and flash it.While the system showed confirmation prompts to install vanilla, unmodified ttsystem images with no problem, I could never get it to update to my modified image, and I had no idea why. I checked the updater logic present in the update file itself and couldn't see any reason why my image would be rejected.It was at this point that I set up an emulator with QEMU, a custom kernel also based on the same 2.6 version, some patches and a very simple CAN emulator for the system to actually boot - albeit reluctantly, wanting to reboot every 3 seconds, which I just patched out by ignoring reboot syscalls.I used this to test installing the modified update image in there. I then realized that I don't actually have the recovery partition that the device boots into to perform the update, and came to the conclusion that there must be some sort of verification layer there that I'm missing.Taking a closer look at the ttsystem image also pretty much confirmed this, as it had a bunch of high-entropy data appended to it, followed by some zero blocks, followed by 40 high-entropy bytes. I assumed this was a signature of some sort (40 bytes could be DSA with SHA-1), but with no access to the actual binary doing the verification, I couldn't really figure out how to attack this or if I even could.Back to the drawing boardI'd been reluctant to put the effort into building the emulator, but it turned out to be extremely useful for testing out various attacks and getting an overview of how the system behaved.For example, I found out that most partitions were mounted either read-only, noexec or both. Mounts from a live system:rootfs on / type rootfs (rw) none on /sys type sysfs (rw,nosuid,noexec) none on /proc type proc (rw,nosuid,noexec) /dev/mmcblk0p5 on /content type ext3 (rw,nosuid,nodev,noexec,noatime,nodiratime,errors=continue,data=ordered) /dev/loop0 on / type ext2 (ro,noatime,nodiratime,errors=continue) none on /dev type tmpfs (rw,nosuid,noexec,size=1024k) none on /tmp type tmpfs (rw,nosuid,noexec,size=2048k) none on /var type tmpfs (rw,nosuid,noexec,size=5120k) none on /dev/pts type devpts (rw,nosuid,noexec,gid=5,mode=620) none on /var/log type tmpfs (rw,nosuid,noexec,size=1024k) /dev/mmcblk0p3 on /mnt/flash type ext3 (rw,sync,nosuid,nodev,noexec,errors=continue,data=ordered) /dev/mmcblk1p1 on /media/sdcard type vfat (rw,sync,nosuid,nodev,noexec,noatime,nodiratime,fmask=0022,dmask=0022,codepage=cp437,iocharset=iso8859-1) /dev/loop1 on /media/loopback type ext3 (rw,nosuid,nodev,noexec,noatime,nodiratime,errors=continue,commit=3600,data=journal) none on /mnt/movi type unionfs (rw,nosuid,nodev,noexec,noatime,nodiratime,dirs=/media/loopback=rw:/media/sdcard=ro)Notably, the base FAT32 filesystem of the SD card was mounted to /media/sdcard, and the system mounted a unionfs on top of it in /mnt/movi, which had a writable layer pointing to an ext3 filesystem which lived as a file on the external SD. I'm not 100% sure what the point of this setup was (maybe so they can use data=journal, which survives power loss better?), but nevertheless all of these mounts were noexec.This seemed like surprisingly strong security for something from 2011.Something else that the emulator helped me with was identifying all of the files that the system tried to read from the external SD card. One of these files was master.script, a script in a custom language for automating certain UI navigation actions. This was loaded every boot and I hoped this would allow me to somehow open the correct settings menu for setting the time.I reversed ttn, the binary responsible for parsing this script, documenting its functionality as I went, but unfortunately I didn't find any way to open the menu I needed.More wild goose chasesI still thought master.script was what I should be putting my effort into, since it had a lot of functionality that could be a potential attack vector.As usual, I checked for any system or popen calls that would allow me to perform command injection. Unfortunately, I didn't find any constructed with user input.I thought I had hit the jackpot when, while reversing the parser, I came across a SHEX/SHELLEXECUTE command. It passed an arbitrary argument to launchserver, which launched whatever command line was provided with execve.This had two obstacles. The first one was that there was still no way to get it to execute a custom executable directly, as the SD card was mounted noexec which prevents executables and scripts on it from running. However, this could be bypassed by not executing the script directly, but rather executing something like /bin/sh /media/sdcard/payload.sh, which would go through /bin/sh on the rootfs, which was not mounted noexec.The second hurdle was bigger, however. It turned out that while launchserver would happily launch anything, SHEX accepts only a single whitespace-delimited token. This means that I could only control which binary was executed, but not pass it any arguments. Combined with the previous obstacle, this then also seemed like a dead end because I could only run scripts or binaries that were already on the rootfs. I did look through most of them, but nothing seemed very helpful.Defeated, I started looking at file writes. Maybe if I could write files to places I shouldn't be able to, that would give me some sort of leverage.Sure enough, I discovered the LOG command, which let me truncate a file (defined with #define LOGFILE log.txt) and write a single line to a file of my choosing. This one actually allowed spaces and regular ASCII characters, but only bytes 0x20 to 0x7E, meaning writing binary data is out of the question. As ttn runs as root, any writes would also be written as root.It also had a classic path traversal vulnerability. Defining LOGFILE with ../ in it allowed me to write outside the intended logfile directory, theoretically allowing me to write printable ASCII to anywhere on the system.However, I once again ran into a wall with how the mount points were set up. I couldn't overwrite anything on the rootfs since it was mounted read-only, and everything else was mounted noexec and would never be executed anyways. I also looked into whether there were any useful config files I could overwrite, but most files were a custom binary format that I couldn't write with LOG or were otherwise unhelpful. This also looked like a dead end.Among other things, master.script allowed displaying images on the screen (GIFs/BMPs). I spent some time setting up a fuzzing environment using Unicorn to see if I could hit any image decoder bugs causing memory corruption, and while I did get quite a few OOB reads, I didn't find any useful writes.Borrowing a trick from kernel exploitsI had been researching, reverse engineering and trying to come up with different strategies to run arbitrary code for a while. Much to my frustration, none of my strategies ended up working, and I took a step back to look at the bigger picture and figure out if I can make any of the puzzle pieces that I already have fit together.Among other things, I knew I could:Execute arbitrary binaries, but with no arguments and only the ones already on the rootfsWrite ASCII to paths of my own choosingThis is when I had a brainwave and was reminded of a trick that kernel exploits often use: Instead of trying to get the userland to execute our script, why don't I get the kernel to execute our script instead?Often, Linux kernel exploits, when being able to write arbitrary memory, overwrite the core_pattern string. Normally, this dictates how coredumps are stored when a process crashes, but it also accepts special syntax for piping these coredumps to a process instead (|/bin/my-coredump-handler). When a crash occurs, the kernel spawns the process specified in core_pattern and pipes the data in there.core_pattern also supports cmdline arguments for the spawned process. I got lucky here, since support for this landed in 2.6.24 whereas the unit's kernel was 2.6.28.Importantly, you're also able to set core_pattern from userland by writing the pattern to /proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern.I can easily use this to point LOGFILE to ../../proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern and LOG the string |/bin/sh /media/sdcard/payload.sh. This would run the rootfs /bin/sh and execute our script with it as root.Being able to execute arbitrary binaries also turned out to be useful even without arguments, since I needed to somehow get a program to crash, triggering a coredump. Using a DoS vuln to crash the script parser or the main UI itself wouldn't work very well, because this would immediately trigger a reboot of the whole system, killing my script.I used my emulator setup to execute pretty much every single binary on the system, and found that /bin/dbus-monitor raised a SIGABRT if it couldn't connect to the system bus (which the unit didn't run), triggering a coredump. This was perfect.Putting it togetherMy final master.script turned out to be quite simple:#define LOGFILE ../../proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern LOG |/bin/sh /media/sdcard/payload.sh SHEX /bin/dbus-monitorI initially confirmed success by simply calling reboot in the payload.sh script. I was very pleasantly surprised when booting the unit with the SD card inserted and pressing "Yes" at the "Execute master.script?" prompt, the unit rebooted, confirming that I had code execution.The first thing I did was use this to create a full backup of the internal eMMC using dd. With a more complete dump of the system, I pretty quickly figured out that the date & time settings that I'm interested in are in /mnt/flash/settings.dat, which is a custom binary format. After some more reverse engineering, I figured out the exact offset in the file which held the currently set timezone, and wrote a script to patch it to be UTC+2.That is how I was finally able to fix my car's timezone.

Normally, this dictates how coredumps are stored when a process crashes, but it also accepts special syntax for piping these coredumps to a process instead (|/bin/my-coredump-handler). When a crash occurs, the kernel spawns the process specified in core_pattern and pipes the data in there.core_pattern also supports cmdline arguments for the spawned process. I got lucky here, since support for this landed in 2.6.24 whereas the unit's kernel was 2.6.28.Importantly, you're also able to set core_pattern from userland by writing the pattern to /proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern.I can easily use this to point LOGFILE to ../../proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern and LOG the string |/bin/sh /media/sdcard/payload.sh. This would run the rootfs /bin/sh and execute our script with it as root.Being able to execute arbitrary binaries also turned out to be useful even without arguments, since I needed to somehow get a program to crash, triggering a coredump. Using a DoS vuln to crash the script parser or the main UI itself wouldn't work very well, because this would immediately trigger a reboot of the whole system, killing my script.I used my emulator setup to execute pretty much every single binary on the system, and found that /bin/dbus-monitor raised a SIGABRT if it couldn't connect to the system bus (which the unit didn't run), triggering a coredump. This was perfect.Putting it togetherMy final master.script turned out to be quite simple:#define LOGFILE ../../proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern LOG |/bin/sh /media/sdcard/payload.sh SHEX /bin/dbus-monitorI initially confirmed success by simply calling reboot in the payload.sh script. I was very pleasantly surprised when booting the unit with the SD card inserted and pressing "Yes" at the "Execute master.script?" prompt, the unit rebooted, confirming that I had code execution.The first thing I did was use this to create a full backup of the internal eMMC using dd. With a more complete dump of the system, I pretty quickly figured out that the date & time settings that I'm interested in are in /mnt/flash/settings.dat, which is a custom binary format. After some more reverse engineering, I figured out the exact offset in the file which held the currently set timezone, and wrote a script to patch it to be UTC+2.That is how I was finally able to fix my car's timezone.

I checked online and found some third parties selling the card I presumably needed, but with shipping to Estonia, it would've cost me roughly 60 EUR, which I really didn't feel like paying.Fine. I'll just root it and do it myself.Easy wins?I couldn't find anyone online who'd jailbroken one of these before. I found some old forum threads with long-expired image links that had some pretty generic information about the unit itself and the general consensus was that it was difficult to root.I didn't expect a Linux 2.6 system from 2011 to be incredibly hard to hack, so I naively went in looking for some easy wins.My first idea was to modify the ext3 update image itself. It seemed like I could easily just mount the filesystem, modify some init scripts to do what I want, and copy it to a blank SD card for the unit to pick up my modified image and flash it.While the system showed confirmation prompts to install vanilla, unmodified ttsystem images with no problem, I could never get it to update to my modified image, and I had no idea why. I checked the updater logic present in the update file itself and couldn't see any reason why my image would be rejected.It was at this point that I set up an emulator with QEMU, a custom kernel also based on the same 2.6 version, some patches and a very simple CAN emulator for the system to actually boot - albeit reluctantly, wanting to reboot every 3 seconds, which I just patched out by ignoring reboot syscalls.I used this to test installing the modified update image in there. I then realized that I don't actually have the recovery partition that the device boots into to perform the update, and came to the conclusion that there must be some sort of verification layer there that I'm missing.Taking a closer look at the ttsystem image also pretty much confirmed this, as it had a bunch of high-entropy data appended to it, followed by some zero blocks, followed by 40 high-entropy bytes. I assumed this was a signature of some sort (40 bytes could be DSA with SHA-1), but with no access to the actual binary doing the verification, I couldn't really figure out how to attack this or if I even could.Back to the drawing boardI'd been reluctant to put the effort into building the emulator, but it turned out to be extremely useful for testing out various attacks and getting an overview of how the system behaved.For example, I found out that most partitions were mounted either read-only, noexec or both. Mounts from a live system:rootfs on / type rootfs (rw) none on /sys type sysfs (rw,nosuid,noexec) none on /proc type proc (rw,nosuid,noexec) /dev/mmcblk0p5 on /content type ext3 (rw,nosuid,nodev,noexec,noatime,nodiratime,errors=continue,data=ordered) /dev/loop0 on / type ext2 (ro,noatime,nodiratime,errors=continue) none on /dev type tmpfs (rw,nosuid,noexec,size=1024k) none on /tmp type tmpfs (rw,nosuid,noexec,size=2048k) none on /var type tmpfs (rw,nosuid,noexec,size=5120k) none on /dev/pts type devpts (rw,nosuid,noexec,gid=5,mode=620) none on /var/log type tmpfs (rw,nosuid,noexec,size=1024k) /dev/mmcblk0p3 on /mnt/flash type ext3 (rw,sync,nosuid,nodev,noexec,errors=continue,data=ordered) /dev/mmcblk1p1 on /media/sdcard type vfat (rw,sync,nosuid,nodev,noexec,noatime,nodiratime,fmask=0022,dmask=0022,codepage=cp437,iocharset=iso8859-1) /dev/loop1 on /media/loopback type ext3 (rw,nosuid,nodev,noexec,noatime,nodiratime,errors=continue,commit=3600,data=journal) none on /mnt/movi type unionfs (rw,nosuid,nodev,noexec,noatime,nodiratime,dirs=/media/loopback=rw:/media/sdcard=ro)Notably, the base FAT32 filesystem of the SD card was mounted to /media/sdcard, and the system mounted a unionfs on top of it in /mnt/movi, which had a writable layer pointing to an ext3 filesystem which lived as a file on the external SD. I'm not 100% sure what the point of this setup was (maybe so they can use data=journal, which survives power loss better?), but nevertheless all of these mounts were noexec.This seemed like surprisingly strong security for something from 2011.Something else that the emulator helped me with was identifying all of the files that the system tried to read from the external SD card. One of these files was master.script, a script in a custom language for automating certain UI navigation actions. This was loaded every boot and I hoped this would allow me to somehow open the correct settings menu for setting the time.I reversed ttn, the binary responsible for parsing this script, documenting its functionality as I went, but unfortunately I didn't find any way to open the menu I needed.More wild goose chasesI still thought master.script was what I should be putting my effort into, since it had a lot of functionality that could be a potential attack vector.As usual, I checked for any system or popen calls that would allow me to perform command injection. Unfortunately, I didn't find any constructed with user input.I thought I had hit the jackpot when, while reversing the parser, I came across a SHEX/SHELLEXECUTE command. It passed an arbitrary argument to launchserver, which launched whatever command line was provided with execve.This had two obstacles. The first one was that there was still no way to get it to execute a custom executable directly, as the SD card was mounted noexec which prevents executables and scripts on it from running. However, this could be bypassed by not executing the script directly, but rather executing something like /bin/sh /media/sdcard/payload.sh, which would go through /bin/sh on the rootfs, which was not mounted noexec.The second hurdle was bigger, however. It turned out that while launchserver would happily launch anything, SHEX accepts only a single whitespace-delimited token. This means that I could only control which binary was executed, but not pass it any arguments. Combined with the previous obstacle, this then also seemed like a dead end because I could only run scripts or binaries that were already on the rootfs. I did look through most of them, but nothing seemed very helpful.Defeated, I started looking at file writes. Maybe if I could write files to places I shouldn't be able to, that would give me some sort of leverage.Sure enough, I discovered the LOG command, which let me truncate a file (defined with #define LOGFILE log.txt) and write a single line to a file of my choosing. This one actually allowed spaces and regular ASCII characters, but only bytes 0x20 to 0x7E, meaning writing binary data is out of the question. As ttn runs as root, any writes would also be written as root.It also had a classic path traversal vulnerability. Defining LOGFILE with ../ in it allowed me to write outside the intended logfile directory, theoretically allowing me to write printable ASCII to anywhere on the system.However, I once again ran into a wall with how the mount points were set up. I couldn't overwrite anything on the rootfs since it was mounted read-only, and everything else was mounted noexec and would never be executed anyways. I also looked into whether there were any useful config files I could overwrite, but most files were a custom binary format that I couldn't write with LOG or were otherwise unhelpful. This also looked like a dead end.Among other things, master.script allowed displaying images on the screen (GIFs/BMPs). I spent some time setting up a fuzzing environment using Unicorn to see if I could hit any image decoder bugs causing memory corruption, and while I did get quite a few OOB reads, I didn't find any useful writes.Borrowing a trick from kernel exploitsI had been researching, reverse engineering and trying to come up with different strategies to run arbitrary code for a while. I got lucky here, since support for this landed in 2.6.24 whereas the unit's kernel was 2.6.28.Importantly, you're also able to set core_pattern from userland by writing the pattern to /proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern.I can easily use this to point LOGFILE to ../../proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern and LOG the string |/bin/sh /media/sdcard/payload.sh. This would run the rootfs /bin/sh and execute our script with it as root.Being able to execute arbitrary binaries also turned out to be useful even without arguments, since I needed to somehow get a program to crash, triggering a coredump. Using a DoS vuln to crash the script parser or the main UI itself wouldn't work very well, because this would immediately trigger a reboot of the whole system, killing my script.I used my emulator setup to execute pretty much every single binary on the system, and found that /bin/dbus-monitor raised a SIGABRT if it couldn't connect to the system bus (which the unit didn't run), triggering a coredump. This was perfect.Putting it togetherMy final master.script turned out to be quite simple:#define LOGFILE ../../proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern LOG |/bin/sh /media/sdcard/payload.sh SHEX /bin/dbus-monitorI initially confirmed success by simply calling reboot in the payload.sh script. I was very pleasantly surprised when booting the unit with the SD card inserted and pressing "Yes" at the "Execute master.script?" prompt, the unit rebooted, confirming that I had code execution.The first thing I did was use this to create a full backup of the internal eMMC using dd. With a more complete dump of the system, I pretty quickly figured out that the date & time settings that I'm interested in are in /mnt/flash/settings.dat, which is a custom binary format. After some more reverse engineering, I figured out the exact offset in the file which held the currently set timezone, and wrote a script to patch it to be UTC+2.That is how I was finally able to fix my car's timezone.

I didn't expect a Linux 2.6 system from 2011 to be incredibly hard to hack, so I naively went in looking for some easy wins.My first idea was to modify the ext3 update image itself. It seemed like I could easily just mount the filesystem, modify some init scripts to do what I want, and copy it to a blank SD card for the unit to pick up my modified image and flash it.While the system showed confirmation prompts to install vanilla, unmodified ttsystem images with no problem, I could never get it to update to my modified image, and I had no idea why. I checked the updater logic present in the update file itself and couldn't see any reason why my image would be rejected.It was at this point that I set up an emulator with QEMU, a custom kernel also based on the same 2.6 version, some patches and a very simple CAN emulator for the system to actually boot - albeit reluctantly, wanting to reboot every 3 seconds, which I just patched out by ignoring reboot syscalls.I used this to test installing the modified update image in there. I then realized that I don't actually have the recovery partition that the device boots into to perform the update, and came to the conclusion that there must be some sort of verification layer there that I'm missing.Taking a closer look at the ttsystem image also pretty much confirmed this, as it had a bunch of high-entropy data appended to it, followed by some zero blocks, followed by 40 high-entropy bytes. I assumed this was a signature of some sort (40 bytes could be DSA with SHA-1), but with no access to the actual binary doing the verification, I couldn't really figure out how to attack this or if I even could.Back to the drawing boardI'd been reluctant to put the effort into building the emulator, but it turned out to be extremely useful for testing out various attacks and getting an overview of how the system behaved.For example, I found out that most partitions were mounted either read-only, noexec or both. Mounts from a live system:rootfs on / type rootfs (rw) none on /sys type sysfs (rw,nosuid,noexec) none on /proc type proc (rw,nosuid,noexec) /dev/mmcblk0p5 on /content type ext3 (rw,nosuid,nodev,noexec,noatime,nodiratime,errors=continue,data=ordered) /dev/loop0 on / type ext2 (ro,noatime,nodiratime,errors=continue) none on /dev type tmpfs (rw,nosuid,noexec,size=1024k) none on /tmp type tmpfs (rw,nosuid,noexec,size=2048k) none on /var type tmpfs (rw,nosuid,noexec,size=5120k) none on /dev/pts type devpts (rw,nosuid,noexec,gid=5,mode=620) none on /var/log type tmpfs (rw,nosuid,noexec,size=1024k) /dev/mmcblk0p3 on /mnt/flash type ext3 (rw,sync,nosuid,nodev,noexec,errors=continue,data=ordered) /dev/mmcblk1p1 on /media/sdcard type vfat (rw,sync,nosuid,nodev,noexec,noatime,nodiratime,fmask=0022,dmask=0022,codepage=cp437,iocharset=iso8859-1) /dev/loop1 on /media/loopback type ext3 (rw,nosuid,nodev,noexec,noatime,nodiratime,errors=continue,commit=3600,data=journal) none on /mnt/movi type unionfs (rw,nosuid,nodev,noexec,noatime,nodiratime,dirs=/media/loopback=rw:/media/sdcard=ro)Notably, the base FAT32 filesystem of the SD card was mounted to /media/sdcard, and the system mounted a unionfs on top of it in /mnt/movi, which had a writable layer pointing to an ext3 filesystem which lived as a file on the external SD. I'm not 100% sure what the point of this setup was (maybe so they can use data=journal, which survives power loss better?), but nevertheless all of these mounts were noexec.This seemed like surprisingly strong security for something from 2011.Something else that the emulator helped me with was identifying all of the files that the system tried to read from the external SD card. One of these files was master.script, a script in a custom language for automating certain UI navigation actions. This was loaded every boot and I hoped this would allow me to somehow open the correct settings menu for setting the time.I reversed ttn, the binary responsible for parsing this script, documenting its functionality as I went, but unfortunately I didn't find any way to open the menu I needed.More wild goose chasesI still thought master.script was what I should be putting my effort into, since it had a lot of functionality that could be a potential attack vector.As usual, I checked for any system or popen calls that would allow me to perform command injection. Unfortunately, I didn't find any constructed with user input.I thought I had hit the jackpot when, while reversing the parser, I came across a SHEX/SHELLEXECUTE command. It passed an arbitrary argument to launchserver, which launched whatever command line was provided with execve.This had two obstacles. The first one was that there was still no way to get it to execute a custom executable directly, as the SD card was mounted noexec which prevents executables and scripts on it from running. However, this could be bypassed by not executing the script directly, but rather executing something like /bin/sh /media/sdcard/payload.sh, which would go through /bin/sh on the rootfs, which was not mounted noexec.The second hurdle was bigger, however. It turned out that while launchserver would happily launch anything, SHEX accepts only a single whitespace-delimited token. This means that I could only control which binary was executed, but not pass it any arguments. Combined with the previous obstacle, this then also seemed like a dead end because I could only run scripts or binaries that were already on the rootfs. I did look through most of them, but nothing seemed very helpful.Defeated, I started looking at file writes. Maybe if I could write files to places I shouldn't be able to, that would give me some sort of leverage.Sure enough, I discovered the LOG command, which let me truncate a file (defined with #define LOGFILE log.txt) and write a single line to a file of my choosing. This one actually allowed spaces and regular ASCII characters, but only bytes 0x20 to 0x7E, meaning writing binary data is out of the question. As ttn runs as root, any writes would also be written as root.It also had a classic path traversal vulnerability. Defining LOGFILE with ../ in it allowed me to write outside the intended logfile directory, theoretically allowing me to write printable ASCII to anywhere on the system.However, I once again ran into a wall with how the mount points were set up. I couldn't overwrite anything on the rootfs since it was mounted read-only, and everything else was mounted noexec and would never be executed anyways. I also looked into whether there were any useful config files I could overwrite, but most files were a custom binary format that I couldn't write with LOG or were otherwise unhelpful. This also looked like a dead end.Among other things, master.script allowed displaying images on the screen (GIFs/BMPs). I spent some time setting up a fuzzing environment using Unicorn to see if I could hit any image decoder bugs causing memory corruption, and while I did get quite a few OOB reads, I didn't find any useful writes.Borrowing a trick from kernel exploitsI had been researching, reverse engineering and trying to come up with different strategies to run arbitrary code for a while. Much to my frustration, none of my strategies ended up working, and I took a step back to look at the bigger picture and figure out if I can make any of the puzzle pieces that I already have fit together.Among other things, I knew I could:Execute arbitrary binaries, but with no arguments and only the ones already on the rootfsWrite ASCII to paths of my own choosingThis is when I had a brainwave and was reminded of a trick that kernel exploits often use: Instead of trying to get the userland to execute our script, why don't I get the kernel to execute our script instead?Often, Linux kernel exploits, when being able to write arbitrary memory, overwrite the core_pattern string. Normally, this dictates how coredumps are stored when a process crashes, but it also accepts special syntax for piping these coredumps to a process instead (|/bin/my-coredump-handler). This would run the rootfs /bin/sh and execute our script with it as root.Being able to execute arbitrary binaries also turned out to be useful even without arguments, since I needed to somehow get a program to crash, triggering a coredump. I then realized that I don't actually have the recovery partition that the device boots into to perform the update, and came to the conclusion that there must be some sort of verification layer there that I'm missing.Taking a closer look at the ttsystem image also pretty much confirmed this, as it had a bunch of high-entropy data appended to it, followed by some zero blocks, followed by 40 high-entropy bytes. I assumed this was a signature of some sort (40 bytes could be DSA with SHA-1), but with no access to the actual binary doing the verification, I couldn't really figure out how to attack this or if I even could.Back to the drawing boardI'd been reluctant to put the effort into building the emulator, but it turned out to be extremely useful for testing out various attacks and getting an overview of how the system behaved.For example, I found out that most partitions were mounted either read-only, noexec or both. Mounts from a live system:rootfs on / type rootfs (rw) none on /sys type sysfs (rw,nosuid,noexec) none on /proc type proc (rw,nosuid,noexec) /dev/mmcblk0p5 on /content type ext3 (rw,nosuid,nodev,noexec,noatime,nodiratime,errors=continue,data=ordered) /dev/loop0 on / type ext2 (ro,noatime,nodiratime,errors=continue) none on /dev type tmpfs (rw,nosuid,noexec,size=1024k) none on /tmp type tmpfs (rw,nosuid,noexec,size=2048k) none on /var type tmpfs (rw,nosuid,noexec,size=5120k) none on /dev/pts type devpts (rw,nosuid,noexec,gid=5,mode=620) none on /var/log type tmpfs (rw,nosuid,noexec,size=1024k) /dev/mmcblk0p3 on /mnt/flash type ext3 (rw,sync,nosuid,nodev,noexec,errors=continue,data=ordered) /dev/mmcblk1p1 on /media/sdcard type vfat (rw,sync,nosuid,nodev,noexec,noatime,nodiratime,fmask=0022,dmask=0022,codepage=cp437,iocharset=iso8859-1) /dev/loop1 on /media/loopback type ext3 (rw,nosuid,nodev,noexec,noatime,nodiratime,errors=continue,commit=3600,data=journal) none on /mnt/movi type unionfs (rw,nosuid,nodev,noexec,noatime,nodiratime,dirs=/media/loopback=rw:/media/sdcard=ro)Notably, the base FAT32 filesystem of the SD card was mounted to /media/sdcard, and the system mounted a unionfs on top of it in /mnt/movi, which had a writable layer pointing to an ext3 filesystem which lived as a file on the external SD. I'm not 100% sure what the point of this setup was (maybe so they can use data=journal, which survives power loss better?), but nevertheless all of these mounts were noexec.This seemed like surprisingly strong security for something from 2011.Something else that the emulator helped me with was identifying all of the files that the system tried to read from the external SD card. One of these files was master.script, a script in a custom language for automating certain UI navigation actions. This was loaded every boot and I hoped this would allow me to somehow open the correct settings menu for setting the time.I reversed ttn, the binary responsible for parsing this script, documenting its functionality as I went, but unfortunately I didn't find any way to open the menu I needed.More wild goose chasesI still thought master.script was what I should be putting my effort into, since it had a lot of functionality that could be a potential attack vector.As usual, I checked for any system or popen calls that would allow me to perform command injection. Unfortunately, I didn't find any constructed with user input.I thought I had hit the jackpot when, while reversing the parser, I came across a SHEX/SHELLEXECUTE command. It passed an arbitrary argument to launchserver, which launched whatever command line was provided with execve.This had two obstacles. The first one was that there was still no way to get it to execute a custom executable directly, as the SD card was mounted noexec which prevents executables and scripts on it from running. However, this could be bypassed by not executing the script directly, but rather executing something like /bin/sh /media/sdcard/payload.sh, which would go through /bin/sh on the rootfs, which was not mounted noexec.The second hurdle was bigger, however. It turned out that while launchserver would happily launch anything, SHEX accepts only a single whitespace-delimited token. This means that I could only control which binary was executed, but not pass it any arguments. Combined with the previous obstacle, this then also seemed like a dead end because I could only run scripts or binaries that were already on the rootfs. I did look through most of them, but nothing seemed very helpful.Defeated, I started looking at file writes. Maybe if I could write files to places I shouldn't be able to, that would give me some sort of leverage.Sure enough, I discovered the LOG command, which let me truncate a file (defined with #define LOGFILE log.txt) and write a single line to a file of my choosing. This one actually allowed spaces and regular ASCII characters, but only bytes 0x20 to 0x7E, meaning writing binary data is out of the question. As ttn runs as root, any writes would also be written as root.It also had a classic path traversal vulnerability. Defining LOGFILE with ../ in it allowed me to write outside the intended logfile directory, theoretically allowing me to write printable ASCII to anywhere on the system.However, I once again ran into a wall with how the mount points were set up. I couldn't overwrite anything on the rootfs since it was mounted read-only, and everything else was mounted noexec and would never be executed anyways. I also looked into whether there were any useful config files I could overwrite, but most files were a custom binary format that I couldn't write with LOG or were otherwise unhelpful. This also looked like a dead end.Among other things, master.script allowed displaying images on the screen (GIFs/BMPs). I spent some time setting up a fuzzing environment using Unicorn to see if I could hit any image decoder bugs causing memory corruption, and while I did get quite a few OOB reads, I didn't find any useful writes.Borrowing a trick from kernel exploitsI had been researching, reverse engineering and trying to come up with different strategies to run arbitrary code for a while. Much to my frustration, none of my strategies ended up working, and I took a step back to look at the bigger picture and figure out if I can make any of the puzzle pieces that I already have fit together.Among other things, I knew I could:Execute arbitrary binaries, but with no arguments and only the ones already on the rootfsWrite ASCII to paths of my own choosingThis is when I had a brainwave and was reminded of a trick that kernel exploits often use: Instead of trying to get the userland to execute our script, why don't I get the kernel to execute our script instead?Often, Linux kernel exploits, when being able to write arbitrary memory, overwrite the core_pattern string. Normally, this dictates how coredumps are stored when a process crashes, but it also accepts special syntax for piping these coredumps to a process instead (|/bin/my-coredump-handler). When a crash occurs, the kernel spawns the process specified in core_pattern and pipes the data in there.core_pattern also supports cmdline arguments for the spawned process. I got lucky here, since support for this landed in 2.6.24 whereas the unit's kernel was 2.6.28.Importantly, you're also able to set core_pattern from userland by writing the pattern to /proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern.I can easily use this to point LOGFILE to ../../proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern and LOG the string |/bin/sh /media/sdcard/payload.sh. This would run the rootfs /bin/sh and execute our script with it as root.Being able to execute arbitrary binaries also turned out to be useful even without arguments, since I needed to somehow get a program to crash, triggering a coredump. Using a DoS vuln to crash the script parser or the main UI itself wouldn't work very well, because this would immediately trigger a reboot of the whole system, killing my script.I used my emulator setup to execute pretty much every single binary on the system, and found that /bin/dbus-monitor raised a SIGABRT if it couldn't connect to the system bus (which the unit didn't run), triggering a coredump. This was perfect.Putting it togetherMy final master.script turned out to be quite simple:#define LOGFILE ../../proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern LOG |/bin/sh /media/sdcard/payload.sh SHEX /bin/dbus-monitorI initially confirmed success by simply calling reboot in the payload.sh script. I was very pleasantly surprised when booting the unit with the SD card inserted and pressing "Yes" at the "Execute master.script?" prompt, the unit rebooted, confirming that I had code execution.The first thing I did was use this to create a full backup of the internal eMMC using dd. With a more complete dump of the system, I pretty quickly figured out that the date & time settings that I'm interested in are in /mnt/flash/settings.dat, which is a custom binary format. After some more reverse engineering, I figured out the exact offset in the file which held the currently set timezone, and wrote a script to patch it to be UTC+2.That is how I was finally able to fix my car's timezone.

As ttn runs as root, any writes would also be written as root.It also had a classic path traversal vulnerability. Defining LOGFILE with ../ in it allowed me to write outside the intended logfile directory, theoretically allowing me to write printable ASCII to anywhere on the system.However, I once again ran into a wall with how the mount points were set up. I couldn't overwrite anything on the rootfs since it was mounted read-only, and everything else was mounted noexec and would never be executed anyways. I also looked into whether there were any useful config files I could overwrite, but most files were a custom binary format that I couldn't write with LOG or were otherwise unhelpful. This also looked like a dead end.Among other things, master.script allowed displaying images on the screen (GIFs/BMPs). I spent some time setting up a fuzzing environment using Unicorn to see if I could hit any image decoder bugs causing memory corruption, and while I did get quite a few OOB reads, I didn't find any useful writes.Borrowing a trick from kernel exploitsI had been researching, reverse engineering and trying to come up with different strategies to run arbitrary code for a while. Much to my frustration, none of my strategies ended up working, and I took a step back to look at the bigger picture and figure out if I can make any of the puzzle pieces that I already have fit together.Among other things, I knew I could:Execute arbitrary binaries, but with no arguments and only the ones already on the rootfsWrite ASCII to paths of my own choosingThis is when I had a brainwave and was reminded of a trick that kernel exploits often use: Instead of trying to get the userland to execute our script, why don't I get the kernel to execute our script instead?Often, Linux kernel exploits, when being able to write arbitrary memory, overwrite the core_pattern string. Normally, this dictates how coredumps are stored when a process crashes, but it also accepts special syntax for piping these coredumps to a process instead (|/bin/my-coredump-handler). When a crash occurs, the kernel spawns the process specified in core_pattern and pipes the data in there.core_pattern also supports cmdline arguments for the spawned process. I got lucky here, since support for this landed in 2.6.24 whereas the unit's kernel was 2.6.28.Importantly, you're also able to set core_pattern from userland by writing the pattern to /proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern.I can easily use this to point LOGFILE to ../../proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern and LOG the string |/bin/sh /media/sdcard/payload.sh. This would run the rootfs /bin/sh and execute our script with it as root.Being able to execute arbitrary binaries also turned out to be useful even without arguments, since I needed to somehow get a program to crash, triggering a coredump. Using a DoS vuln to crash the script parser or the main UI itself wouldn't work very well, because this would immediately trigger a reboot of the whole system, killing my script.I used my emulator setup to execute pretty much every single binary on the system, and found that /bin/dbus-monitor raised a SIGABRT if it couldn't connect to the system bus (which the unit didn't run), triggering a coredump. This was perfect.Putting it togetherMy final master.script turned out to be quite simple:#define LOGFILE ../../proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern LOG |/bin/sh /media/sdcard/payload.sh SHEX /bin/dbus-monitorI initially confirmed success by simply calling reboot in the payload.sh script. I was very pleasantly surprised when booting the unit with the SD card inserted and pressing "Yes" at the "Execute master.script?" prompt, the unit rebooted, confirming that I had code execution.The first thing I did was use this to create a full backup of the internal eMMC using dd. With a more complete dump of the system, I pretty quickly figured out that the date & time settings that I'm interested in are in /mnt/flash/settings.dat, which is a custom binary format. After some more reverse engineering, I figured out the exact offset in the file which held the currently set timezone, and wrote a script to patch it to be UTC+2.That is how I was finally able to fix my car's timezone.

For example, I found out that most partitions were mounted either read-only, noexec or both. Mounts from a live system:rootfs on / type rootfs (rw) none on /sys type sysfs (rw,nosuid,noexec) none on /proc type proc (rw,nosuid,noexec) /dev/mmcblk0p5 on /content type ext3 (rw,nosuid,nodev,noexec,noatime,nodiratime,errors=continue,data=ordered) /dev/loop0 on / type ext2 (ro,noatime,nodiratime,errors=continue) none on /dev type tmpfs (rw,nosuid,noexec,size=1024k) none on /tmp type tmpfs (rw,nosuid,noexec,size=2048k) none on /var type tmpfs (rw,nosuid,noexec,size=5120k) none on /dev/pts type devpts (rw,nosuid,noexec,gid=5,mode=620) none on /var/log type tmpfs (rw,nosuid,noexec,size=1024k) /dev/mmcblk0p3 on /mnt/flash type ext3 (rw,sync,nosuid,nodev,noexec,errors=continue,data=ordered) /dev/mmcblk1p1 on /media/sdcard type vfat (rw,sync,nosuid,nodev,noexec,noatime,nodiratime,fmask=0022,dmask=0022,codepage=cp437,iocharset=iso8859-1) /dev/loop1 on /media/loopback type ext3 (rw,nosuid,nodev,noexec,noatime,nodiratime,errors=continue,commit=3600,data=journal) none on /mnt/movi type unionfs (rw,nosuid,nodev,noexec,noatime,nodiratime,dirs=/media/loopback=rw:/media/sdcard=ro)Notably, the base FAT32 filesystem of the SD card was mounted to /media/sdcard, and the system mounted a unionfs on top of it in /mnt/movi, which had a writable layer pointing to an ext3 filesystem which lived as a file on the external SD. I'm not 100% sure what the point of this setup was (maybe so they can use data=journal, which survives power loss better?), but nevertheless all of these mounts were noexec.This seemed like surprisingly strong security for something from 2011.Something else that the emulator helped me with was identifying all of the files that the system tried to read from the external SD card. One of these files was master.script, a script in a custom language for automating certain UI navigation actions. This was loaded every boot and I hoped this would allow me to somehow open the correct settings menu for setting the time.I reversed ttn, the binary responsible for parsing this script, documenting its functionality as I went, but unfortunately I didn't find any way to open the menu I needed.More wild goose chasesI still thought master.script was what I should be putting my effort into, since it had a lot of functionality that could be a potential attack vector.As usual, I checked for any system or popen calls that would allow me to perform command injection. Unfortunately, I didn't find any constructed with user input.I thought I had hit the jackpot when, while reversing the parser, I came across a SHEX/SHELLEXECUTE command. It passed an arbitrary argument to launchserver, which launched whatever command line was provided with execve.This had two obstacles. The first one was that there was still no way to get it to execute a custom executable directly, as the SD card was mounted noexec which prevents executables and scripts on it from running. However, this could be bypassed by not executing the script directly, but rather executing something like /bin/sh /media/sdcard/payload.sh, which would go through /bin/sh on the rootfs, which was not mounted noexec.The second hurdle was bigger, however. It turned out that while launchserver would happily launch anything, SHEX accepts only a single whitespace-delimited token. This means that I could only control which binary was executed, but not pass it any arguments. Combined with the previous obstacle, this then also seemed like a dead end because I could only run scripts or binaries that were already on the rootfs. I did look through most of them, but nothing seemed very helpful.Defeated, I started looking at file writes. However, this could be bypassed by not executing the script directly, but rather executing something like /bin/sh /media/sdcard/payload.sh, which would go through /bin/sh on the rootfs, which was not mounted noexec.The second hurdle was bigger, however. It turned out that while launchserver would happily launch anything, SHEX accepts only a single whitespace-delimited token. This means that I could only control which binary was executed, but not pass it any arguments. Combined with the previous obstacle, this then also seemed like a dead end because I could only run scripts or binaries that were already on the rootfs. I did look through most of them, but nothing seemed very helpful.Defeated, I started looking at file writes. Maybe if I could write files to places I shouldn't be able to, that would give me some sort of leverage.Sure enough, I discovered the LOG command, which let me truncate a file (defined with #define LOGFILE log.txt) and write a single line to a file of my choosing. This one actually allowed spaces and regular ASCII characters, but only bytes 0x20 to 0x7E, meaning writing binary data is out of the question. As ttn runs as root, any writes would also be written as root.It also had a classic path traversal vulnerability. Defining LOGFILE with ../ in it allowed me to write outside the intended logfile directory, theoretically allowing me to write printable ASCII to anywhere on the system.However, I once again ran into a wall with how the mount points were set up. I couldn't overwrite anything on the rootfs since it was mounted read-only, and everything else was mounted noexec and would never be executed anyways. I also looked into whether there were any useful config files I could overwrite, but most files were a custom binary format that I couldn't write with LOG or were otherwise unhelpful. This also looked like a dead end.Among other things, master.script allowed displaying images on the screen (GIFs/BMPs). I spent some time setting up a fuzzing environment using Unicorn to see if I could hit any image decoder bugs causing memory corruption, and while I did get quite a few OOB reads, I didn't find any useful writes.Borrowing a trick from kernel exploitsI had been researching, reverse engineering and trying to come up with different strategies to run arbitrary code for a while. Much to my frustration, none of my strategies ended up working, and I took a step back to look at the bigger picture and figure out if I can make any of the puzzle pieces that I already have fit together.Among other things, I knew I could:Execute arbitrary binaries, but with no arguments and only the ones already on the rootfsWrite ASCII to paths of my own choosingThis is when I had a brainwave and was reminded of a trick that kernel exploits often use: Instead of trying to get the userland to execute our script, why don't I get the kernel to execute our script instead?Often, Linux kernel exploits, when being able to write arbitrary memory, overwrite the core_pattern string. Normally, this dictates how coredumps are stored when a process crashes, but it also accepts special syntax for piping these coredumps to a process instead (|/bin/my-coredump-handler). When a crash occurs, the kernel spawns the process specified in core_pattern and pipes the data in there.core_pattern also supports cmdline arguments for the spawned process. I got lucky here, since support for this landed in 2.6.24 whereas the unit's kernel was 2.6.28.Importantly, you're also able to set core_pattern from userland by writing the pattern to /proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern.I can easily use this to point LOGFILE to ../../proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern and LOG the string |/bin/sh /media/sdcard/payload.sh. This would run the rootfs /bin/sh and execute our script with it as root.Being able to execute arbitrary binaries also turned out to be useful even without arguments, since I needed to somehow get a program to crash, triggering a coredump. Using a DoS vuln to crash the script parser or the main UI itself wouldn't work very well, because this would immediately trigger a reboot of the whole system, killing my script.I used my emulator setup to execute pretty much every single binary on the system, and found that /bin/dbus-monitor raised a SIGABRT if it couldn't connect to the system bus (which the unit didn't run), triggering a coredump. This was perfect.Putting it togetherMy final master.script turned out to be quite simple:#define LOGFILE ../../proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern LOG |/bin/sh /media/sdcard/payload.sh SHEX /bin/dbus-monitorI initially confirmed success by simply calling reboot in the payload.sh script. I was very pleasantly surprised when booting the unit with the SD card inserted and pressing "Yes" at the "Execute master.script?" prompt, the unit rebooted, confirming that I had code execution.The first thing I did was use this to create a full backup of the internal eMMC using dd. With a more complete dump of the system, I pretty quickly figured out that the date & time settings that I'm interested in are in /mnt/flash/settings.dat, which is a custom binary format. After some more reverse engineering, I figured out the exact offset in the file which held the currently set timezone, and wrote a script to patch it to be UTC+2.That is how I was finally able to fix my car's timezone.

I was very pleasantly surprised when booting the unit with the SD card inserted and pressing "Yes" at the "Execute master.script?" prompt, the unit rebooted, confirming that I had code execution.The first thing I did was use this to create a full backup of the internal eMMC using dd. With a more complete dump of the system, I pretty quickly figured out that the date & time settings that I'm interested in are in /mnt/flash/settings.dat, which is a custom binary format. After some more reverse engineering, I figured out the exact offset in the file which held the currently set timezone, and wrote a script to patch it to be UTC+2.That is how I was finally able to fix my car's timezone.

The second hurdle was bigger, however. It turned out that while launchserver would happily launch anything, SHEX accepts only a single whitespace-delimited token. This means that I could only control which binary was executed, but not pass it any arguments. Combined with the previous obstacle, this then also seemed like a dead end because I could only run scripts or binaries that were already on the rootfs. I did look through most of them, but nothing seemed very helpful.Defeated, I started looking at file writes. Maybe if I could write files to places I shouldn't be able to, that would give me some sort of leverage.Sure enough, I discovered the LOG command, which let me truncate a file (defined with #define LOGFILE log.txt) and write a single line to a file of my choosing. This one actually allowed spaces and regular ASCII characters, but only bytes 0x20 to 0x7E, meaning writing binary data is out of the question. As ttn runs as root, any writes would also be written as root.It also had a classic path traversal vulnerability. Defining LOGFILE with ../ in it allowed me to write outside the intended logfile directory, theoretically allowing me to write printable ASCII to anywhere on the system.However, I once again ran into a wall with how the mount points were set up. I couldn't overwrite anything on the rootfs since it was mounted read-only, and everything else was mounted noexec and would never be executed anyways. I also looked into whether there were any useful config files I could overwrite, but most files were a custom binary format that I couldn't write with LOG or were otherwise unhelpful. This also looked like a dead end.Among other things, master.script allowed displaying images on the screen (GIFs/BMPs). I spent some time setting up a fuzzing environment using Unicorn to see if I could hit any image decoder bugs causing memory corruption, and while I did get quite a few OOB reads, I didn't find any useful writes.Borrowing a trick from kernel exploitsI had been researching, reverse engineering and trying to come up with different strategies to run arbitrary code for a while. Much to my frustration, none of my strategies ended up working, and I took a step back to look at the bigger picture and figure out if I can make any of the puzzle pieces that I already have fit together.Among other things, I knew I could:Execute arbitrary binaries, but with no arguments and only the ones already on the rootfsWrite ASCII to paths of my own choosingThis is when I had a brainwave and was reminded of a trick that kernel exploits often use: Instead of trying to get the userland to execute our script, why don't I get the kernel to execute our script instead?Often, Linux kernel exploits, when being able to write arbitrary memory, overwrite the core_pattern string. Normally, this dictates how coredumps are stored when a process crashes, but it also accepts special syntax for piping these coredumps to a process instead (|/bin/my-coredump-handler). When a crash occurs, the kernel spawns the process specified in core_pattern and pipes the data in there.core_pattern also supports cmdline arguments for the spawned process. I got lucky here, since support for this landed in 2.6.24 whereas the unit's kernel was 2.6.28.Importantly, you're also able to set core_pattern from userland by writing the pattern to /proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern.I can easily use this to point LOGFILE to ../../proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern and LOG the string |/bin/sh /media/sdcard/payload.sh. This would run the rootfs /bin/sh and execute our script with it as root.Being able to execute arbitrary binaries also turned out to be useful even without arguments, since I needed to somehow get a program to crash, triggering a coredump. This would run the rootfs /bin/sh and execute our script with it as root.Being able to execute arbitrary binaries also turned out to be useful even without arguments, since I needed to somehow get a program to crash, triggering a coredump. Using a DoS vuln to crash the script parser or the main UI itself wouldn't work very well, because this would immediately trigger a reboot of the whole system, killing my script.I used my emulator setup to execute pretty much every single binary on the system, and found that /bin/dbus-monitor raised a SIGABRT if it couldn't connect to the system bus (which the unit didn't run), triggering a coredump. With a more complete dump of the system, I pretty quickly figured out that the date & time settings that I'm interested in are in /mnt/flash/settings.dat, which is a custom binary format. After some more reverse engineering, I figured out the exact offset in the file which held the currently set timezone, and wrote a script to patch it to be UTC+2.That is how I was finally able to fix my car's timezone.

InfoQ Homepage News Shopify Overexposed Scans GKE Ingresses and Cloud Run for Exposure

Nov 02, 2026 3 min read

Shopify has introduced Overexposed. This internal scanner locates Kubernetes Ingresses on GKE and Cloud Run services. It checks for those that are accessible from the internet without authentication. After a first version based on repository config files produced false alarms and blind spots, the team rebuilt it on GCP Cloud Asset Inventory and an anonymous HTTP probe. In just a few weeks of tuning, this reduced inconclusive Ingress verdicts by around 80%.

The original scanner checked the infrastructure repository for Ingresses. It focused on public hostnames without authentication settings and then probed them. Shopify says this failed in three ways. Teams that configured proxy authentication annotations directly triggered false positives. Admission controllers that rewrite settings at admission time, but do not run in every cluster, meant a correct-looking config could have no effect. Ingresses created by other repositories or platform tooling were never seen. The authors summarize the lesson as: the repository shows intent; the cluster shows what is enforced.

The current version follows a schedule. It queries Cloud Asset Inventory. This inventory includes Ingresses accepted by GKE after admission, along with Cloud Run services and load balancers. A second search retrieves access policies without needing cluster credentials. The inventory also surfaced Cloud Run services in projects the first scanner had never covered.

Each candidate then receives a single anonymous request. The scanner sends HEAD first, falls back to GET, follows at most three redirects and checks each one. It also tests path variations such as /ADMIN, since path rules can be case-sensitive. Results map to six verdicts: exposed, expected, protected, not found, unreachable and inconclusive. "Expected" applies when an endpoint is open but matches a reviewed, in-code allowlist entry by exact host and path. Allowlisted endpoints are still probed on every run, and an entry that turns out to be protected or gone is flagged as stale.

Shopify stresses that status codes are context-dependent. A 404 behind an Ingress means the proxy answered and the path is missing. On Cloud Run, Google's front end can return a 404 before the application runs, so the scanner classifies it as inconclusive. A 403 is also not treated as proof of protection. For Cloud Run, the scanner distinguishes ingress settings from IAM: a service is public only if allUsers holds the invoker role or the invoker check is disabled. Services behind a load balancer use a URL map. This map decides which backend handles each path. It also shows where authentication, like Identity-Aware Proxy, is required.

In early runs, roughly three in four results were inconclusive in one July run. The team grouped results by reason, added verdicts where evidence supported them, and replayed rule changes against saved scan results before shipping. Uncertain evidence stays inconclusive rather than defaulting to protected. The scanner stores verdicts, reasons and team ownership, but not response bodies or credentials.

Because the scanner makes outbound requests to arbitrary hostnames, Shopify hardened it against SSRF. It validates every IP returned by DNS, rejects private and loopback addresses, connects directly to the checked IP to prevent DNS rebinding, and repeats checks on each redirect. The authors recommend also restricting the scanner's network egress, including cloud metadata endpoints.

The team built Overexposed with AI coding agents and AI code review. To catch tests that pass while checking the wrong thing, they apply mutation testing to security guards and keep one canary target per verdict.

Shopify’s experience illustrates a split that applies to exposure scanning in general. Rule-based checks, such as Trend Micro’s Cloud Run rule, look for allUsers bindings. This is affordable and easily integrable into CI. This tool report intent, not enforcement, so it miss resources created outside the repository and settings that an admission controller later rewrites.

Inventory-based approaches, such as Cartography and the Cloud Asset Inventory queries behind Shopify’s Overexposed, start from what the cloud actually runs, which closes those blind spots. Cartography still derives an exposed_internet flag from configuration, so it can’t confirm what an outsider sees. Overexposed adds an anonymous probe, an allowlist, and evidence-backed verdicts to the inventory. It sees uncertain evidence as inconclusive, not protected.

For teams creating something similar, use inventory as the main reference. Keep config analysis as an early signal in CI. Add a probe only if inventory can’t show whether access control works.

#9910. The Agent Said It Was Done. The Database Disagreed.

Microsoft ThinkingBox grades AI agents on the records they leave behind, not the sentences they generate, and then asks whether they can do it twenty times in a row. It is now available through Hugging Face.

Figure 1: ThinkingBox runs an agent against isolated MCP tool sessions, then grades the terminal backend state and side effects it leaves behind. From our ThinkingBox paper.

A customer writes in. Her $745 kitchen appliance has been stuck in a courier "exception" at a Nashville distribution center, fifteen days past its estimated delivery date.

The AI agent does careful work. Nine tool calls: it pulls the order, checks tracking, looks up her customer profile, searches the refund policy twice, confirms no ticket exists, opens one, documents the timeline, and reads the policy correctly; her account segment genuinely does not qualify for late-delivery compensation.

Then it closes the ticket as resolved and replies “ Since your query is resolved, is there anything I may assist you with? ”

Two things are wrong. The carrier exception is still open, so the required end state was on hold, pending resolution. And the customer never got a real answer to what she actually asked.

An AI grader checking tool calls would see nine well-formed ones. The grader checking whether the agent wrote to the database would see that too. The database is what disagrees.

That gap is what ThinkingBox measures. Across 507 stateful business workflows, each run 20 times against various LLM models, it grades agents on terminal backend state and side effects. This post covers what we found, what consistency costs, and how to run the benchmark yourself through OpenEnv.

You can run this one yourself: the example above is adapted from a benchmark task sandbox_external_retail_group1.py:test_case_ST003_006, and the executable check that fails is a single field: the ticket's status is solved where the required end state is hold. The full trace is in Appendix D.4, Case 3 of our paper.

Want to try it before reading the results? Skip to section Run it yourself.

Final responses and valid tool calls are only proxies. An agent can sound correct while leaving the wrong value, changing the wrong record, or creating an extra side effect. Only the records it leaves behind settle the question.

The gap is substantial. In a common-set ablation covering 121,680 valid trials across 12 LLM models, 79,853 attempts failed the executable checks. Of those failures, 67.24% still terminated cleanly, invoked a state-changing tool, and reported no final tool error. Executable checks nevertheless found wrong field values in 77.61% of them, unintended extra effects in 43.30%, and missing required effects in 25.36%. Those state-check findings overlap.

A trajectory is a claim. Database state is the evidence. Repetition is the trust test.

An agent that processes a refund correctly once and mishandles it the next four times is not a working refund agent. So every task runs 20 independent times, each from an identical clean backend, and we report three different things:

Table 1: The three numbers we report, and the question each one answers.

We use observed 20/20 in this blog post as the literal count of how many of the 507 tasks passed 20 out of 20. No estimator, no smoothing.

Starting with the familiar view. The table below reports pass@1, the single-attempt score estimate, broken out by domain. This is the number most leaderboards publish, and on its own it reads like an ordinary capability ranking.

Table 2: ThinkingBox-Bench pass@1 (%) by domain. Each model is evaluated on every task for 20 repeated trials. Bold marks the group leader; underline marks the runner-up. The standard errors for the single attempt score estimates are provided in Table 4 in our ThinkingBox paper.

Claude Opus 5.5 leads overall at 67.16%, two-thirds of a point above Claude Opus 5. Kimi-K3 is the strongest open-weights model, within a point of GPT-6-Astra. Domain matters just as much: Claude Opus 4.6 scores 68.62% on retail but 8.30% on auto insurance.

One good run tells you a model can do the work. It does not tell you whether it will do it again. So run every task 20 times and ask how much of that score survives.

Figure 2: How much of each model's single-attempt score survives 20 repeats.

Only three hold on to most of their pass@1 scores: GPT-6 Astra retains 78% of its single-attempt rate, and Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Opus 5 each retain 71%. At the other end, GLM-5.1, Kimi-K2.6 and DeepSeek-V4-Pro each keep about 8%.

The gap between what a model can do once and what it does every time is the whole story.

Figure 3: Breadth and consistency pull apart. Twelve of the eighteen models are shown; six below 33% pass@1 are omitted for legibility.

Kimi-K3 has the broadest coverage of any model we tested. It solves 93.89% of the benchmark at least once: 476 of 507 tasks. Only 31 tasks defeat it entirely, the lowest count in the field. On retail workflows it leads outright at 82.24% pass@1, ahead of every proprietary model.

Kimi-K3 is also among the least consistent. Just 68 of 507 tasks, 13.41%, succeed in all 20 attempts.

Claude Opus 5 inverts this. It solves fewer tasks at least once (79.09%; 106 defeat it entirely) but completes 47.53% of the benchmark on every single attempt.

A newer model does not fix this. Claude Opus 5.5 scores higher than Claude Opus 5 on every-attempt average, 67.16% against 66.50%, and solves more tasks at least once. It passes exactly the same number of tasks on all 20 attempts: 241. Half a point of headline accuracy bought no additional dependability at all.

If you are choosing a model for work that touches real records, pass@20 is the wrong column to look at.

Capability comparisons usually stop at the score. For anyone deploying, the relevant question is what a successful unit of work costs. We measure that as cost per successful task attempt. We say task attempt because every benchmark task is run repeatedly and cost is incurred per attempt, so pass@1 is the matching quality denominator.

We took each model's recorded token usage from its full 507 × 20 campaign and priced it at undiscounted list rates available on OpenRouter+, reversing promotional discounts and excluding endpoints that declare quantization. Input, output and cache rates all come from one provider endpoint per model.

Then we divided one run's cost by the number of attempts that succeeded:

Cost per successful task attempt = estimated cost for 507 attempts, one per task ÷ (507 × pass@1)

This is a comparative efficiency index, not an invoice, and not the price of serving one production request. It also prices single successes, not consistency. We price consistency next.

Example: GPT-5.4 costs $43.49 for 507 attempts (one attempt per task) and has 65.36% pass@1, so $43.49 ÷ (507 × 0.6536) = $0.131 per successful task attempt.

A model is on the frontier if no other model is both no more expensive and at least as accurate. Three models qualify; every other model is dominated on at least one axis.

Figure 4: Cost per successful task attempt against pass@1. Ringed dots are pareto cost frontier models.

The frontier has three steps. GPT-5.6 Sol has the lowest cost per success at $0.127; GPT-5.4 raises pass@1 by 3.45 percentage points for $0.004 more per success; Claude Opus 5.5 adds another 1.80 points at $0.276 per success. Each of the three remains on the cost frontier line because no cheaper model matches its pass@1.

Claude Opus 5 is the clearest case: at $0.475 per successful attempt and 66.50% pass@1, it is both more expensive and less accurate than Claude Opus 5.5 at $0.276 and 67.16%.

Cost per success rewards a model that is cheap and often right. It does not reward a model that is right every time. So we also compute cost per dependable task: the cost of the full 20-run campaign divided by the number of tasks the model passed on all 20 attempts.

Cost per dependable task = estimated cost of 20 runs of 507 attempts ÷ tasks passing 20/20

Example: GPT-6-Astra costs 20 × $86.03 = $1,720.60 for the campaign and passes 231 tasks on every attempt, so $1,720.60 ÷ 231 = $7.45 per dependable task.

Table 3: The nine lowest costs per dependable task among models with at least one observed 20/20 task, sorted low to high. Estimated $, not actual cloud bills.

Now rank by consistency. GPT-5.4 is the cheapest at $6.80, though only 128 tasks meet the bar. GPT-6 Astra reaches 231 at $7.45, and Claude Opus 5.5 the joint-highest 241 at $7.80.

None of the three dominates the others: each additional dependable task costs more. Claude Opus 5 also passes 241, but at $13.30, so Opus 5.5 dominates it outright. GPT-5.6 Sol, the cheapest per single success at $0.127, costs $9.76 per dependable task. The cheapest way to get a right answer is not the cheapest way to get a dependable one.

We assign each failed trace one deterministic diagnostic signature, and the headline is actionable: roughly four in five failures are tool handling, not reasoning. Across an ablation study in Table 5 of our paper:

These are unweighted averages of per-model shares and observable labels, not unique causal explanations.

The practical pattern is simple: agents usually get far enough to attempt the workflow, then fail to recover from tool errors, failed preconditions, or empty lookups. That is a retry and error-recovery problem before it is a model problem.

Difficulty also changes by domain: across the models listed in Table 2 above, retail averages 59.52% pass@1 while auto insurance averages 33.83%.

What to do about it. Treat the 20/20 rate as a design input, not a verdict. The same signal the benchmark grades on is available in production: check the terminal state before you commit, not the model's summary of it.

Classify tool and system errors so retries target the recoverable ones. Cut the tool surface to what the workflow needs. And require human approval on the changes you cannot cheaply reverse. We have not measured the lift from any of these on this benchmark, which is exactly the kind of thing the environment now makes testable.

ThinkingBox is the agent sandbox, while ThinkingBox-Bench is a dataset benchmark to evaluate agents. The diagram at the top of this post shows the loop; here is what each part does.

Figure 5: The sandbox loop from panel A in Figure 1 above: isolated tool session, terminal database state, side effects, executable judges.

Each task defines a starting backend state, a user goal, the available MCP tools, the domain policy, and executable checks over the terminal state. A simulated user holds private context (a booking reference, a preference, or a date of birth) and releases it only when asked.

Every attempt gets an isolated MCP session with freshly initialized state. Two attempts of the same task never share a database row or cached tool state, which is what makes 20-trial comparison meaningful.

At the end, a side-effect extractor derives what actually changed, and deterministic judges compare it against the required end state, accepting any trajectory that produces the right outcome while rejecting wrong, missing or extra effects. For requirements with no clean database value ("did the agent disclose this is not guaranteed?"), a narrow binary rubric question handles the semantics. 477 of the 507 tasks are graded on state alone; 30 add response rubrics.

The trust boundary: the model sees tasks, dialogue and tool schemas. Golden state, assertions, grading internals and credentials stay on the evaluator side.

ThinkingBox is now on Hugging Face, both the harness and the dataset. ThinkingBox-Bench now sits behind the OpenEnv interface, and each finished episode returns a binary pass/fail reward. The released adapter is designed for evaluation; separate, non-benchmark scenarios can use the same interface in training workflows.

Tested on Linux and WSL, with Python 3.11+, uv and Docker. You also need a thinkingbox-data checkout at the pinned release and model endpoints for the agent, simulated user and judge. One endpoint can serve all three roles, which is the simplest way to start. The OpenEnv image starts only the OpenEnv API; everything else you run yourself.

In a second terminal, start Typesense 30.1 and wait for its health check:

In a third terminal, start the Session Proxy and MCP servers.

Back in the first terminal, start the OpenEnv server against a ThinkingBox YAML config naming your three models (config guide):

Gate on readiness before running anything. It returns 503 until its observable data, configuration and Session Proxy checks pass. It cannot observe Typesense or live-probe every model endpoint, so confirm those separately:

Now score a real episode. example_usage.py only resets and lists tools; for agent actions, effects and assertions use the packaged evaluator:

The OpenEnv adapter writes operational failures to an errors sidecar so they can be rerun rather than silently mixed with model outcomes. A canonical result must resolve or explicitly account for those attempts; we counted system errors as unsuccessful trials.

Runs are gated on a pinned framework commit, a pinned data release and a bundle hash, so a canonical result is verifiable rather than asserted.

The useful part of this work is not our pass@1 leaderboard. It is the environment.

If you are evaluating an agent that touches real records:
