#9837. LinearB Launches Agentic Studio to Steer AI Coding Agents in a $127 Billion Market by 2032

AI, Web3, Cybersecurity, Startup Funding & Enterprise SaaS. Top Journalist, Analyst & Thought Leadership Media Leader.

AI, Web3, Cybersecurity, Startup Funding & Enterprise SaaS. Top Journalist, Analyst & Thought Leadership Media Leader.

AI, Web3, Cybersecurity, Startup Funding & Enterprise SaaS. Top Journalist, Analyst & Thought Leadership Media Leader.

Developers who used AI on at least 75% of their coding days merged a median of 95.7% more pull requests per week in May 2026 than they did in June 2025 according to LinearB's benchmarks of 2.7 million pull requests from 253 engineering organizations, yet at the top-performing organizations in that same sample only 79% of the pull requests opened by autonomous agents merge within 30 days against 92% for changes written by humans alone.

LinearB, a Leader in the first Gartner Magic Quadrant for Developer Productivity Insight Platforms, launched Agentic Studio to close that gap by giving engineering leaders and coding agents the same view of everything that has happened across software delivery. The launch matters to anyone paying for AI coding tools because the benchmark data shows the extra code piling up in review queues and the token bill climbing fastest at the top of the distribution.

LinearB has spent years collecting data from the tools engineers use every day, such as GitHub and Jira, while linking each code change to the ticket that requested it and the release that shipped it. Agentic Studio puts that history to work for managers, who can type a plain question such as where delivery is stuck or whether AI spending is paying off and receive an answer with a suggested next step.

Coding agents get the same history through an MCP server, which is a standard way for AI tools to plug into outside data, along with add-ons that LinearB calls agent skills. An agent about to edit a file can now see who owns that code, how often it has been rewritten and whether it caused recent incidents, which tells the agent how carefully it needs to work.

The first skill, called effort, is in early access and uses that history to decide how hard an agent should try on each change. A simple, low-risk edit gets a quick pass that uses fewer tokens, the units AI providers bill by, while a complex or risky change gets more effort with careful, tested edits. The skill works with any coding agent, Agentic Studio is available now to all LinearB customers and the next skills will focus on code review and merging.

Companies are pouring money into AI coding tools, with enterprises spending $4.0 billion on them in 2025 against $550 million a year earlier according to Menlo Ventures. That sevenfold jump makes coding the largest single use of AI inside companies, at 55% of the $7.3 billion spent on departmental AI.

MarketsandMarkets expects the market for AI code assistants to grow from $8.14 billion in 2025 to $127.05 billion by 2032, a rise of about 48% a year. As writing code gets cheaper, the pressure moves to everything that happens after the code is written, which is why the tools that measure engineering work are growing fast too, with Gartner estimating that category at about $400 million and expanding more than 40% a year.

More code does not mean faster delivery, because every change still has to be checked by a human reviewer before it ships. LinearB's 2026 Software Engineering Benchmarks Report, which covers 8.1 million pull requests from 4,800 teams in 42 countries, shows that AI-assisted changes run to 408 lines of code against 157 for changes written without AI, measured at the 75th percentile, which makes them 2.6 times larger (our arithmetic).

Changes written by agents face a different problem, since they wait 17.6 hours for a reviewer to pick them up against 3.4 hours for human changes, which is 5.2 times longer (our arithmetic). Once a reviewer starts, the review itself takes 6.4 hours, so an agent's change spends almost three times as long waiting in the queue as it does being read. Across the whole dataset 84.4% of changes written without AI were accepted within 30 days against 32.7% of AI changes.

Pull request size and review wait by type.

The productivity gains are real for heavy users, since among the 83,000 developers in LinearB's 2026 AI benchmarks those who used AI on at least three out of every four coding days merged a median 95.7% more pull requests per week in May 2026 than in June 2025. Developers who used no AI at all merged 3.6% fewer over the same period.

The gains grow step by step with usage, with developers using AI on half their coding days gaining 65.4% and occasional users gaining 24.4%. LinearB says these figures show a correlation that does not prove AI alone caused the gains. It also notes that the acceptance rate of heavy users' changes slipped 4.4% over the year. AI use is now close to universal, with 88.3% of organizations using AI tools daily or weekly, yet 44.7% still do not measure what those tools deliver.

Merged pull request growth by AI usage band.

Even the best teams use AI less than the hype suggests. At elite organizations, the top 10% in LinearB's sample, AI helps write only 54% of pull requests, AI writes 45% of the code that gets merged and fully autonomous agents open just 4.7% of all changes.

The biggest difference between the best teams and the rest is AI code review, where an AI tool checks a change before a human does. Elite organizations use it on 57% of pull requests against 8% at fair organizations, the top 60%, which is a sevenfold gap. It is also the easiest win on the table, because changes with an AI review are accepted at the highest rate of any type, lifting acceptance by up to five percentage points, while LinearB's August analysis found a lift of two to three points across almost every type of change.

More AI output comes with a much bigger bill, since organizations merge 2.6 pull requests per developer each week, twice the 1.3 at fair organizations, yet spend $481 per developer each month on AI tokens against $50, which is 9.6 times as much.

In plain terms, doubling output has cost close to ten times as much in AI usage, which is the trade-off that boards and finance teams now ask engineering leaders to explain. LinearB labels these token figures as rough averages, though the direction is clear: this is the gap the effort skill is designed to narrow by saving expensive AI effort for the changes that need it.

Acceptance is where agents still fall short, since at elite organizations 79% of the changes opened by autonomous agents are merged within 30 days against 92% of changes written only by people, a gap of 13 points (our arithmetic).

The gap widens at weaker organizations, where agent acceptance drops to 58% at good organizations and 37% at fair ones, leaving agent work 28 and 44 points behind the overall rate (our arithmetic). LinearB's explanation is ownership, because a change that no developer feels responsible for often never gets merged. That is why Agentic Studio gives agents code ownership history, so an agent knows whose code it is touching before it opens a change.

Token bills are rising fastest among the heaviest users, since at the 90th percentile, meaning the top tenth of spenders, developers now use $35.20 of AI tokens per coding day, up nearly 75% in three months, while the typical developer's spend has barely moved. That works out to $481 a month or $5,772 a year per developer (our arithmetic), which LinearB says is still under 4% of what a developer costs in total.

Gartner expects spending on AI coding tools to pass the average developer's salary by 2028 as token use keeps climbing. LinearB's own worked example, which is an illustration and not customer data, shows why the cost of each delivered change matters more than the raw bill, since a 350-developer company that quadruples its token spend from $300,000 to $1.2 million a month while lifting output from 3.3 to 5.67 merged changes per developer each week cuts its cost per delivered change by 29%, from $864 to $613.

Kraken offers an early example of the data at work, since the company used LinearB's MCP server with an AI assistant to find out what was slowing its code reviews and learned that the cause was time zones and reviewer availability, not large changes. Over the next four months it cut its slowest review times, measured at the 90th percentile, by more than half.

Emburse uses the data at board level, with chief technology officer Ken Ringdahl putting LinearB charts directly into board decks because his board wants to know how the company uses AI and what return it gets. LinearB says its AI assistant and MCP access have the highest user retention of any features it has released.

LinearB plans its next agent skills for code review and merging, followed by tools that help teams govern AI-written code safely and cut what they spend on AI. Chief executive and co-founder Ori Keren describes the company's data as a knowledge graph of the entire software delivery process that coding tool makers do not have, while co-founder and chief operating officer Dan Lines says the goal is to move leaders from reading dashboards to knowing what to do next.

For engineering leaders, LinearB's data points to three places where AI coding is losing value today, which are the review queue, the agent change that nobody owns and the top of the token bill. Agentic Studio is LinearB's attempt to fix all three by giving people and agents the same context, in a market that Gartner sizes at about $400 million and growing more than 40% a year.

#9836. Turning Database Grading into RL Rewards: Post-Training Agents with ThinkingBox

This is the follow up to our first blog post, The Agent Said It Was Done. The Database Disagreed. ThinkingBox-Training is now available on GitHub.

We built ThinkingBox to evaluate an agent's work by comparing the final database state with the expected outcome. We then used the same kind of executable signal as a reward on training tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench. For Qwen3.8-27B, average success rose from 51.70% to 60.78%, while tasks completed correctly on all twenty attempts rose from 38 to 107 with 50 GRPO steps.

Figure 1. ThinkingBox turns executable checks of terminal database state into rewards for post-training agents on tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench.

We built ThinkingBox to catch agents that say they are done when they are not.

Each of its 507 tasks in ThinkingBox-Bench (our benchmark dataset) hands an agent a real backend and a set of tools, lets it work, then checks what really changed in the database. In the first post, we caught a model closing a customer's ticket as resolved while the carrier exception behind it was still open. Nine competent-looking tool calls, one wrong database row.

Then we noticed what we had built. For most tasks, an executable check can return 1 or 0 directly from the final database state. That is not just a grader. This can be a reward function.+

So we constructed a training pool from ThinkingBox-format tasks outside the benchmark and used their executable outcomes as rewards. The catch was choosing which tasks are suitable for agent training: most tasks are either already solved or hopeless for the model in front of you, and both teach it nothing.

Difficulty is policy-relative: a task is hard for the current model only until that model learns it.

We call this offline policy-relative difficulty. We estimated each task's success probability once using the base policy before training and kept the selected training pool fixed throughout the run.

We used offline policy-relative difficulty to build the training pool, then fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B with GRPO for 50 steps. To recap, we evaluate each of the 507 benchmark tasks 20 times. pass@1 measures average success across all 10,140 attempts. pass@20 measures the share of tasks solved at least once. Observed 20/20 measures the share of tasks that pass every recorded attempt.

Table 1. Qwen3.8-27B results before and after 50 steps of GRPO on the offline-selected training pool.

Training sharply increased repeatable success, with a small decline in at-least-once coverage. The rest of the post explains how we selected practice tasks, built the reward loop, and measured that tradeoff.

What does that improvement look like on one task? A traveler requests a room downgrade, but company policy requires manager approval first. Before training, the agent changed the booking and issued refunds without approval in 15 of 20 attempts. After RL fine-tuning, it preserved the booking and payment state in all 20.

Figure 2. One corporate hotel-booking task, 20 attempts per model. The base Qwen3.8-27B model changed the booking without required manager approval in 15 attempts. The RL fine-tuned model preserved booking and payment state in all 20; all expected records matched in 19.

In a hurry? The headline result is above. The implementation is in Run the training stack.

ThinkingBox-Bench grades agents on the database records they leave behind. Each of its 507 tasks starts a real backend, hands the agent a set of MCP tools and a simulated LLM user with private context, and at the end runs executable checks against the terminal database state. Checks are against the backend record that needs to be correct, not the specific tool calls. This incentivizes the model to discover possibly new solution paths rather than “rediscover” the human-backed solution, that might be suboptimal albeit correct.

In our first post we ran eighteen models through that benchmark twenty times each and reported a gap that headline accuracy hides. Kimi-K3 solved 93.89% of tasks at least once but completed only 68 of 507 tasks (13.41%) on all twenty recorded attempts. Claude Opus 5 inverted it: narrower coverage, far more consistency.

And bigger or better model did not close it. Claude Opus 5.5 scored 0.66 percentage points higher than Claude Opus 5 on pass@1, yet passed exactly the same number of tasks, 241, on all twenty attempts. That gain in headline accuracy bought zero additional dependability.

If you are choosing a model for work that touches production database records, pass@1 should not be read alone. Observed 20/20 shows which tasks succeed on every attempt, which is closer to what production reliability requires.

The executable terminal-state verdict was also the training reward. Before unpacking the training loop, here is what changed on the sealed benchmark.

After training Qwen3.8-27B, we evaluated the selected step-50 checkpoint on the 507-task benchmark it had never trained on. The 507 tasks represent an out-of-distribution test set: their domains, databases, and most MCP tools were not encountered during RL training.

Table 2. ThinkingBox-Bench pass@1 (%) by domain, for selected models from our first blog's Table 2 and our fine-tuned model for different domains and overall. Observed 20/20 numbers are over the entire benchmark with 507 tasks. Each model is evaluated on all 507 tasks for 20 repeated trials. Bold marks the column leader; underline marks the runner-up.

The headline result is the observed-20/20 row in Table 1. A 27B model that initially completed 38 (7.5%) of ThinkingBox-Bench on every attempt now completes 107 (21.1%) on every attempt, almost thrice. For comparison, observed 20/20 for Kimi-K3 is 68, GPT-5.4 with 128, GPT-6 Astra has 231, and Claude Opus 5.5 leads with 241.

Average success and repeatability produce different orderings. In Table 2, we notice that GPT-5.6 Sol scored slightly higher on pass@1 than the RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B (61.91% versus 60.78%) but passed fewer tasks on all 20 recorded attempts: 82 versus 107. Claude Sonnet 4.6 scored lower on pass@1, at 59.19%, yet passed nearly the same number of tasks every time, at 102. Neither metric alone captures the full picture.

The observed pattern is consistent with sharpening: repeatable success rose while at-least-once coverage fell slightly. This is in-line with prior work. One explanation is that probability distribution moved toward trajectories that work repeatedly while some low-probability paths disappeared.

Overall, the model did not become broader. It became more repeatable. The next question is where those gains landed.

Figure 3. Domain-level base scores, RLFT scores, and percentage-point changes. Green change cells show gains and red cells show declines; blue shading indicates the score level within each metric.

Pass@1 and observed 20/20 rose in all five domains. Pass@20 was mixed: it increased in neobank and consulting, but declined in retail, travel, and auto insurance. Auto insurance had the largest breadth loss (−7.0 points), while retail had the largest observed-20/20 gain (+24.5 points).

The first post priced consistency using simple math: divide the estimated cost of the full 20-run campaign by the number of tasks the model passed every single time.

Cost per dependable task = estimated cost of the 507 × 20 campaign ÷ tasks passing 20/20

Applying the same cost math to the fine-tuned checkpoint's measured token usage:

Table 3. Estimated evaluation cost and dependability for base and RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B. Cost per successful attempt divides total estimated campaign cost (507 x 20) by the number of passing attempts.

At $8.00 per dependable task, the fine-tuned model came close to GPT-5.4 ($6.80), GPT-6 Astra ($7.45), and Claude Opus 5.5 ($7.80) in the companion comparison.

Figure 4 prices cost per successful attempt against pass@1.

Figure 4. The golden arrow traces Qwen3.8-27B base pareto cost position to the RLFT (diamond): pass@1 rises from 51.70% to 60.78% while estimated cost per successful attempt falls from $0.177 to $0.139. Ringed circles mark the Pareto cost frontier.

The move places the fine-tuned checkpoint close to GPT-5.6 Sol, although GPT-5.6 Sol remains cheaper and slightly higher on pass@1. Four models priced in our paper fall outside the plotted range.

The dollar values are a comparative serving index, not invoice or cloud bills. Serving the fine-tuned checkpoint would be the same as the base model. The calculation includes model inference cost, and excludes training run and policy-probe cost for curating the training dataset.

These results tell us what moved. The next sections explain the training loop and why selecting the right tasks matters the most.

Figure 5. The six stages, now in context: candidate tasks feed in, the first three run once offline, the last three repeat for every group in the training run. The trained checkpoint is evaluated against ThinkingBox-Bench.

Selection runs once, offline, against the base policy model, i.e in this case Qwen3.8 27B; training then uses that fixed pool that has been curated. The dashed amber arrow in Figure 5 marks the path we did not take: re-probing difficulty during the training run.

Every rollout is a complete episode, not a text completion. It gets a fresh backend, an isolated MCP session, and GPT-5 Chat as the simulated user. Most rewards come from deterministic terminal-state checks; a minority of narrow rubric requirements can invoke the configured judge (GPT-5 Chat).

Training and evaluation must interpret Qwen output identically. That includes reasoning extraction, tool calls, argument typing, rendering, and isolated task state. Otherwise the reward measures a different agent from the one evaluated. The shared interpretation code is in trainer/core/tb_interpret.py.

For the reference run, we ran full-parameter RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B on 187 tasks using token-mean GRPO. Each update generated 18 groups of 8 rollouts, or 144 episodes, across 24 H100s. Training ran synchronously with parameter and optimizer offload; AdamW used a 1e-6 learning rate and zero weight decay. We ran the training for 50 steps.

Zero-variance groups were replaced DAPO-style during training. System errors were handled separately: a backend timeout is not an incorrect agent outcome, so affected groups were refilled rather than scored as failures.

That explains how retained tasks were trained. The remaining question is which tasks entered the training pool.

Before diving deep into the selection of training tasks, a disclaimer:

No ThinkingBox-Bench task was included in the RL training pool. The benchmark was reserved for evaluation.

ThinkingBox-Bench is out-of-distribution relative to the RL training pool: its domains, databases, policies, and most tools were not encountered during RL training. The two sets still share the ThinkingBox framework, simulated-user machinery, executable terminal-state grading, a few common tools, and a similar task style. These shared elements limit the scope of the transfer claim.

Why selection matters comes down to one arithmetic fact about GRPO. If all eight rollouts fail, the reward vector is [0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0]. If all eight succeed, it is [1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1]. In either case, centering within the group produces no task-reward advantage because no trajectory did better than another.++

A mixed group such as [0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1] supplies the contrast GRPO can learn from. That distinction is expensive for a stateful agent: every rollout provisions an isolated backend, runs a real tool session, and calls a separate model to play the user.

The question that shaped this work was therefore not only which model or optimizer? It was: which candidate tasks should enter the fixed training pool?

We used an offline pass-rate filter on the posterior to select the training pool. It estimates which tasks are likely to produce contrasting terminal rewards under the base policy.

So we probe. Each candidate task is run repeatedly against the base policy model. The plain-language rule is simple: tasks the model always fails are unlikely to teach it yet; tasks it always passes are already learned; tasks it solves sometimes are where outcomes can provide contrast.

Each candidate task is run n times, producing k successes. We model its latent success probability with Jeffreys posterior probability:

success probability | k successes in n probes ~ Beta(k + ½, n − k + ½)

Figure 6. Offline policy-relative difficulty is estimated from repeated base-policy probes and used to retain tasks likely to produce contrasting rewards.

We partition the unit interval into five buckets with boundaries at 0.08, 0.40, 0.60, and 0.90, chosen as hyperparameters for these runs. Each task is assigned to the bucket containing the greatest posterior mass:

Further details are in Appendix C.4 of our ThinkingBox paper.

Figure 7. Zooming in, one task through all six stages: GPT-5.4 screening, base-model probes, difficulty classification, a rollout group, terminal-state grading, and a GRPO update.

Figure 7 follows one candidate task that can potentially enter the training pool. For the Qwen3.8 27B full-parameter pool, GPT-5.4 first served as a solvability screen. The base policy then succeeded on few of the probes e.g 3 of 8, producing a Beta(3.5, 5.5) posterior. Its largest mass, 54.0%, fell in the Difficult band.

When sampled for training, the task produced the mixed reward group [0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1]. Successful trajectories therefore received above-mean task advantage and failed trajectories below-mean advantage, giving GRPO contrast to learn from. A different policy model could place the same task in a different difficulty band.

The final Qwen3.8-27B curated training pool contained 187 tasks.

Nothing about the trajectory. The reward is the task's own executable verdict.

When an episode ends, the sandbox extracts what actually changed in the backend and runs the task's deterministic checks against the terminal state. Any trajectory that produces the correct end state passes. Wrong, missing, or extra side effects fail. The reward is 1 or 0.

In the benchmark, the database grader can be thought of as the “examiner”: it caught agents that reported success and left the wrong record. In training, the same kind of check can be seen as the “teacher” on a different, disjoint set of tasks.

We release the data-selection, rollout, reward, and Verl integration used to train Qwen3.8-27B in microsoft/thinkingbox-training. The repository README is the entry point. The detailed guides are:

Tested on Linux and WSL with Python 3.12 and uv. You need NVIDIA GPUs with a compatible CUDA/NCCL stack, a local Qwen3.8-27B checkpoint, and OpenAI-compatible endpoints for the simulated user and judge. The validated reference configuration uses 3 nodes x 8 H100 GPUs; smaller custom configurations depend on model size, context length, and rollout concurrency.

The public sample task list exercises the interface. It is not the private 187-task training pool used for the reported run. Supply an authorized training source that remains disjoint from the public benchmark.

Keep the three repositories side by side:

The released stack targets Linux, Python 3.12, Verl 0.9.0, and the pinned package lock:

The final two commands should report a verified patched Verl checkout and no broken requirements. Do not run another automatic package sync afterward: it can replace the patched source installation with the vanilla Verl wheel.

Start with the publicly provided samples, or add your own authorized dataset in ThinkingBox format. Then run the repository's preparation script:

The script aggregates policy probes, applies offline policy-relative difficulty filters and benchmark exclusions, and writes the selected train.yaml and test.yaml files. docs/data-preparation.md documents the input fields, loader contract, and complete command.

Follow docs/reference-q38-run.md to start Typesense and the MCP servers, configure the simulated user and judge, set the model, task-list, checkpoint, and topology variables, and prepare the Ray cluster. Keep credentials in runtime secret injection rather than committed files or shell history.

Before allocating a training job, use the guide's dry-run command:

It must exit zero without starting Ray or allocating GPUs. Read the emitted python -m verl.trainer.main_ppo command and every resolved override before launching the run.

The launcher configures training; it does not provision hosts. On the reference three-node topology, export the same environment on every node, mount CHECKPOINT_DIR at the same absolute path, then start Ray:

After ray status reports all 24 GPUs, launch once from the head node:

The first ThinkingBox post covers Typesense, the MCP Session Proxy, and OpenEnv setup. Merge the trained checkpoint following docs/evaluation.md, then serve it with vLLM.

From the OpenEnv repository root, set MERGED_MODEL to the merged model directory and THINKINGBOX_DATA to the pinned benchmark checkout. The historical checkpoint evaluation used this eight-A100 serving configuration:

In a separate terminal, start the OpenEnv compatibility proxy for the Qwen chat template from the ThinkingBox Training checkout. It listens on port 8014 and forwards to vLLM on 8001:

Keep it running during evaluation. From another terminal, check readiness:

Update the agent entry in the existing thinkingbox.yaml; retain its MCP, simulated-user, and judge configuration:

Start OpenEnv as in the first post, with OPENENV_TB_CONFIG pointing to this thinkingbox.yaml and OPENENV_TB_DATASET to $THINKINGBOX_DATA. Once /ready succeeds, run the full protocol of 507 tasks × 20 attempts:

The full profile validates all 10,140 expected task/repetition keys before aggregation.

The useful part of this work is not one Qwen3.8-27B checkpoint. It is the training loop and training data curation that turns executable outcomes into rewards.

If you are training or evaluating an agent that touches real database records:

Further details can be found in the following links:

ThinkingBox code is MIT-licensed; the benchmark data is CDLA-Permissive-2.0.

Disclaimer: every task in the public benchmark is a synthetic reconstruction. The workflows and policies are modeled on real enterprise agent patterns; the customers are not real.

ThinkingBox, ThinkingBox-Bench and ThinkingBox-Training is built by the Microsoft Copilot Studio team in partnership with Toloka with collaborators from the University of Pittsburgh, Northwestern University, Columbia University and UC Irvine who interned at Microsoft. ++ That zero-gradient problem has a standard batch-time fix: oversample, discard the degenerate groups, refill. The full-parameter run did exactly that, similar to DAPO with replacement of zero-variance groups. But refilling still pays full price for every wasted rollout before throwing it away.

#9835. Widespread PHP Flaw May Cause Many Site Outages Today

Expect to see quite a few websites serving error pages today: Nearly 70 percent of websites need to update their core software to fix a pair of vulnerabilities that allow an attacker to seize full control over affected servers. Experts say there are working exploits for the flaws, and that these critical bugs are already being exploited in the wild.

The flaws at issue are present in PHP, the programming language that powers sites running on a large number of web publishing systems, including Drupal, Magento, Joomla and WordPress. Earlier today, PHP released an emergency security update to fix two critical bugs that can allow an attacker to execute code of their choosing on a vulnerable server.

Reuters reports that government websites in Europe and elsewhere went offline today after the PHP vulnerabilities were disclosed. Cloudflare said it has already detected some exploitation of the flaw, and that at 3:02 am (UTC) it implemented web application firewall rules to protect websites from attack traffic seeking to exploit the bugs, which could cause a denial of service condition, remote code execution, and data exposure.

OpenAI, which was involved in the vulnerability research and outreach, said “given the severity of these flaws and PHP’s widespread use, we consider this one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory.”

Censys, a company that tracks the technology used by Internet hosts, said a recent scan identified approximately 2.58 million Internet facing hosts and 54.9 million web properties running PHP.

Security experts at Wiz said every PHP version released in the last decade is affected by at least one of these vulnerabilities [full disclosure: Wiz is an advertiser on this blog].

“These findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history,” reads a blog post published today by a team of researchers at Wiz, which was one of several organizations credited with discovering the vulnerabilities. “The underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve. Frontier AI models substantially reduced that barrier, turning a longstanding flaw into an exploit.”

The Wiz researchers say it is likely the PHP vulnerabilities will be mass-exploited to install web-based backdoors or “web shells,” which give attackers a web-based panel that allows them to remotely control infected sites. Wiz said that prior to the PHP bugs being publicly disclosed, the company worked with the PHP team, Calif and OpenAI to measure the size of the problem and coordinate patch verification and disclosure.

The PHP zero-day vulnerabilities are being tracked by their CVE numbers, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, and they affect all web servers running PHP 5.4 or later. The bugs are fixed in PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35.

According to Wiz, PHP is so deeply embedded in many web applications that we are likely to see organizations struggling to patch these vulnerabilities for some time to come, comparing this PHP vulnerability pair with the Log4Shell weakness that emerged in 2021 — a widespread, severe-as-it-gets security flaw in Log4j, a popular Java logging framework.

“A vulnerability in core PHP reaches far beyond a single application,” the Wiz researchers wrote. “PHP runs across clouds, hosting providers, content-delivery networks and millions of independently managed servers. Reducing exposure before the technical details became public required coordinated work across that entire ecosystem.”

The SANS Internet Storm Center is keeping an eye on major software platforms that are shipping updates to deal with these PHP flaws. For example, Ubuntu just released updated PHP packages. For a technical deep-dive on these vulnerabilities that tells the timeline of the discovery of these bugs in a comic book style, check out this post from Calif, another technology company credited with finding the PHP flaws.

A snapshot of php2shell.censys.com, the website Censys set up to track the PHP vulnerabilities.

This is a fast-moving story. Updates will be noted here with timestamps.

Update, 2:30 pm ET: Add figures from Censys and a link to Calif’s writeup.

#9832. Does Your Model Run on AWS Trainium? Look It Up

In a previous post, we introduced TorchNeuron, the native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium (the torch-neuronx package). With it, Transformers runs its own modeling code on Trainium, as it does on any other device, so any Transformers model on the Hub may run. Which ones actually do?

The torch-neuronx model support Space answers that question for the most popular models on the Hub. It tells you whether a model runs unmodified on Trainium, and gives you the script to run it yourself.

The Space opens on the Selected view: our own selection of models picked among the top models on the Hub by downloads and by trending score. Each row gives the result, the number of Trainium cores the model is sharded over, the wall time of the run (compilation included) and the peak device memory.

To look up a given model, switch to the Trending or Downloads view and type part of its name. These views follow the Hub's own rankings, one task at a time, whether a model was tested or not. When a model was left out on purpose, the Space tells you why (most of the time it was not prioritized, sometimes it is truly incompatible). You can also pick the versions of the Neuron compiler (neuronx-cc) and of Transformers to look at.

At the time of writing, only Transformers models are tested, and our selection is limited to text-generation and image-text-to-text models. We plan to expand to diffusers, sentence transformers, and other transformers tasks.

Select a model to see how to run it. The Space lists the Neuron stack the model was tested on, the packages to install on top of it, and the run.py script that ran. The script follows the recipe of the TorchNeuron announcement: it loads the model with from_pretrained, sharded when it needs to be, then generates with a static cache and torch.compile(backend="neuron").

On a Trainium2 (trn2) instance with that stack, for example in the AWS Neuron Deep Learning Container, install the packages, then run:

No need for torchrun: the script launches its own torch.distributed ranks when the model is sharded.

A first run starts by compiling the model's graphs. To skip that step, copy the graphs the same compiler built during the test, from the public NEFF cache bucket. The Space gives you the command, with the right compiler version:

Each test loads the model on a trn2 instance, sharded over the smallest number of Trainium cores that can hold its weights. Most models are sharded with tensor parallelism. Mixture-of-experts models without a tensor-parallel plan use expert parallelism only. The test then generates 32 tokens and checks them. On a single core, the tokens are compared with those of a CPU run of the same checkpoint. When the model is sharded, a small judge model checks that the text is fluent English.

At the time of writing, only models that fit on 4 Trainium2 devices are tested, which means 16 cores at most. A PASS says nothing about throughput, or about longer generations.

Everything the Space shows comes from the public aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-model-support dataset, with one Parquet file per pair of neuronx-cc and library versions.

Each row holds a model's result, the error when it failed, the versions of the whole stack and the run.py that ran. You can query it directly:

The dataset card gives the exact meaning of each result.

Next time you wonder whether a model runs on Trainium, look it up.

#9831. Tech Firms Dismantle Botnet That Turned 1.3M TV Boxes Into Proxies

Google said today it worked with industry partners to dismantle a botnet made up of more than 1.3 million Android TV set-top boxes that ship with malicious software which secretly rents the user’s Internet connection out to strangers and conducts advertising fraud. Experts involved in the takedown say the action is likely to sever the botnet’s access to more than 10 million additional compromised systems, including other Internet of Things (IoT) products such as Android-based healthcare devices and karaoke machines.

A report from the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) said Google has severed ties with Videostrong Technology Co., a TV box manufacturer in China that GTIG and other industry experts concluded was responsible for including malware that enrolled more than 1.3 million set-top boxes in a botnet dubbed “XCPE” (named after one of the malware’s core code components).

The global distribution of XCPE botnet infections. Image: Google Threat Intelligence Group.

The report said the XCPE botnet loaded the user’s device with software that makes their Internet address available for resale by multiple “residential proxy” services, which allow customers to rent Internet addresses as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects.

“Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates’ malware modules onto infected devices,” the GTIG post reads, noting that Google took legal action to take down the domains and servers Videostrong used to control the botnet and install additional malware. “A device manufacturer intentionally infecting their users with malware is an unacceptable breach of trust, and represents a serious risk to those users. Without users’ knowledge or consent, infected devices were offered as a distribution mechanism for a wide array of criminal actors.”

The report notes that while TV boxes made up the the majority of the botnet, the same XCPE malware was found in other Android-based IoT products, including telehealth devices, karaoke machines, and even digital signage systems.

Google said it requires all Android device makers to pass compatibility and security tests to ensure their products don’t harm users, but that Videostrong nevertheless found a way to load their malicious software immediately after a user boots up one of these devices for the first time (Google says it has since addressed that weakness).

The GTIG report calls out a number of residential proxy providers whose software development kits were routinely downloaded by devices infected by the XCPE botnet. Those include AppSalt, also known as Honeygain, which is owned by the Vilnius, Lithuania-based Oxylabs. In October 2026, Oxylabs was relaunched under a new brand called Source, after receiving $130 million in funding from private equity firm Warburg Pincus that reportedly valued the business at $3.6 billion. Oxylabs did not respond to a request for comment.

Another provider linked to the botnet was NetNut, a once sprawling residential proxy company operated by the publicly-traded Israeli company Alarum Technologies. In July 2026, the FBI worked with industry partners to seize hundreds of domains associated with NetNut, saying the company was responsible for operating a separate botnet called Popa that enslaved TV boxes as residential proxies. Other proxy providers named in the GTIG report include EarnFM, Traffmonetizer, Jaguar, LINKFOG, BMW/IPWeb and GaGaNode.

Google’s announcement credits a number of industry partners, including Synthient, a startup that tracks proxy providers. In January 2026, Synthient published research into the rapid spread of the Kimwolf botnet, which at the time was hammering networks worldwide with record-smashing DDoS attacks. Synthient documented how Kimwolf infected millions of Android set-top boxes virtually overnight, using a widespread vulnerability in these residential proxy services to compromise other Android-based devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting TV box users.

Synthient’s research caused dozens of residential proxy providers to patch their networks, which helped to fragment the Kimwolf botnet into much smaller pieces that made its incessant and disruptive DDoS attacks far easier for network operators to manage. It also attracted the attention of the Motion Picture Association (MPA), a trade group representing the major Hollywood studios, which partnered with Synthient to purchase and tear apart a number of popular Android TV set-top boxes — including some that were being infected by Kimwolf and other IoT botnets.

In a report published today, Synthient examined a popular, pre-infected TV box sold under the brand MECOOL by a publicly traded company in China called Skyworth Technology, concluding that MECOOL also bundled the malware from Videostrong Technology Co. and likewise installed AppSalt/Honeygain and other proxy components.

The MECOOL storefront and marketing. Image: Synthient.com.

Synthient founder Ben Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity that Videostrong’s malware also distributed software for the proxy service Grass. In our November 2025 story, “Is Your Android TV Streaming Box Part of a Botnet?” we quoted a researcher from Censys who found the popular Superbox TV streaming device bundled Grass’s residential proxy software. We also quoted the Grass founder, who denied any affiliation with the TV box maker.

That November 2025 story noted that Superbox and similar Android TV set-top boxes gain new customers primarily by engaging influencers on Tiktok and other social networks who praise the product’s ability to offer hundreds of (pirated) pay TV streaming services for a one-time fee.

The popular Youtube channel Linus Tech Tips discussing MECOOL TV streaming boxes.

The GTIG report estimates the XCPE botnet takedown should sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices, noting that the various proxy and ad fraud affiliates of Videostrong “each have diversified distribution channels for their modules beyond XCPE.”

Synthient’s Brundage echoed that conclusion, calling the 1.3 million number “highly conservative.”

“The scale of affected devices is likely way higher,” he said. “This is probably the largest operation against backdoored TV boxes that we’ve seen.”

Further reading: Plume Security Labs white paper on the XCPE botnet (PDF) Black Lotus Labs writeup on LinkedIn TrendAI’s analysis Synthient’s list of affected devices, broken down by model number

#9830. Sellvia in 2026: The Tech Behind Its Digital Stores, Built-In Ads, and Orders

Business Developement Manager with a demonstrated history of working in the public relations and communication.

Business Developement Manager with a demonstrated history of working in the public relations and communication.

Business Developement Manager with a demonstrated history of working in the public relations and communication.

Opening an ecommerce store used to involve several separate projects. A seller needed a website, hosting, product pages, payment tools, marketing software, and a system for keeping track of orders. None of those tasks was impossible, but the number of services involved made a small online business surprisingly complicated to operate.

Sellvia takes a more integrated approach. Instead of asking users to assemble a store from independent services, the platform provides a managed storefront, access to a product catalog, promotional tools, and a dashboard for everyday operations.

That approach is timely. Sellvia appeared at No. 591 on the 2026 Inc. 5000 list of fast-growing private companies in the United States. Beyond the ranking, the more interesting story is how the platform brings several parts of digital commerce into one workflow.

Sellvia is an ecommerce platform that helps users launch an online store and manage its day-to-day operations. Its turnkey store offering is based on WordPress with Sellvia's own plugin and managed hosting.

The company supplies a ready-to-use store structure rather than leaving the owner to configure a server and assemble a large collection of plugins. Product management, store activity, and available marketing tools are reached through the Sellvia Dashboard.

This design changes the work involved in getting started. A new owner can spend more time choosing products, improving descriptions, and planning how to reach customers. They spend less time on hosting arrangements and the technical maintenance of separate systems.

The platform is especially interesting for someone who wants to run a store without becoming a WordPress administrator. Sellvia manages much of the underlying environment, while users work with the controls provided in the dashboard.

One of Sellvia's practical advantages is access to an existing product catalog.

Digital products can include ebooks, downloadable guides, educational material, courses, and templates. Unlike physical merchandise, these products do not require a warehouse or parcel delivery. Customers receive access to digital content after completing the relevant purchase process.

Take a store specializing in productivity and professional development. The owner might organize useful digital resources around planning, career skills, or personal organization. The work becomes selecting coherent offers and presenting them clearly instead of sourcing physical inventory and arranging shipping.

Product quality and relevance still matter. A broad catalog is most useful when the store has a clear audience and a sensible way of helping visitors choose among available products.

This is also why digital commerce is an attractive starting point for an integrated platform: product presentation, customer purchase, and content delivery can be coordinated electronically.

The key to understanding Sellvia is to look beyond the storefront itself.

The storefront is the public-facing part of the business. It presents products, organizes categories, and gives visitors a place to browse.

The product catalog supplies the items the owner can select and publish. This reduces the preparation involved in building a store from an empty website.

Sellvia Ads provides a managed promotional service within Sellvia's ecosystem. Users can review the available promotion settings and activity through their account rather than building the entire advertising workflow from scratch.

Order management brings transaction records and order activity into the dashboard, helping users see which orders need attention and which have progressed through the applicable processing steps.

Reporting connects these activities. Instead of judging the business only by how the homepage looks, users can monitor product activity, promotion, and orders in one working environment.

These functions have different jobs, but they share a practical purpose: reducing the number of disconnected tools a store owner needs to manage.

Marketing is often the next challenge after a store goes live. Having a finished website does not mean that people will automatically discover its products.

Sellvia Ads addresses part of that challenge with a managed promotion service. Its published terms describe promotion through Sellvia-operated digital properties and internal placement systems. Available budgets and service options are managed from the platform environment.

That makes Sellvia Ads different from an ordinary advertising account in which a merchant manually controls every external placement. It is important to understand that the internal promotion service does not necessarily function as a campaign sending visitors directly to the owner's branded website.

For someone new to advertising, a managed service can reduce the number of settings they need to learn at the beginning. It also provides a convenient starting point for examining how promotional activity relates to product demand.

The useful metrics are the ones tied to business decisions: what promotion was used, which products generated activity, and how actual orders compare with promotional spending. Advertised exposure is not the same as a completed order, and keeping those measurements separate leads to better decisions.

The digital-order journey is short enough to understand without technical jargon.

First, a product is selected from the catalog and presented to customers through the relevant store or sales interface. The product page should explain what the buyer receives and make the offer easy to evaluate.

Next, the customer completes the checkout process available for that purchase. The precise payment flow depends on the store's configured arrangement.

Once the purchase has been processed, the buyer can receive access to the digital material through the applicable delivery process. The order is also recorded in the systems used to manage store activity.

These steps show the practical value of selling downloadable resources: there is no shipping label, carrier pickup, or warehouse dispatch between a completed digital purchase and access to the purchased material.

The store owner should still test the experience personally. Product pages, checkout instructions, access links, and order records should be clear and consistent, particularly on mobile devices.

A useful ecommerce dashboard should support decisions, not merely display numbers.

Sellvia groups important store functions in a central workspace. Users can work with the catalog, review order information, access available promotional controls, and inspect reporting provided for their account.

For example, an owner who has added several digital guides can check whether visitors are engaging with those offers and whether the products are generating orders. When experimenting with promotion, the same owner can compare activity over time and decide which subjects deserve more attention.

Centralization matters because small operational tasks accumulate. Every additional service normally introduces another login, another set of settings, and another place where data might need to be checked. A connected dashboard reduces that fragmentation.

For additional explanations of the interface and individual features, Sellvia.info provides platform-focused guides and resources.

Sellvia's published September 2026 terms describe three base subscription levels:

The standard introductory offer described in those terms includes a 14-day trial. The availability of higher tiers and promotional offers may be subject to additional conditions.

The base subscription covers the relevant store infrastructure and platform access. Services such as advertising and certain order-related operations can have separate charges, so the subscription amount should not be mistaken for the total cost of operating a store.

A sensible first budget separates recurring software costs from optional promotion. That makes it much easier to test the platform methodically and understand the economics of a specific product category.

Before investing heavily in advertising, run through the service as both a store owner and a customer.

Review the catalog and select products that fit a recognizable audience. Check that each description makes the content and intended buyer clear. Open the storefront on a phone and make sure the navigation and product pages are readable.

Then inspect the purchase path that applies to your configuration, including what happens after checkout and how buyers obtain their digital content.

Finally, review the dashboard's order and promotion tools. Identify the information that will help you compare products and measure spending. These simple checks reveal much more about everyday usability than a feature list alone.

This kind of evaluation is also a useful way to understand the platform's central benefit: the work of running a digital store is organized around one connected operating environment.

Sellvia's model reflects a wider change in ecommerce software. Increasingly, the appeal of a platform is not just how quickly it creates a website but how much routine operational work it brings together afterward.

A hosted store, existing product catalog, built-in promotion, order management, and accessible reporting each solve a different problem. Their combined value is that owners spend less time coordinating software and more time understanding products and customers.

That does not replace sound business decisions. Choosing useful products, describing them accurately, managing expenses, and serving customers still matter.

But for someone who wants a practical way to begin selling digital products, Sellvia provides an integrated starting point. Its 2026 ecosystem shows how the storefront has become one component of a broader digital-commerce workspace.

#9828. Can we trust LLMs to judge whether a research idea is novel?

Today we’re releasing Old Ideas, Novel Problems, a new study of how reliably large language models can evaluate the novelty of scientific research ideas. Alongside the paper, we’re publishing a benchmark, data, and code for testing novelty judges, plus an automated pipeline researchers can use to build new evaluation sets.

At Ai2, we’ve been developing AI systems that support different parts of scientific discovery. DataVoyager helps researchers explore and analyze structured data, AutoDiscovery generates and tests hypotheses, and Theorizer synthesizes evidence across large bodies of literature into candidate scientific theories. Together with Asta, these projects point toward systems that can help researchers move from understanding prior work to proposing, testing, and refining new ideas.

But generating research ideas is only part of the challenge of automating scientific discovery. Those ideas also need to contribute something genuinely new, which means these systems need a way to distinguish a novel direction from one that mostly repackages existing work.

That judgment is often handed to another LLM—what we call a novelty judge. Novelty judges assess whether a research idea is new relative to prior work, either on its own or in comparison with another idea. There’s no standard way to build one; research teams choose a model, prompt, evaluation format, reasoning budget, and sometimes a literature-retrieval system. Those choices can materially affect the verdict. Yet these judges are often validated only on human-written papers rather than the AI-generated ideas they are actually meant to evaluate.

Our new benchmark results suggest novelty evaluation itself is far from reliable. Across six LLM judges – GPT-5.1, GPT-5.2, GPT-5.4, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Claude Opus 4.5, and Claude Opus 4.6 – seemingly small changes to the evaluation setup produce dramatically different judgments of the same ideas. In one experiment, changing just a few words in a prompt shifts a model’s accuracy in identifying which of two ideas is more novel by more than 50 percentage points. Retrieval and additional reasoning do not consistently improve judgments, and two purpose-built novelty evaluation systems perform worse than a simple prompted Claude Opus 4.6 baseline.

If AI is going to play a larger role in scientific discovery, we need more dependable ways to tell whether it is actually proposing something new. Our work provides tools for studying that problem, while showing how much remains unresolved.

To test how reliably novelty judges can distinguish more novel research ideas from less novel ones, we first needed examples where there was strong evidence about the originality of the underlying scientific contribution.

So we built an automated pipeline around ICLR 2026 peer reviews. Rather than treating paper acceptance as a proxy for novelty, we mined the reviews themselves for passages where reviewers explicitly discussed a contribution’s originality. That distinction is key; a paper can be accepted without being particularly novel as long as it is strong enough in other aspects. Likewise, a rejected paper with an original contribution can have other weaknesses.

We created a high-novelty pool of 154 human-authored research ideas by selecting accepted papers in the top-rated 10% of their ICLR research area whose reviewers positively identified novelty and where no reviewer disputed it. We applied the reverse criteria to build a lower-novelty pool: 145 ideas from rejected papers in the bottom 10% whose reviewers raised originality concerns without any reviewer positively identifying novelty. In a separate check of the review-mining process, an annotator agreed with the extracted novelty-signal polarity in 47 of 50 cases; none of the disagreements would have changed whether a reviewer was counted as praising or disputing the paper’s novelty.

Together, these two pools form our first evaluation setting, Human-Only, which tests whether novelty judges can tell apart human-authored ideas with strong evidence of higher or lower novelty. But in practice, novelty judges are increasingly being used to evaluate AI-generated ideas. So we created a second setting, Human+Generated.

For this pool, we paired the same 154 validated human ideas with 154 ideas produced by a simple LLM generator. We assumed the generated ideas were less novel than their human-authored counterparts; these are weak labels, not verified judgments for every idea. The generator received only a research area and an instruction to propose a novel idea, with no literature search, tools, iteration, or feedback. This gave us a conservative comparison between ideas from a basic generator and contributions from top-10% ICLR papers whose reviewers had explicitly endorsed their originality.

As additional checks, an expert independently reviewed 30 Human+Generated pairs, heavily weighted toward cases our strongest judge got wrong, and we rewrote the human- and AI-generated ideas into a common structure to test whether judges were simply reacting to differences in writing style. The expert preferred the human idea in all 30 pairs and judged none of the generated ideas novel.

Importantly, many of our core findings don’t depend on the labels at all. If two reasonable evaluation setups give opposite answers for the same pair of ideas, that disagreement itself reveals instability.

Using our collections of human-authored and AI-generated research ideas, we tested how well six LLM judges – GPT-5.1, GPT-5.2, GPT-5.4, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Claude Opus 4.5, and Claude Opus 4.6 – could evaluate novelty through both pointwise (i.e., absolute novelty ratings) and pairwise (i.e., comparing two ideas to find the most novel) comparisons. We varied one factor at a time: the prompt, reasoning budget, whether the judge could see related papers, how the ideas were formatted, how many judgments were combined into a final verdict, and – for AI-generated ideas – which model generated them.

The largest shifts in performance came from how we prompted the model to judge novelty.

For example, we showed GPT-5.4 the same Human+Generated pairs – each containing one validated human-authored idea and one AI-generated idea – with two prompts. One prompt told the model that reviewers had found exactly one idea in each pair to be novel and asked it to identify which one; the other simply asked which idea was novel. When we switched to the simpler prompt, accuracy dropped from 93.5% to 40.9% – below chance – and the model changed its verdict on more than half of the same pairs.

By contrast, the same prompt change shifted accuracy by only about seven percentage points on the Human-Only dataset, which pairs human-authored ideas with stronger and weaker evidence of novelty. That suggests a novelty judge can appear relatively stable on human-authored research but behave very differently on AI-generated ideas.

That said, human-authored ideas weren’t immune. We saw substantial shifts on the Human-Only dataset as well; the same change moved Claude Opus 4.6 accuracy by 21 points. The shifts were just less severe than on the AI-generated ideas.

There was also no universally better prompt. For example, when judging ideas individually, dropping an instruction that warned judges not to treat trivial or incremental contributions as novel improved accuracy for some judges while reducing it for others. A prompt that works well for one model may not transfer to another, in other words.

We also tested a common use of novelty judges: comparing ideas from two AI generators. We paired ideas from Claude Opus 4.5 with Claude Sonnet 4.5, and GPT-5.4 with GPT-5.1. Across the tested prompt changes, roughly a quarter to a third of verdicts changed on average across six judges. This disagreement can be measured without assuming which generator produces more novel ideas, showing how the choice of judge prompt can affect comparisons between ideation systems.

More search and reasoning didn’t necessarily produce better novelty judgments. We gave GPT-5.6 Sol an extra-high reasoning budget and live, iterative search restricted to arXiv, then compared it with standard-retrieval judges that each saw five pre-retrieved abstracts. (All judges in this comparison ran once per idea on Human+Generated.) The agentic judge scored 0.78 macro-F1 – 11 points behind Claude Opus 4.6 at 0.89, and in roughly the same range as simpler Claude Opus 4.5 and GPT-5.4 setups – while costing roughly 10× more per decision at current API prices. (In this context, macro-F1 measures how well a judge identifies novel and non-novel ideas; higher is better.)

Purpose-built evaluators weren’t more accurate either, despite costing substantially more. On the Human+Generated set, a simple Claude Opus 4.6 prompt using low reasoning and majority voting across three calls achieved 0.854 macro-F1 at a total evaluation cost of $2.59. By comparison, Idea Novelty Checker, a literature-grounded retrieval and reranking pipeline, scored 0.642 at $30.66, while Sakana AI’s AI Scientist, whose novelty evaluator iteratively searches Semantic Scholar, scored 0.772 at $82.05. (Both dedicated evaluators used Claude Opus 4.6, with one call per decision.)

In other words, the simple prompted baseline was both more accurate and considerably cheaper than either purpose-built system.

Taken together, these results suggest that novelty evaluation is particularly brittle on the AI-generated ideas these systems are increasingly being asked to judge.

Our results suggest that LLM-based novelty evaluation remains a major open problem. Judges that appear reliable on human-authored research may behave differently on AI-generated ideas; prompts that help one model can hurt another; and more search or compute does not necessarily produce more consistent judgments.

Future work should test judges on the kinds of ideas they will actually evaluate, measure sensitivity across prompts and models, improve how prior literature is incorporated, and build benchmarks that can evolve as the scientific literature grows and AI systems improve. Our benchmark and reusable data pipeline are a starting point—researchers can apply them to new peer reviews, other scientific communities, and future generations of novelty judges.

Automated ideation depends on more than generating plausible research directions; we also need ways to tell when those ideas are genuinely new. By making the weaknesses of current novelty judges easier to measure, we hope this release helps researchers build more robust ways to evaluate AI-generated research ideas.

Thanks to Kyle and the AllenAI team for this benchmark! The finding that agentic search and complex evaluators underperform simpler baselines strongly resonates with what I observed in my own research: https://coronring.github.io/blog/stop-taking-ai-advice-on-where-to-submit/

Earlier this month, I ran a complementary study asking current models (GPT-6 Luna and Claude Opus 5.5) where to submit 132 full, blinded AI papers from the 2026 cycle (NeurIPS, EMNLP, COLM, Findings, and workshops) strictly after the model knowledge cutoff date: Stop taking AI advice on where to submit your paper.

While Novelty-Bench examines the idea-level novelty judge, evaluating full manuscripts revealed the exact same underlying failure modes:

Your work provides the benchmark tools needed to quantify this at the ideation stage, and our results suggest the problem persists all the way downstream to full paper evaluation. Very glad to see rigorous attention brought to this issue and love to chat on it!

#9827. When AI Works Perfectly, What Happens to Human Life?

The medical report says there is nothing wrong. Every number falls within its expected range. No abnormality has been detected. The system has done what it was designed to do.

And yet, on the morning before work, the body hesitates. It knows something that the report cannot describe. Or perhaps it knows nothing at all. Perhaps the sensation is ordinary anxiety, fatigue, or a passing discomfort. The distinction matters, but the person experiencing it cannot yet make that distinction.

The report is correct. The discomfort remains. There is no contradiction in the data. Only a contradiction in the life that must continue after the data has been delivered.

This is where a story might begin. Not with a malfunctioning machine, but with a functioning one.

Much of our imagination about artificial intelligence remains organized around failure. We fear the incorrect diagnosis, the discriminatory algorithm, the autonomous system that escapes its instructions. We imagine machines that deceive, disobey, or misunderstand us. These dangers are real enough to deserve serious attention.

But another kind of future is harder to picture. A future in which the systems become remarkably good. They identify illness earlier. They match workers with appropriate jobs. They calculate risks, recommend careers, preserve memories, and relieve us of countless small decisions. The machinery of everyday life becomes smoother. There are fewer mistakes to correct, fewer uncertainties to endure, fewer reasons to question the next recommendation.

And yet, somewhere inside this increasingly orderly world, a person stops. Not because the system has failed. Because the system's success has revealed something it was never built to understand. What happens when the answer is correct, but the question was incomplete?

This question became the starting point for LIFE, a ten-part work of linked fiction developed by SHIRO & Co., an independent creative and research practice in Tokyo. LIFE is not a story about artificial intelligence taking over the world. It is about the quieter possibility that the world might remain recognizable even as something essential becomes difficult to name.

Engineers have good reasons to dislike friction. Friction slows processes, introduces uncertainty, increases costs, and creates opportunities for failure. To remove it is often to improve a system.

But in human life, friction has another meaning. It is the pause before saying something irreversible. It is the embarrassment of being inexperienced, the uncertainty of beginning a relationship, the inability to explain why a familiar place suddenly feels different. It is the interval between knowing what is reasonable and deciding what one can live with.

Not all of these experiences are valuable. Some are painful, unnecessary, even destructive. But neither are they all defects awaiting correction.

Consider a young person applying for a first job. The recruitment system asks for experience. It evaluates qualifications accurately, compares candidates fairly according to its criteria, and produces a defensible decision. The applicant has no experience. The answer is no. Nothing in the system needs to be broken for the rejection to make sense. Yet a question remains: where does experience begin, in a society that increasingly requires it before granting entry?

The problem is not simply that a machine has evaluated a person. It is that the criteria of evaluation may quietly determine which kinds of lives are allowed to begin. We can improve the algorithm. We can revise its criteria. We can introduce exceptions. But sooner or later we encounter a question that is not exclusively computational. Who is willing to make room for someone who has not yet become useful?

In another story, a thirteen-year-old faces a future already arranged according to stability and probability. The recommendations are sensible. Certain paths offer better prospects. Others carry greater risks. The system has no reason to conceal what it knows. Parents might find such guidance reassuring.

But there is an awkward fact about childhood: the person whose future is being predicted does not yet fully exist. Not in the sense that the child is incomplete or lacks a voice. Rather, the future person will be shaped by encounters, disappointments, friendships, accidents, and desires that have not yet occurred. A recommendation can describe likely outcomes. It cannot contain every possibility that will emerge from living.

There is a profound difference between helping someone imagine a future and deciding, in advance, which future is worth imagining. This distinction is easy to lose when prediction becomes increasingly persuasive. The more accurate a recommendation appears, the more difficult it can become to disagree with it. Eventually, refusing the optimal choice may begin to look like an error.

Yet the freedom to become someone unexpected has always depended, at least partly, on the right to make choices whose value cannot be demonstrated beforehand.

Memory presents another difficulty. Imagine an old message, left on an online bulletin board twenty years ago. The original conversation has ended. The participants have changed, disappeared, or perhaps died. The message remains.

Then a reply arrives. It resembles a continuation of the conversation, but the voice is not the voice of the person who originally wrote it.

Technically, information has been preserved and reproduced. Something has survived. But what exactly? A person's words are not the same as that person's continued presence. A voice is not a life. A convincing response does not restore the circumstances in which an earlier conversation took place.

Still, the response may move us. We may recognize something in it. We may even find comfort. It would be too simple to declare that such experiences are false, just as it would be too simple to treat them as equivalent to human continuity. Between those positions lies a region that ordinary technological language struggles to describe.

Literature has lived in that region for centuries. It knows that memory can be inaccurate and still meaningful. That absence can remain present. That a silence may carry more of a relationship than a complete transcript.

AI introduces new possibilities for preserving traces of human life. It does not settle what those traces mean.

LIFE exists as ten interconnected stories, accompanied by microdramas that approach its questions through brief audiovisual experiences.

At first glance, microdrama might seem an unlikely format for philosophical inquiry. There is little time for explanation. No space for an elaborate argument. Often, barely enough room for a situation to unfold.

But that limitation is precisely what makes the form interesting.

A person looks at a screen. A sentence appears. Someone hesitates before responding. The scene ends. The viewer has been given almost no explanation, yet something continues beyond the final image.

Unlike an explanatory video, a microdrama does not necessarily tell its audience what to think. It can place a contradiction before them and leave the work of interpretation unfinished. This is not a rejection of analysis. It is another way of beginning it.

For people who design AI systems, fiction offers an unusual perspective. Technical evaluations ask whether a system behaves correctly under specified conditions. Stories ask what happens to a person who must continue living after the system has behaved correctly. The distinction matters. A model may complete its task. A human experience does not necessarily end there.

When software behaves according to its specification, we have a basis for calling it correct.

But human situations rarely arrive with complete specifications. A request may be clearly expressed while the underlying desire remains uncertain. A recommendation may be justified while the consequences are emotionally unbearable. A decision may satisfy every formal requirement and still leave someone unable to move forward.

This does not make correctness irrelevant. It makes correctness insufficient as a complete description of human experience.

As AI systems become more deeply involved in consequential decisions, a distinction becomes necessary between producing an answer and possessing the authority to act on it. An observation is not yet a recommendation. A recommendation is not yet a decision. And a decision is not always the end of the matter.

Sometimes the appropriate response is to ask another question. Sometimes it is to acknowledge that the available evidence cannot settle the issue. Sometimes it is to allow a person to refuse a reasonable recommendation without having to prove that the system was wrong.

This is not a romantic argument for irrationality. It is a recognition that human judgment involves more than selecting the best option from a defined set. It also involves deciding whether the available options adequately describe the situation. The ability to say not yet may be as important as the ability to say yes or no.

The ten stories of LIFE move through health, work, intimacy, education, aging, memory, and observation. Their settings change, but a similar tension returns. The systems work. The world continues. And something remains outside the record.

It might be a bodily sensation, an unchosen future, a voice that no longer belongs to its speaker, or a feeling for which no useful category exists.

None of these things proves that technology should retreat from human life. Nor does their existence mean that suffering, uncertainty, and inefficiency should be preserved for their own sake.

The question is more modest, and perhaps more difficult. Can we build increasingly capable systems without treating everything they cannot resolve as an imperfection? Can a system be useful without becoming authoritative? Can technology leave space for experiences that do not improve a metric, complete a workflow, or produce a satisfactory conclusion?

Literature offers no engineering specification for such a world. It has something else to offer: attention to what happens between the events we know how to measure.

A machine produces an answer. A person reads it. The screen goes quiet. Outside, the day continues. There are trains to catch, messages to answer, people to meet, things that cannot be postponed.

The answer may be correct. The person still has to live. And perhaps that is where the story begins.

LIFE is a ten-part literary anthology with accompanying microdrama experiences, developed by SHIRO & Co., an independent creative and research practice based in Tokyo. The project examines everyday life in a society where AI systems function as intended, yet human experiences continue to resist complete representation.
